2027-06-06.title: Fourth Sunday of the Apostles
2027-06-06.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Judge rightly: hear the small and the great alike
Wash yourselves; learn to do good
Run so as to win the imperishable wreath
Love your enemies; be merciful as your Father is merciful
2027-06-06.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), from Pentecost to the beginning of the Season of Summer (Kaitha): the Church remembers the apostles who, filled with the Holy Spirit, preached Christ and founded the Churches, among them the Church of India founded by Mar Thoma. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed at the three hours of the day. The calendar gives longer forms: Deuteronomy 1:16–33; 1 Corinthians 9:13–27; Luke 6:12–46. In the Latin calendar today is the Tenth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
2027-06-06.verse: Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.
theo: On the Fourth Sunday of the Apostles the readings move from the altar to the whole of life: to the courtroom, the market, the playing field and the place where we meet our enemies. The first reading continues Moses' farewell on the plains of Moab. He remembers how he organised the people in the wilderness and appointed judges, and what he told them: “Give the members of your community a fair hearing, and judge rightly between one person and another, whether citizen or resident alien. You must not be partial in judging: hear out the small and the great alike; you shall not be intimidated by anyone, for the judgment is God’s.” Three things stand out. Justice must reach the outsider as well as the citizen. The poor man's case must be heard as carefully as the powerful man's. And the judge must not be afraid, because he judges in God's place and will answer to God. Every Christian who holds even a small authority hears these words: the teacher who marks answer papers, the officer who processes a file, the panchayat member, the parish committee, parents settling a quarrel between their children. Kerala today has hundreds of thousands of workers from other states; the resident alien of Deuteronomy is the migrant labourer on our building sites, who must receive his wages and his rights as fairly as anyone else. The Season of the Apostles shows us a Church that organised itself in the same spirit: when the Greek-speaking widows were neglected in the daily distribution, the apostles appointed seven men to see that they received justice (Acts 6:1–6).

Isaiah's words are among the sharpest in the whole Bible. He addresses Jerusalem with the names of the two most notorious cities of the Old Testament: “Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom! Listen to the teaching of our God, you people of Gomorrah!” Then God speaks of the very worship that the people thought pleased him: “What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? … I cannot endure solemn assemblies with iniquity… When you stretch out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you; even though you make many prayers, I will not listen; your hands are full of blood.” God is not against sacrifice and prayer; he commanded them. He is against worship that leaves life untouched, festivals celebrated with the money of the cheated, prayers lifted by hands that oppress. A great parish feast, with illuminations and fireworks, means little to God if the workers who built the stage were not paid, or if a family in the parish has no food. Then come the commands: “Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean; remove the evil of your doings from before my eyes; cease to do evil, learn to do good; seek justice, rescue the oppressed, defend the orphan, plead for the widow.” And, unexpectedly, the most tender invitation: “Come now, let us argue it out, says the Lord: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be like snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool.” God's anger is the anger of a lover who wants his people back. The door of the sacrament of Reconciliation is that invitation made concrete: come now, and the scarlet will become white.

In the Epistle Paul explains how he lives as an apostle. Though he owed no one anything, he made himself everyone's servant in order to win them: “To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews… To the weak I became weak, so that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that I might by all means save some.” He did not change the Gospel, but he changed himself, his habits, his way of speaking, his food and his customs, so that nothing in him would block the Gospel. The apostles who carried the faith to the nations did the same. Mar Thoma's children in India lived for centuries as Indians in culture, Christians in faith and Oriental in worship: they kept the customs of their land, its dress and its family life, and they kept the faith of the apostle. Then Paul turns to sport, which the Corinthians loved, for their city hosted the Isthmian Games: “Do you not know that in a race the runners all compete, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may win it. Athletes exercise self-control in all things; they do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable one.” Children going back to school this week, students preparing for entrance examinations, young people training for a match know what discipline costs. Paul asks the same seriousness for the soul: a rule of prayer, fasting on the days the Church asks, mastery of the tongue and the eyes, “so that after proclaiming to others I myself should not be disqualified.”

The Gospel is from Luke's Sermon on the Plain, which the calendar gives in a longer form beginning with the choice of the Twelve apostles. Jesus has just named his apostles, and the first thing he teaches them is the hardest: “But I say to you that listen, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.” Four commands, each going further than the last: love in the heart, good in action, blessing on the lips, and prayer before God for the one who harms us. Then Jesus gives the rule that sums up the law: “Do to others as you would have them do to you.” And he asks three questions that strip away our self-satisfaction: “If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them.” Christian love begins where ordinary decency ends. Finally Jesus gives the reason: “Your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind to the ungrateful and the wicked. Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.” We do not love our enemies because they deserve it, but because God has loved us when we did not deserve it. The Indian Church has seen this Gospel lived in our own time. When Blessed Rani Maria, a Franciscan Clarist sister from near Perumbavoor, was murdered in Madhya Pradesh in 1995, her family forgave the man who killed her, and her sister visited him in prison and called him brother. Mercy did what punishment alone could not do: it changed his heart. Justice in Deuteronomy, a washed heart in Isaiah, discipline in Paul and mercy in Luke belong together. The disciple of Jesus is just, clean of heart, disciplined and, above all, merciful as the Father is merciful.
conn: Justice without partiality.

“You must not distort justice; you must not show partiality; and you must not accept bribes, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and subverts the cause of those who are in the right” (Deuteronomy 16:19).
The resident alien.
“The alien who resides with you shall be to you as the citizen among you; you shall love the alien as yourself, for you were aliens in the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 19:34).
Worship and justice.

“He has told you, O mortal, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8); “leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister” (Matthew 5:24).
Whiter than snow.
“Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm 51:7).
The race.

“let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus the pioneer and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:1–2); “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7).
Father, forgive them.
“Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34); Stephen: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60).
Overcome evil with good.
“Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).
altar: Isaiah warns against hands full of blood lifted in prayer. At the Holy Qurbana, before we come to the altar, we exchange the sign of peace: the Lord asks us to come reconciled. Let us bring to this altar hands washed by repentance and hearts that have forgiven.

Here the One who prayed for those who crucified him offers himself to the Father for all, friends and enemies alike. Receiving his Body, we receive his mercy, and we are sent out to be merciful as the Father is merciful.
outline: Opening
From the altar into the courtroom, the market, the playing field and the place where we meet our enemies.
Point 1 · Hear the small and the great alike
Impartial justice for the citizen and the resident alien.
Point 2 · Wash yourselves; learn to do good
Worship without justice is empty; scarlet can become white.
Point 3 · All things to all, and the race for the imperishable wreath
The apostle who adapts himself, and the discipline of the soul.
Point 4 · Be merciful as your Father is merciful
Love of enemies, the golden rule, the children of the Most High.
Closing image
A sister in a prison in Indore, tying a rakhi on the wrist of the man who killed her sister, and calling him brother.
Take-home line
“Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.”
live: Judge rightly (Deuteronomy 1:17)
In whatever authority you hold this week, at work, at school or at home, give the small and the great the same hearing.
Seek justice (Isaiah 1:17)
Pay every worker the full wage on time, including the migrant labourer and the domestic helper; and help one family in need through your parish.
Run to win (1 Corinthians 9:24)
Choose one spiritual discipline for this week, a fixed time of prayer, a fast or guarding your tongue, and keep it like an athlete.
Pray for those who abuse you (Luke 6:28)
Name in prayer each day this week a person who has hurt you, and ask God to bless them.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Jesus did not say only, Do not hate your enemy, but, Love him; not only, Do not harm him, but, Do him good; and not only, Do not curse him, but, Pray for him. This is the summit of virtue, by which we become like God, who makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good.
St Ambrose (in substance)
Christ the Lord came to teach us to bear injuries, not to return them. Mercy is the fullness of virtue; be merciful, as your Father is merciful, and you will be his children.
St Augustine (in substance)
God does not want our sacrifices if our hands are full of injustice. The sacrifice that pleases him is a heart washed by repentance and hands open to the poor.
magis: Catechism 1807
Justice is the moral virtue that consists in the constant and firm will to give their due to God and neighbour; you shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great.
Catechism 2443
God blesses those who come to the aid of the poor and rebukes those who turn away from them; love for the poor is incompatible with immoderate love of riches.
Catechism 1844
By charity we love God above all things and our neighbour as ourselves for love of God; it is the bond of perfection.
Catechism 2844
Christian prayer extends to the forgiveness of enemies; it transfigures the disciple by configuring him to his Master. Forgiveness is a high point of Christian prayer.
Catechism 2015
The way of perfection passes by way of the Cross; there is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle.
saints: Today
Fourth Sunday of the Apostles. In the Latin calendar, the Tenth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
Next days
Tue 8 June: St Mariam Thresia. Wed 9 June: Mar Aprem (St Ephrem). Fri 11 June: St Barnabas, the Apostle.
2027-06-06.prayer: Lord God, judge of all the earth, you told the judges of Israel to hear the small and the great alike, and you told your people to wash their hands of injustice before they lift them in prayer. Make us just in every judgment and clean of heart; though our sins are like scarlet, make them white as snow. Give us the discipline of athletes who run for the imperishable wreath, and the humility of your apostle who became all things to all. Lord Jesus, you prayed for those who crucified you: teach us to love our enemies, to bless those who curse us, and to be merciful as our Father is merciful. Glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-06-20.title: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles
2027-06-20.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The commandments of the Lord give life
All the nations shall stream to the mountain of the Lord
Do everything for the glory of God
Unless you repent, you will all perish
2027-06-20.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations and founded the Churches. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar gives longer forms: Deuteronomy 4:1–10; Isaiah 2:1–19; 1 Corinthians 10:14–32; Luke 12:57–13:17 (with the parable of the barren fig tree and the healing of the bent woman on the sabbath). In the Latin calendar today is the Twelfth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
2027-06-20.verse: No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all perish as they did.
theo: Five weeks after Pentecost the readings of the Season of the Apostles put a question to us: what does it look like to live as God's people in the middle of the nations? The first reading answers from the plains of Moab. Moses, about to die, gathers Israel at the edge of the promised land: “So now, Israel, give heed to the statutes and ordinances that I am teaching you to observe, so that you may live to enter and occupy the land”. Notice the purpose: so that you may live. God's commandments are not a fence around our happiness but the shape of life itself. “You must neither add anything to what I command you nor take away anything from it”: neither the religion that piles up human rules nor the religion that quietly drops the hard ones. And then two great questions. “For what other great nation has a god so near to it as the Lord our God is whenever we call to him? And what other great nation has statutes and ordinances as just as this entire law that I am setting before you today?” The law is the sign of God's nearness. Israel's wisdom will not be its armies or its wealth; the nations will look at a people who live by God's word and say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and discerning people!” The longer reading adds a command for every Christian family: “make them known to your children and your children’s children”. June in Kerala is the month the schools reopen and the Sunday catechism classes begin a new year. Faith that is not handed on at home does not survive the second generation.

Isaiah lifts our eyes from the plains of Moab to a mountain at the end of days: “In days to come the mountain of the Lord’s house shall be established as the highest of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; all the nations shall stream to it.” Rivers flow down from mountains; here the nations flow up, drawn by a light. “Many peoples shall come and say, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob; that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths.’ For out of Zion shall go forth instruction, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” The Church has always read this as a prophecy of Pentecost. From Jerusalem the word went out with the apostles, to Samaria, to Antioch, to Rome and, as our tradition holds, to the coasts of India with Mar Thoma. St Justin Martyr, writing in Rome in the second century, quoted this very passage and said (in substance) that from Jerusalem twelve unlearned men went out into the world and proclaimed the word of God to every race. And the fruit of that word is peace: “they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.” We have not yet seen that day in full; the news of every week tells us so. But wherever the Gospel is truly received, swords begin to become ploughs: enemies are reconciled, families make peace, communities divided by caste, language or politics learn to sit at one table. The prophet ends with an invitation, not a command: “O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord!”

Paul brings the vision down to the dinner table. Corinth was full of temples, and much of the meat in the market had first been offered to idols. Some Christians said, “All things are lawful.” Paul quotes the slogan and corrects it: “but not all things are beneficial. ‘All things are lawful,’ but not all things build up. Do not seek your own advantage, but that of the other.” The question is not only what I am allowed to do, but what builds up my brother and sister. Paul is not anxious about the meat itself: “the earth and its fullness are the Lord’s.” But if someone at table says, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat, “out of consideration for the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience”, the other person's conscience. Love sometimes gives up what liberty allows. In our own country, where Christians live with Hindu and Muslim neighbours, share their festivals and receive their hospitality, Paul's principle is a wise guide: receive every good gift with thanksgiving and respect, never do anything that would be taken as worship of another god, and never wound the conscience of a weaker brother or sister. Then comes the sentence that turns ordinary life into liturgy: “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.” Eating, working, studying, cooking, driving the autorickshaw, answering emails: all of it can be offered. The Holy Qurbana does not end at the church door; it continues at the dinner table.

The Gospel is sharp. Jesus has been speaking about the signs of the times, and he asks: “And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?” If you are on your way to court with an opponent, “on the way make an effort to settle the case”, before it is too late. Then some people tell him a terrible piece of news: Pilate has killed some Galileans while they were offering sacrifice, mingling their blood with the blood of their animals. Behind the report is an old assumption: those who suffer such things must have deserved them. Jesus rejects it firmly. “Do you think that because these Galileans suffered in this way they were worse sinners than all other Galileans? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all perish as they did.” He adds a disaster of his own: “those eighteen who were killed when the tower of Siloam fell on them”, an accident, not a crime. Were they worse offenders? No. Jesus will not let us turn the suffering of others into a judgment on them; he turns it into a call to ourselves. When a landslide buries a village in the monsoon, or a boat overturns in the backwaters, we must not say, ‘they were punished.’ We must weep with them, help them, and ask: am I ready to meet God? The longer reading gives the other side of the picture: a fig tree that has borne no fruit for three years, an owner who says, “Cut it down!”, and a gardener who pleads, “Sir, let it alone for one more year, until I dig around it and put manure on it.” Repentance is urgent because life is short; it is possible because God is patient. The Fathers saw in the gardener Christ himself, who intercedes for us and digs around our roots with his word and sacraments. Today is the year of grace. On this Sixth Sunday of the Apostles, let us walk in the light of the Lord, do everything for his glory, and turn back to him while we are still on the way.
conn: So that you may live.
“If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15): the law of Moses becomes, in Christ, the law of love.
A god so near.
“And the Word became flesh and lived among us” (John 1:14): God's nearness, which Moses praised, has a human face.
Out of Zion shall go forth instruction.
The Risen Lord: “you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8).
Swords into plowshares.
“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9); “The effect of righteousness will be peace” (Isaiah 32:17).
Food will not bring us close to God.
Paul had already written, “‘Food will not bring us close to God.’ We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do” (1 Corinthians 8:8).
Repent.
The first preaching of Jesus: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent, and believe in the good news” (Mark 1:15).
One more year.
“The Lord is not slow about his promise, as some think of slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting any to perish, but all to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).
altar: The nations stream to the mountain of the Lord's house; every Holy Qurbana is a small fulfilment of Isaiah's vision, as people of many families, languages and histories climb the steps of the sanctuary to be taught his ways.

Whether we eat or drink, do everything for the glory of God: at this altar we eat and drink the Body and Blood of Christ for the glory of the Father, so that every meal at home may become a thanksgiving.
outline: Opening
A people in the middle of the nations: how do we live so that others see God?
Point 1 · A god so near
The commandments as the shape of life; handing them on to our children.
Point 2 · All the nations shall stream to it
Pentecost, the apostles, and swords beaten into ploughshares.
Point 3 · Do everything for the glory of God
Liberty, love and the conscience of the other at table.
Point 4 · Unless you repent
Not a judgment on the suffering, but a call to ourselves; the patient gardener.
Closing image
A fig tree with fresh earth dug around it, waiting one more year.
Take-home line
“O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord!”
live: Make them known to your children (Deuteronomy 4:9)
Parents: sit with your children this week as the catechism year begins and read one Gospel passage with them.
Walk in the light of the Lord (Isaiah 2:5)
Take one step towards peace this week with someone you are in conflict with.
Do everything for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31)
Before each meal this week, pray aloud as a family and offer the day's work to God.
Unless you repent (Luke 13:3)
Go to confession before the feast of Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June.
fathers: St Justin Martyr (in substance)

From Jerusalem twelve men went out into the world. They were unlearned and could not speak with eloquence, but by the power of God they proclaimed to every race of people that they had been sent by Christ to teach the word of God. And we who once killed one another now not only refuse to make war on our enemies, but gladly die confessing Christ.
St Gregory the Great (in substance)

The fig tree that bears no fruit is human nature; for three years the Lord sought fruit from it, before the law, under the law and under grace. The gardener who digs around the tree is the one who rebukes the barren soul, and the manure is the memory of our sins, which, laid at the roots with tears, makes the soul fruitful again.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Do you see how even eating can become an act of worship? Let the table be such that God may be glorified at it: with thanksgiving before and after, with sobriety, with a share for the poor, and with words that build up and do not wound.
magis: Catechism 2062

The commandments express the implications of belonging to God through the covenant; moral existence is a response to the Lord's loving initiative, an acknowledgement of homage and thanksgiving to God.
Catechism 2317

Injustice, excessive inequality and envy threaten peace and cause wars; insofar as people are sinners, the threat of war hangs over them, but insofar as they are united by charity, violence is overcome, and Isaiah's word is fulfilled: they shall beat their swords into plowshares.
Catechism 1431
Interior repentance is a radical reorientation of our whole life, a return to God with all our heart, an end of sin and a turning away from evil.
Catechism 1789
Some rules apply in every case: one may never do evil so that good may result; and charity always proceeds by way of respect for one's neighbour and his conscience.
Second Vatican Council, Gaudium et Spes 78
Peace is not merely the absence of war; it is rightly called an enterprise of justice and the fruit of love, and it must be built up ceaselessly.
saints: Today

Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. In the Latin calendar, the Twelfth Sunday in Ordinary Time. In India and many other countries this Sunday is also kept as Father's Day: a day to thank God for our fathers, living and dead.
Next days

Mon 21: St Aloysius Gonzaga (listed). Tue 22: Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, martyrs. Thu 24: the Birth of John the Baptist. Sun 27: Seventh Sunday of the Apostles. Tue 29: Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles, a day of obligation.
2027-06-20.prayer: Lord our God, there is no other people with a God so near as you are to us whenever we call upon you. Teach us your statutes, that we may live, and help us to hand on your word to our children and our children's children. Draw all the nations to the mountain of your house, and let the word that went out from Jerusalem with the apostles make swords into ploughs in our land and in our homes. Whether we eat or drink, or whatever we do, may we do everything for your glory. Lord Jesus, patient gardener, dig around our roots and give us one more year of grace, that we may turn back to you and bear fruit. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.

2027-06-27.title: Seventh Sunday of the Apostles
2027-06-27.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: You heard the sound of words but saw no form
The Holy God shows himself holy by righteousness
Let all that you do be done in love
Strive to enter through the narrow door
2027-06-27.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. Today is the last Sunday of the Season of the Apostles. The calendar gives longer forms: Deuteronomy 4:10–24; Isaiah 5:8–25; 1 Corinthians 15:58–16:24; Luke 13:22–35. Looking ahead: the Dukhrana of St Thomas on Saturday 3 July, and the Season of Kaitha (Qaita) from Sunday 4 July. In the Latin calendar today is the Thirteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
2027-06-27.verse: Strive to enter through the narrow door; for many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able.
theo: The Season of the Apostles ends today as it began, with a word heard from the fire. At Pentecost the Spirit came on the apostles in tongues of fire; in the first reading Moses reminds Israel of the day they stood at Horeb “while the mountain was blazing up to the very heavens, shrouded in dark clouds.” God had said to Moses, “Assemble the people for me, and I will let them hear my words, so that they may learn to fear me as long as they live on the earth, and may teach their children so.” Then the decisive line: “Then the Lord spoke to you out of the fire. You heard the sound of words but saw no form; there was only a voice.” Israel's God is not a statue that can be carried or bought; he is a living God who speaks and makes a covenant, written on two tablets of stone. Faith comes by hearing, and it lives by being taught to children. In Kerala this month the schools have reopened, and in our parishes the faith formation classes have begun again on Sunday mornings. Moses would call that holy work. The voice without form has now taken a face: “No one has ever seen God. It is God the only Son, who is close to the Father’s heart, who has made him known” (John 1:18). The apostles heard that voice, saw that face and handed both on to us.

Isaiah's reading follows the Song of the Vineyard, in which God looked for justice in his people and found bloodshed, looked for righteousness and heard a cry (Isaiah 5:7). Now come the woes. “Ah, you who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is room for no one but you, and you are left to live alone in the midst of the land!” Greed that swallows the land of the poor ends in loneliness: large and beautiful houses “without inhabitant”. Many Kerala villages know the sight of great locked houses whose owners live abroad and whose aged parents are alone. Then: “Ah, you who rise early in the morning in pursuit of strong drink, who linger in the evening to be inflamed by wine,” with music at every feast, “but who do not regard the deeds of the Lord.” Our State knows the cost of that woe in broken families and early deaths. And the deepest woe: “Ah, you who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness.” When a society renames sin as progress and calls goodness foolish, it has lost its way. Yet in the middle of the woes stands the Holy One: “the Lord of hosts is exalted by justice, and the Holy God shows himself holy by righteousness.” God is not defeated by our confusion; his holiness will shine in justice.

Paul's letter closes with practical matters, and they show us the apostolic Church at work. “Now concerning the collection for the saints”: the churches founded among the Gentiles were gathering money for the poor of the mother Church in Jerusalem. “On the first day of every week, each of you is to put aside and save whatever extra you earn.” Here, in one of the earliest Christian writings, the first day of the week, the day of the Resurrection, is already the day of giving, just as Acts tells us it was the day “when we met to break bread” (Acts 20:7). Paul then shares his plans: “I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.” An open door and many adversaries: that is the life of every apostle. He commends young Timothy, “let no one despise him”, and speaks warmly of Apollos. And he gives five commands that could sum up the whole Season of the Apostles: “Keep alert, stand firm in your faith, be courageous, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love.” Our Sunday offering, our help to the mission dioceses of North India and to the poor of our own parish, belongs to this same apostolic love.

In the Gospel Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem, and someone asks the question people still ask: “Lord, will only a few be saved?” Jesus does not answer with a number. He turns curiosity into a call: “Strive to enter through the narrow door.” The word for strive is the word for an athlete's struggle; salvation is a gift, but it is received by those who make the effort of conversion. Then a hard picture: the owner of the house has shut the door, and those outside knock: “Lord, open to us.” “We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.” They had been near Jesus, had shared meals with him and heard him preach, yet he says, “I do not know where you come from.” Nearness without conversion is not enough. Baptism, a Christian name, a seat in church on feast days: these are graces, but they do not replace a life turned to God. And then the door opens wide: “Then people will come from east and west, from north and south, and will eat in the kingdom of God.” The apostles carried this invitation to every direction of the earth, and Mar Thoma brought it to our shores. “Indeed, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.” Those who came late may be first at the table. As the Season of the Apostles closes, the Church asks us: have we entered through the narrow door ourselves, and are we holding it open for those still outside?
conn: A voice without form.
“No one has ever seen God. It is God the only Son, who is close to the Father’s heart, who has made him known” (John 1:18); “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).
Teach your children.

“Keep these words that I am commanding you today in your heart. Recite them to your children and talk about them when you are at home and when you are away, when you lie down and when you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:6–7).
The vineyard and the woes.

Isaiah's woes follow the Song of the Vineyard: “he expected justice, but saw bloodshed; righteousness, but heard a cry!” (Isaiah 5:7). Jesus takes up the vineyard in the parable of the wicked tenants (Matthew 21:33–43).
The first day of the week.

“On the first day of the week, when we met to break bread, Paul was holding a discussion with them” (Acts 20:7). The collection for Jerusalem: “Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to share their resources with the poor among the saints at Jerusalem” (Romans 15:26).
The narrow door.
“For the gate is narrow and the road is hard that leads to life, and there are few who find it” (Matthew 7:14); “I am the gate. Whoever enters by me will be saved” (John 10:9).
From east and west.
“For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations” (Malachi 1:11).
altar: The voice that Israel heard from the fire at Horeb speaks to us at every Holy Qurbana in the readings, and the One who has made the Father known gives himself to us in his Body and Blood. Here already people from east and west, north and south, sit at the table of the kingdom.

The first day of the week is the day of the Qurbana and the day of giving. The bread and wine we offer, and the offering we place in the box, are one act of love: the Lord receives both and sends us out to let all that we do be done in love.
outline: Opening
The last Sunday of the Season of the Apostles: from the fire of Horeb and Pentecost to the table of the kingdom.
Point 1 · Only a voice
God speaks and makes a covenant; faith is heard and taught to children.
Point 2 · The woes of the vineyard
Greed for land, strong drink, and calling evil good; the Holy God shows himself holy by righteousness.
Point 3 · Let all be done in love
The collection on the first day of the week; a wide door and many adversaries.
Point 4 · The narrow door
Not how many, but am I entering? East and west at the table.
Closing image
A small tin box beside the family altar, filled each Sunday.
Take-home line
“Strive to enter through the narrow door.”
live: Teach the children (Deuteronomy 4:10)
Parents: sit with your children for ten minutes this week and ask what they learned in the faith formation class; pray together afterwards.
Refuse the woes (Isaiah 5:8, 11, 20)
Name one place where you have called evil good, or where drink or greed has a hold in your home, and take one step to change it.
Give on the first day (1 Corinthians 16:2)
Set aside a fixed amount every Sunday this coming season for the poor or the missions, before any other spending.
Strive (Luke 13:24)
Choose one concrete effort of conversion for the week: confession, reconciliation with someone, or a daily time of prayer.
fathers: St Ambrose of Milan (in substance)

How far, you rich, will you stretch your mad greed? Will you alone live on the earth? Why do you drive out the one who shares your nature and claim the creation for yourself? The earth was made for all in common, rich and poor alike. When you give to the poor, you do not give from what is yours; you return what is his.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Paul says, on the first day of the week let each put something aside. Let us do the same: let there be a little box for the poor in your house, beside the place where you stand to pray. Each time you pray, put something in it. Then your house will be a church, and the money of the poor will guard your house better than any weapon.
St Cyril of Alexandria (in substance)

The Lord did not answer the question of how many are saved, because it was of no use to the hearer. He showed the way instead. The narrow door is the life of virtue, which is entered with effort; but those who have entered find it opens on a wide and joyful dwelling with Christ.
magis: Catechism 1036

The affirmations of Sacred Scripture and the teachings of the Church on hell are a call to responsibility: Enter by the narrow gate, for the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction.
Catechism 2178
The practice of the Christian assembly on the Lord's Day dates from the beginnings of the apostolic age; the Letter to the Hebrews reminds the faithful not to neglect to meet together.
Catechism 2226
Education in the faith by the parents should begin in the child's earliest years; parents have the mission of teaching their children to pray and to discover their vocation as children of God.
Catechism 2290
The virtue of temperance disposes us to avoid every kind of excess: the abuse of food, alcohol, tobacco or medicine.
Catechism 2403
The right to private property does not do away with the original gift of the earth to the whole of mankind; the universal destination of goods remains primordial.
saints: Today
Seventh Sunday of the Apostles, the last Sunday of the season. In the Latin calendar, the Thirteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
Next days
Mon 28: St Irenaeus. Tue 29: St Peter and St Paul, the Apostles, an important feast and a day of obligation. Sat 3 July: the Dukhrana of St Thomas. Sun 4 July: the Season of Kaitha begins.
2027-06-27.prayer: Lord God, you spoke to your people out of the fire at Horeb, and at Pentecost you sent the fire of your Spirit on the apostles. Through this season you have taught us the faith they handed on: keep it alive in our homes, and help us to teach it to our children. Deliver us from greed, from strong drink and from calling evil good; show yourself holy among us by righteousness. Make us generous on the first day of every week, alert, firm in faith, courageous and strong, and let all that we do be done in love. Lord Jesus, you are the narrow door: give us strength to enter, and gather people from east and west, north and south, to your table in the kingdom. Glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-06-29.title: Saint Peter and Saint Paul, the Apostles
2027-06-29.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Elisha raises the son of the Shunammite woman
Love is the fulfilling of the law
2027-06-29.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. Today, the Seventh Tuesday of the Apostles, is the feast of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, the Apostles: an important feast and a day of obligation in the Syro-Malabar calendar. Both sets of readings printed in the calendar are shown: the four readings of the feast (the calendar notes the fuller passages 2 Kings 4:8–37 and 2 Corinthians 10:1–7 with 11:21–33, and joins Matthew 16:13–19 to the Gospel) and the weekday readings of the Seventh Tuesday. Verify locally the times of the Holy Qurbana. The Latin Church keeps the solemnity of Sts Peter and Paul today; in Rome the Pope blesses the pallium for new metropolitan archbishops.
2027-06-29.verse: He said to him the third time, “Simon son of John, do you love me?” Peter felt hurt because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” And he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.
theo: Today the whole Church, East and West, keeps one feast for two apostles. Peter, the fisherman of Galilee, and Paul, the scholar of Tarsus who had persecuted the Church, were very different men. They once disagreed openly at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14). Yet they preached one Gospel, served one Lord, and gave their lives for him in the same city. According to the ancient tradition of the Church, Peter was crucified in Rome during the persecution under Nero, and was buried on the Vatican hill, where the Basilica of St Peter stands over his tomb; tradition adds that he asked to be crucified head downward, judging himself unworthy to die as his Master had died. Paul, a Roman citizen, was beheaded on the road to Ostia and buried where the Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls now stands. St Augustine said that the two apostles have one feast because they were one: though they suffered on different days, they were as one. For us in India this feast has a family warmth. Peter and Paul were the brothers in mission of Mar Thoma, our Father in faith, whose Dukhrana we will keep on Saturday. And our Syro-Malabar Church, with its own Major Archbishop and Synod, lives in full communion with the Bishop of Rome, the successor of Peter. Today we pray especially for Pope Leo XIV. It is a day of obligation: the Church gathers around the altar with the apostles.

The first two readings are a pair, like the two apostles. In the Second Book of Kings a wealthy woman of Shunem has welcomed the prophet Elisha, building a small room on her roof for him. He promises her a son: “At this season, in due time, you shall embrace a son.” The boy is born, grows, goes out to his father among the reapers, cries “Oh, my head, my head!”, and dies on his mother's lap at noon. She lays him on the prophet's bed, rides to Mount Carmel and will not let Elisha go. “So he went in and closed the door on the two of them, and prayed to the Lord.” He stretches himself on the child, mouth to mouth, eyes to eyes, hands to hands, the child grows warm, sneezes seven times and opens his eyes. “Take your son.” In the Acts of the Apostles the same story happens again through Peter. At Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, in Greek Dorcas, “devoted to good works and acts of charity,” has died. The widows stand weeping, showing the tunics and clothing she had made for them. Peter, like Elisha, puts everyone outside; he kneels and prays; then he says, “Tabitha, get up.” She opens her eyes and sits up. “He gave her his hand and helped her up.” The apostle does what the prophet did, and more: he does what Jesus did, for in the house of Jairus Jesus had taken a girl by the hand and said, “Talitha cum,” which means, “Little girl, get up!” (Mark 5:41). And this morning's weekday Gospel shows where Peter first saw that gesture: in his own house at Capernaum, when Jesus came to his mother-in-law, sick with fever, “and took her by the hand and lifted her up.” The authority of Peter is the power of the risen Lord, given for the poor, the widows and the dead.

Paul's reading is a page from his own life, written to Corinthians who were being impressed by boastful preachers. Paul says he will speak “as a fool”, and boast as the others do: “Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I.” Then he lists, not his successes, but his sufferings: labours and imprisonments, floggings, near death many times; beaten with rods three times, stoned once, shipwrecked three times, “for a night and a day I was adrift at sea”; dangers from rivers, bandits, Gentiles and his own people, in city and wilderness and at sea; hunger, thirst, cold and sleeplessness. He even mentions the synagogue punishment of the forty lashes minus one, which he, a Jew among Jews, accepted five times rather than abandon his people or his Lord. And above all this: “I am under daily pressure because of my anxiety for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not indignant?” Then the surprising conclusion: “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.” The great apostle remembers that his ministry began with a humiliating escape, let down in a basket through a window in the wall of Damascus. Paul's glory is not his eloquence but his wounds, carried for Christ and for the Churches. At the end of his life he could write, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7).

The Gospel takes us to the shore of the Sea of Tiberias after the Resurrection. Jesus has prepared a charcoal fire with fish and bread for the disciples. The last time Peter stood by a charcoal fire was in the courtyard of the high priest, where he denied his Master three times (John 18:18). Now, by another charcoal fire, Jesus asks him three times: “Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?” “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” “Feed my lambs.” The second time: “Tend my sheep.” The third time Peter is hurt, and he answers with all his heart: “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” “Feed my sheep.” Three confessions of love heal three denials, and each confession is answered by a commission. Jesus does not give Peter a lesser task because he fell; he gives him his whole flock, the lambs and the sheep, the little ones and the great. The calendar joins to this Gospel the scene at Caesarea Philippi: “you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:18–19), and Luke adds the Lord's prayer for him: “I have prayed for you that your own faith may not fail; and you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Here is the Petrine ministry that the Catholic Church believes continues in the Bishop of Rome: a primacy of faith and love, of feeding and of strengthening, a ministry of unity for the whole Church. Pope St Gregory the Great called himself the servant of the servants of God, and every Pope since has carried that title. Then Jesus tells Peter how he will die: “when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will fasten a belt around you and take you where you do not wish to go.” And the last word: “Follow me.” The shepherd who feeds the sheep will one day lay down his life for them, like the Good Shepherd himself.

The weekday readings, read on the Seventh Tuesday of the Apostles, complete the picture. Paul tells the Romans: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law.” Love is the only debt we can never finish paying, and it is the whole law. And Mark shows us Peter's house at Capernaum: Jesus heals his mother-in-law, “and she began to serve them,” and that evening “the whole city was gathered around the door,” bringing the sick and the possessed. Pilgrims to Capernaum today are shown, under a modern church, the remains of a house that early Christians honoured and that many archaeologists identify with Peter's house. The Church built on Peter is meant to be such a house: a home where Jesus heals, where those who are healed serve, and at whose door the whole city can gather. On this feast let us thank God for the two pillars of the Church, pray for the Pope, our Major Archbishop and all our bishops, and renew our own answer to the question that Jesus asks every disciple: do you love me?
conn: Little girl, get up.
Peter's “Tabitha, get up” (Acts 9:40) echoes the words of Jesus in the house of Jairus: “He took her by the hand and said to her, ‘Talitha cum,’ which means, ‘Little girl, get up!’” (Mark 5:41).
Two charcoal fires.

Peter denied Jesus by a charcoal fire: “Peter also was standing with them and warming himself” (John 18:18); after the Resurrection, “they saw a charcoal fire there, with fish on it, and bread” (John 21:9).
The rock and the keys.

“And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18); the key of the house of David: “he shall open, and no one shall shut” (Isaiah 22:22).
Strengthen your brothers.
“I have prayed for you that your own faith may not fail; and you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32).
Pillars and partners.
James, Cephas and John, “who were acknowledged pillars,” gave Paul and Barnabas “the right hand of fellowship” (Galatians 2:9).
The good fight.
Paul at the end: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7).
altar: At every Holy Qurbana the Church names the Pope and our bishops: in that prayer the communion of the whole Church around the successor of Peter is made present at our parish altar. The apostles who broke bread in the Upper Room hand on to us the same Body and Blood.

Peter heard three times, “Do you love me?” before he heard, “Feed my sheep.” At the altar the Good Shepherd feeds us with himself, so that we in turn may feed others, and one day follow him wherever he leads.
outline: Opening
Two very different apostles, one feast, one faith, one city of martyrdom.
Point 1 · Do you love me? Feed my sheep
Three denials healed by three confessions; the Petrine ministry of love and unity.
Point 2 · Tabitha, get up
Elisha, Peter and Jesus: the hand that lifts up the dead and the poor.
Point 3 · I will boast of my weakness
Paul's wounds and his daily anxiety for all the Churches.
Point 4 · On this rock
The keys, the rock, and our communion with the successor of Peter.
Closing image
Peter's house at Capernaum, with the whole city at the door.
Take-home line
“Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.”
live: Answer the question (John 21:17)
Tonight, before sleep, answer Jesus aloud in your own words: “Lord, you know that I love you.” Then ask him whom he wants you to feed.
Lift someone up (Acts 9:41)
Like Peter with Tabitha, give your hand this week to someone who is down: a widow, a sick person, a discouraged friend.
Carry the Church (2 Corinthians 11:28)
Pray every day this week for the Pope, for our Major Archbishop and for your own bishop by name, and for one Church in difficulty.
Owe only love (Romans 13:8)
Pay one debt you have delayed, of money, of a visit or of an apology, and keep only the debt of love.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

One day is consecrated to the passion of the two apostles, but these two were one. Though they suffered on different days, they were one. Peter went first; Paul followed. Let us love their faith, their lives, their labours, their sufferings, their confession and their preaching.
St Augustine (in substance)

The threefold confession of love answered the threefold denial of fear, so that the tongue might serve love no less than it had served fear. Feed my sheep means: if you love me, do not think of feeding yourself, but feed my sheep as mine, not as yours; seek my glory in them, not your own.
St Leo the Great (in substance)

These are the men through whom the light of the Gospel of Christ shone on you, Rome. They are your holy fathers and true shepherds, who founded you far better than those who built your walls. In the blessed Peter the whole Church is strengthened, so that the firmness of faith praised in him may be shared by all.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Paul rejoiced in sufferings as others rejoice in honours. He counted the lashes as gains and the chains as ornaments. Who is weak, he says, and I am not weak? He carried in his heart all the Churches of the world, as a father carries all his children.
magis: Catechism 552
Simon Peter holds the first place in the college of the Twelve; Jesus entrusted a unique mission to him. Because of the faith he confessed, Peter will remain the unshakeable rock of the Church.
Catechism 553

Jesus entrusted a specific authority to Peter: the power of the keys designates authority to govern the house of God, which is the Church. After his Resurrection Jesus confirmed this mandate: Feed my sheep.
Catechism 881

The Lord made Simon alone, whom he named Peter, the rock of his Church; this pastoral office of Peter and the other apostles belongs to the Church's very foundation and is continued by the bishops under the primacy of the Pope.
Catechism 882
The Pope, Bishop of Rome and Peter's successor, is the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity both of the bishops and of the whole company of the faithful.
Second Vatican Council, Orientalium Ecclesiarum 3

The particular Churches of East and West are of equal dignity; none is superior to the others by reason of its rite, and all are entrusted to the pastoral government of the Roman Pontiff, the successor of Peter.
saints: Today
Saint Peter and Saint Paul, the Apostles: an important feast and a day of obligation. Also the Seventh Tuesday of the Apostles. The Latin Church keeps the solemnity today.
Next days
Wed 30: in the Latin calendar, the First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church. Sat 3 July: the Dukhrana of St Thomas. Sun 4 July: the Season of Kaitha begins.
2027-06-29.prayer: Lord God, you built your Church on the faith of the apostles and gave us today the joy of honouring Saint Peter and Saint Paul, who gave their lives for Christ in Rome. You made Peter, who had denied his Master, the shepherd of your flock, and Paul, who had persecuted your Church, its tireless apostle. Hear the prayer of your Church gathered on this feast: keep us one in faith and love around the successor of Peter. Strengthen our Pope Leo, our Major Archbishop, our bishops and priests, that they may feed your sheep with love. Give us Peter's love and Paul's zeal, the hand that lifts up the fallen and the heart that carries all the Churches. When our own hour comes, may we too have fought the good fight, finished the race and kept the faith. Glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-06-13.title: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles
2027-06-13.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: God's anger on those who do injustice
Trust in the providence of God
2027-06-13.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar gives longer forms: Deuteronomy 1:33–2:1, 1 Corinthians 14:1–19 and Luke 12:16–34 (with the parable of the rich fool).
2027-06-13.verse: “Do not be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
theo: On this Fifth Sunday of the Apostles the readings set before us two ways of facing the future: fear and trust. The first reading takes us to Kadesh, on the southern edge of the promised land. Moses reminds the people of the day when the spies came back from Canaan with fruit in their hands and fear in their hearts. The land was good, but its cities were walled and its people tall, and Israel refused to go up. Moses had pleaded with them: the Lord your God “goes before you on the way to seek out a place for you to camp, in fire by night, and in the cloud by day, to show you the route you should take.” They had seen the sea divided and the manna fall, yet they would not trust. So the Lord said that this generation would not see the good land, “except Caleb son of Jephunneh,” because of “his complete fidelity to the Lord.” Then came the second mistake, the mirror image of the first. Having refused to go when God said go, the people now insisted on going when God said stay: “We have sinned against the Lord! We are ready to go up and fight.” The Lord warned them: “Do not go up and do not fight, for I am not in the midst of you.” They went anyway, and the Amorites “chased you as bees do.” Fear refuses to move with God; presumption rushes ahead without him. Both are failures of the same thing, which is trust. And notice the tender detail in the middle of the judgment: the little ones, whom the frightened parents expected to become booty, are the very ones who will enter the land. God's promise was never withdrawn; it passed to the next generation.

Isaiah's oracle is a lament over Jerusalem, “the faithful city,” which has become unfaithful like a wife who has betrayed her husband. Strong language, but the charge is specific. The city's silver “has become dross,” its wine “is mixed with water.” Its leaders love bribes; “they do not defend the orphan, and the widow’s cause does not come before them.” For the prophets, unfaithfulness to God shows itself first in injustice to the weak. Yet the fire Isaiah announces is the fire of a refiner, not of a destroyer: “I will smelt away your dross as with lye and remove all your alloy. And I will restore your judges as at the first, and your counselors as at the beginning. Afterward you shall be called the city of righteousness, the faithful city.” God burns away what is false in order to recover what is precious. Only those who cling to their idols, the sacred oaks and gardens of the old fertility cults, are left like “a garden without water.” In the monsoon month, when every compound in Kerala turns green and every well fills, the image speaks clearly: a soul without God is a garden in which the rain has stopped.

Paul writes to a lively and gifted Church in Corinth, where some prized the gift of tongues above everything. He does not despise any gift of the Spirit, but he gives them an order: “Pursue love and strive for the spiritual gifts, and especially that you may prophesy.” Prophecy here means speaking God's word in a way others can understand, so that they are built up, encouraged and consoled. A gift that only edifies its owner is less than a gift that edifies the Church. Paul's examples are homely: a flute or a harp that does not give distinct notes, a bugle that “gives an indistinct sound,” so that no one knows it is time to prepare for battle. “So with yourselves; since you are eager for spiritual gifts, strive to excel in them for building up the church.” In this Season of the Apostles, when we thank God for the Spirit given at Pentecost, Paul reminds every prayer group, every choir, every catechist and every preacher of the test: does what I do build up the Church in love? A clear word spoken kindly in a family is worth more than an impressive word that leaves everyone confused.

In the Gospel Jesus turns to his disciples and speaks the words that have comforted anxious people ever since: “do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear.” He points to the ravens, birds that the Law counted unclean and that no farmer ever fed: “they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds!” He points to the lilies, which “neither toil nor spin; yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not clothed like one of these.” Worry adds nothing: “can any of you by worrying add a single hour to your span of life?” Jesus does not forbid work or planning; the birds hunt and the lilies grow. What he forbids is the anxious grasping that makes us forget the Father. “Instead, strive for his kingdom, and these things will be given to you as well.” Then comes the tenderest sentence of the passage: “Do not be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.” The apostles were a little flock indeed, a handful of fishermen and tax collectors. The Church in India has often been a little flock too, from the first communities that tradition traces to Mar Thoma. The kingdom is not something we must seize; it is the Father's pleasure to give it. Therefore the disciple can be generous: “Sell your possessions, and give alms. Make purses for yourselves that do not wear out.” The longer form of the Gospel adds the rich man who planned bigger barns and heard, “You fool! This very night your life is being demanded of you.” The Kadesh generation, the faithless city and the rich fool all made the same mistake: they trusted in what they could see. Jesus ends with a question for every heart: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
conn: Fire by night and cloud by day.
“The Lord went in front of them in a pillar of cloud by day, to lead them along the way, and in a pillar of fire by night, to give them light” (Exodus 13:21).
Caleb's whole heart.
“But my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me wholeheartedly, I will bring into the land” (Numbers 14:24).
They could not enter.
The Letter to the Hebrews reads the story of Kadesh as a warning: “So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:19).
The refiner's fire.
Of the coming Lord Malachi says: “he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver” (Malachi 3:3); faith is “more precious than gold that, though perishable, is tested by fire” (1 Peter 1:7).
Sons and daughters shall prophesy.
“I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2:28), fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:17).
Strive first for the kingdom.
Matthew's form of the same teaching: “But strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well” (Matthew 6:33).
Do not worry about anything.
“Do not worry about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6).
altar: Israel was fed in the wilderness by a God who went before them in fire and cloud. At the Holy Qurbana the same Father feeds his little flock with the Bread of life, the treasure that no thief can steal and no moth destroy.
When the priest raises the Body and Blood of the Lord, he lifts our hearts with them. There, where our treasure is, our hearts are taught to stay.
outline: Opening
Two ways of facing tomorrow: fear that refuses and presumption that rushes, or the trust of a little flock.
Point 1 · The God who goes before you
Kadesh: refusing to go, then going without God; Caleb's complete fidelity; the little ones who enter.
Point 2 · The refiner's fire
A faithful city that forgot the orphan and the widow; God burns away dross to recover silver.
Point 3 · Pursue love, build up the Church
Gifts given for others; a bugle with a clear sound.
Point 4 · Do not be afraid, little flock
Ravens and lilies; strive for the kingdom; treasure in heaven.
Closing image
A garden in the monsoon rain, and a garden where the rain has stopped.
Take-home line
“Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
live: Follow wholeheartedly (Deuteronomy 1:36)
Name one thing you have been afraid to do although you know God is asking it, and take the first step this week.
Defend the orphan and the widow (Isaiah 1:23)
Find out about one widow, orphan or elderly person living alone in your parish ward and do something concrete for them this week.
Build up the Church (1 Corinthians 14:12)
Before you speak in a meeting, a family discussion or a WhatsApp group this week, ask: will this build up or only show off?
Do not worry (Luke 12:22–31)
Each night this week write down one worry and place it before the Father in prayer; then give one alms you had not planned.
fathers: St Basil the Great (in substance)

Preaching on the rich man who wanted bigger barns, Basil said: the bread you hoard belongs to the hungry, the coat in your chest to the naked, the shoes rotting in your house to the barefoot, the money you bury to the needy. The barns that hold your wealth are the stomachs of the poor.
St Augustine (in substance)

Do you want to keep your treasure safe? Send it ahead. The poor are like porters who carry what you give into heaven, where no thief breaks in. What you keep you will leave behind; what you give goes before you.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Paul does not say simply, love; he says, pursue love, as a hunter pursues his quarry without tiring. Love is the root from which every gift draws its sap; the gift that builds up others is the one love chooses.
magis: Catechism 305
Jesus asks for childlike abandonment to the providence of our heavenly Father, who takes care of his children's smallest needs: therefore do not be anxious, but seek first his kingdom.
Catechism 2830
Asking for our daily bread expresses filial trust; it is not passivity, but the confidence of children who know the Father gives what they need.
Catechism 2547
The Lord grieves over the rich, because they find their consolation in the abundance of goods; detachment from riches is necessary for entering the kingdom of heaven.
Catechism 799–800

Charisms, extraordinary or simple and humble, are graces of the Holy Spirit that directly or indirectly benefit the Church, ordered as they are to her building up; they are to be accepted with gratitude, and charity is their true measure.
saints: Today

Fifth Sunday of the Apostles. In the Latin calendar the Eleventh Sunday in Ordinary Time; the memorial of St Antony of Padua (c. 1195–1231), the Franciscan preacher so dearly loved in Kerala, gives way to the Sunday this year.
Next days
Wed 16: in the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church the Apostles' Fast begins. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Thu 24: the Birth of John the Baptist.
2027-06-13.prayer: Lord God, you went before your people in fire by night and cloud by day, and you never withdrew your promise. Forgive us when fear has kept us from following you and when pride has made us rush ahead without you. Refine us as silver is refined, and make our homes and our parish faithful and just to the orphan and the widow. Holy Spirit, give us gifts that build up your Church, and above all give us love. Lord Jesus, teach your little flock not to be afraid, to seek the kingdom first, and to keep our treasure, and so our hearts, with you. Glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-06-01.title: Third Tuesday of the Apostles · St Justin, Martyr
2027-06-01.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The kingdom of God is not in talk but in power
Do not put a stumbling block before the little ones
2027-06-01.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), from Pentecost to the beginning of the Season of Summer (Kaitha): the Church remembers the apostles who, filled with the Holy Spirit, preached Christ and founded the Churches, among them the Church of India founded by Mar Thoma. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed at the three hours of the day. St Justin, martyr: Genesis 18:23–32; Wisdom 10:9–14; 1 Corinthians 1:18–25; Luke 12:2–8. In the Latin calendar St Justin is also remembered today.
2027-06-01.verse: For the kingdom of God depends not on talk but on power.
theo: The first day of June opens with a father's letter. Paul writes to a quarrelsome community he loves, and he does not hide his feelings: “For though you might have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers. Indeed, in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.” The guardian in a Greek household was the slave who walked the children to school and kept an eye on them; he could be strict and useful, but he was not their father. Paul claims something deeper. He did not merely supervise the Corinthians; he begot them in faith by preaching Christ to them. That is why he can say, without pride, “I appeal to you, then, be imitators of me.” Faith is handed on not only by teaching but by a life that can be copied. Paul sends Timothy, “my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ Jesus.” This is the apostolic pattern of the whole Season of the Apostles: a father in the faith, a son trained by him, and a community that learns the ways of Christ by watching those who walk in them. In these days, when schools reopen across Kerala and children set out with new bags and new books, the Church reminds parents, godparents, teachers and priests that they are more than guardians. Children learn the faith first from the way we pray, speak and forgive at home.

Then Paul turns to those who have grown arrogant, thinking that he will never come back: “But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power. For the kingdom of God depends not on talk but on power.” Corinth loved clever speech. Some had made themselves important by talking well about spiritual things. Paul asks a simple question: what has your talk produced? The kingdom of God is shown by the power of the Spirit that changes lives, heals divisions and makes people holy. Words about God are cheap; a life changed by God is costly and convincing. Then the tender ending: “What would you prefer? Am I to come to you with a stick, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?” A good father can correct, but he would much rather come with gentleness. The choice, Paul says, is partly theirs.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks some of the sternest words he ever spoke, and he speaks them in defence of the little ones: “If any of you put a stumbling block before one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for you if a great millstone were fastened around your neck and you were drowned in the depth of the sea.” The millstone was the heavy stone turned by a donkey to grind grain. Jesus does not use such language lightly. To lead a child, or any simple believer, into sin or out of faith is a grave evil. The Church has had to hear these words with shame in our own time, when some who should have been fathers in the faith harmed the little ones entrusted to them; every parish and institution is bound to protect children and vulnerable people, to listen to them and to act. Then Jesus turns the warning inward: “If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away.” He is not asking for mutilation; he is asking for decisiveness. Whatever in my life leads me into sin, a habit, a company, an app on the phone, must be cut off firmly, because eternal life is worth more than anything we give up.

Today the Church remembers St Justin, one of the first great Christian thinkers. Born in Samaria early in the second century, he searched for the truth among the philosophers of his day, until an old man he met by the sea pointed him to the prophets and to Christ. He became, as he said, a philosopher of the true philosophy, opened a school in Rome, and wrote to the emperor to defend the Christians. In those writings he left the earliest full description of the Sunday Eucharist outside the New Testament: the reading of the memoirs of the apostles and the prophets, the homily, the prayers, the bread and wine brought to the presider, the great thanksgiving, the Amen of the people, and the gifts carried to the absent. Around the year 165 he was arrested with several companions and beheaded under the prefect Rusticus for refusing to sacrifice to the gods. The readings of his feast fit his life: “the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Corinthians 1:18), and “everyone who acknowledges me before others, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God” (Luke 12:8). Justin's power was not in talk, though he talked well; it was in the witness of his blood.
outline: Opening
A new month and a new school year: who are the fathers and mothers in faith for our children?
Point 1 · Not many fathers
Paul begets the Corinthians through the Gospel and sends Timothy to remind them of his ways.
Point 2 · Not talk but power
The kingdom is shown by changed lives; a stick or gentleness.
Point 3 · The little ones
The millstone, the duty to protect, and cutting off what causes sin.
Point 4 · St Justin
The philosopher who found Christ, described the Sunday Qurbana and died for the faith.
Take-home line
“The kingdom of God depends not on talk but on power.”
live: Be imitators (1 Corinthians 4:16)
Parents and godparents: pray once this week with your children, aloud and unhurried, so that they can copy what they see.
Protect the little ones (Matthew 18:6)
Know your parish's child-protection guidelines and speak up if a child is in danger.
Cut off what causes stumbling (Matthew 18:8)
Name one habit, company or app that leads you into sin, and remove it this week.
fathers: St Justin Martyr (in substance)

On the day called Sunday all who live in the cities or in the country gather in one place. The memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read as long as time permits; the presider exhorts us to imitate these good things; we stand and pray; bread and wine and water are brought, he gives thanks as best he can, and the people say Amen. Then each one receives, and the deacons carry a portion to those who are absent.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Nothing is more precious than a soul. To build up a child in virtue is a greater work than any painter or sculptor can do. Do not say that the child is too young: a young plant is easily bent, and what you teach now will remain.
magis: Catechism 2223

Parents have the first responsibility for the education of their children; they bear witness to this responsibility first by creating a home where tenderness, forgiveness, respect, fidelity and service are the rule.
Catechism 2285
Scandal takes on a particular gravity by reason of the authority of those who cause it or the weakness of those who are scandalized; Jesus pronounced a curse on it in Matthew 18:6.
Catechism 1345
As early as the second century St Justin Martyr gave the basic lines of the order of the Eucharistic celebration, which have stayed the same until our own day.
saints: Today

St Justin (c. 100–c. 165), philosopher and martyr, born at Flavia Neapolis (Nablus) in Samaria, teacher in Rome, author of two Apologies and the Dialogue with Trypho; beheaded with companions under the prefect Junius Rusticus.
This week

1–6 June: the third and fourth weeks of the Season of the Apostles. Tue 1: St Justin, martyr. Thu 3: in the Latin calendar, St Charles Lwanga and his companions, the Martyrs of Uganda. Fri 4: the Feast of the Sacred Heart of Jesus (Third Friday of the Apostles), and First Friday. Sat 5: the Feast of the Immaculate Heart of Mary (Third Saturday of the Apostles); in the Latin calendar also St Boniface. Sun 6: Fourth Sunday of the Apostles. June is the month of the Sacred Heart in popular devotion; in Kerala it is also the month the schools reopen and the monsoon rains arrive.
2027-06-01.prayer: Father of all, you gave the Corinthians a father in the faith through the Gospel, and you gave St Justin the wisdom to find in Christ the truth he was seeking. Give our children faithful fathers and mothers, teachers and priests, whose lives they can copy. Keep the little ones from every stumbling block, and give us courage to cut off whatever leads us into sin. Let your kingdom be seen among us not in talk but in the power of your Holy Spirit. Through Christ our Lord, to whom with you and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: St Justin tells us that already in the second century the Christians gathered on Sunday to hear the apostles and prophets, to give thanks over bread and wine, and to say Amen. Every Holy Qurbana is that same gathering, and the Amen we say before Communion is the Amen of Justin and his companions, who sealed it with their blood.

2027-06-02.title: Third Wednesday of the Apostles
2027-06-02.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Shine like stars in the world
This is truly the Saviour of the world
2027-06-02.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), from Pentecost to the beginning of the Season of Summer (Kaitha): the Church remembers the apostles who, filled with the Holy Spirit, preached Christ and founded the Churches, among them the Church of India founded by Mar Thoma. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed at the three hours of the day. In the Latin calendar today is the optional memorial of Sts Marcellinus and Peter, martyrs.
2027-06-02.verse: They said to the woman, “It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world.”
theo: The Gospel today is the last scene of one of the great encounters of John's Gospel. At Jacob's well, at noon, Jesus has asked a Samaritan woman for a drink, and he has given her living water instead. She has left her water jar and run back to her town with a strange message: come and see a man who told me everything I have ever done. Now we hear what happened next: “Many Samaritans from that city believed in him because of the woman’s testimony.” This is remarkable on every side. Jews and Samaritans did not share vessels or prayers; the woman herself, it seems, was not well regarded in her own town; and yet her word is enough to bring a whole crowd out to the well. She did not preach a sermon. She told what had happened to her. That is the first form of witness that the Season of the Apostles asks of each of us: not a lecture about religion, but the honest story of what the Lord has done in my life. Only a few years later the deacon Philip would go down to a city of Samaria and proclaim the Messiah there, “so there was great joy in that city” (Acts 8:8); in a sense the woman at the well had already prepared the ground.

Then the Samaritans do something beautiful: “So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them; and he stayed there two days. And many more believed because of his word.” They do not only want to see the wonder-worker; they want him as a guest. And Jesus, who was on a journey to Galilee, stays. Faith grows in the time spent with him. Finally they say to the woman: “It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world.” This is the goal of all witness. The witness brings people to Jesus and then steps back, so that they may meet him themselves. A mother's prayers, a catechism teacher's patience, a friend's invitation to a retreat are all the woman's word; but sooner or later each person must hear him for themselves, in the Scriptures, in the Holy Qurbana, in silent prayer. And notice who first gives Jesus this great title: not the disciples, not the leaders in Jerusalem, but Samaritans, outsiders. The Saviour of the world is recognised first by those whom the world kept at a distance.

Paul's letter to the Philippians speaks to a community that already believes and must now grow. “Therefore, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed me, not only in my presence, but much more now in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who is at work in you, enabling you both to will and to work for his good pleasure.” Two truths are held together here.
