We must work; salvation is not something that happens to us while we sleep. Yet the very wanting and the very working are God's gift in us. The Catholic faith has always kept this balance: grace comes first and carries us, and grace calls for our answer. Then Paul gives a practical rule: “Do all things without murmuring and arguing, so that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, in which you shine like stars in the world.” The murmuring of Israel in the wilderness is in the background. A grumbling Christian is a dim star. A family that does not complain at every inconvenience, an office worker who does not join the gossip, a young person who refuses the cynical joke, shine in a dark sky. The secret, Paul says, is “holding fast to the word of life”: the same word of Jesus that the Samaritans heard for themselves.
outline: Opening
A woman runs to her town; a whole people comes to the well.
Point 1 · The witness of one woman
Not a sermon but a story: what the Lord has done for me.
Point 2 · We have heard for ourselves
They ask him to stay; faith grows in time spent with Jesus.
Point 3 · God at work in you
Work out your salvation; grace comes first and calls for our answer.
Point 4 · Shine like stars
Without murmuring, holding fast to the word of life.
Take-home line
“This is truly the Savior of the world.”
live: Tell your story (John 4:39)
Share with one person this week, simply, one thing the Lord has done in your life.
Ask him to stay (John 4:40)
Spend an extra ten minutes with the Gospel or before the Blessed Sacrament on two days this week.
Without murmuring (Philippians 2:14)
Go one whole day without complaining, and notice how often you are tempted.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

First they believed because of the woman's report; then, when he stayed with them, they believed because of his presence. So it happens now with those outside the Church: Christ is announced to them by friends, they come, and he remains with them; and he stays two days, that is, he gives them the two commandments of love.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

The woman did what the apostles were later sent to do. She did not hide what had been said about her life, but went running into the city and called everyone. Her shame became her preaching, and from her word a whole city came to the Lord.
magis: Catechism 425
The transmission of the Christian faith consists primarily in proclaiming Jesus Christ in order to lead others to faith in him.
Catechism 2001
The preparation of man for the reception of grace is already a work of grace; God completes in us what he has begun.
Catechism 905
Lay people fulfil their prophetic mission by evangelization, that is, the proclamation of Christ by word and the testimony of life.
saints: Today
Latin calendar: Sts Marcellinus, priest, and Peter, exorcist, martyrs at Rome in the persecution of Diocletian (about 304); their names are among the martyrs remembered in the Roman Canon.
This week

1–6 June: the third and fourth weeks of the Season of the Apostles. Tue 1: St Justin, martyr. Thu 3: in the Latin calendar, St Charles Lwanga and his companions, the Martyrs of Uganda. Fri 4: the Feast of the Sacred Heart of Jesus (Third Friday of the Apostles), and First Friday. Sat 5: the Feast of the Immaculate Heart of Mary (Third Saturday of the Apostles); in the Latin calendar also St Boniface. Sun 6: Fourth Sunday of the Apostles. June is the month of the Sacred Heart in popular devotion; in Kerala it is also the month the schools reopen and the monsoon rains arrive.
2027-06-02.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Saviour of the world, you sat by the well and gave living water to a Samaritan woman, and through her word you drew a whole town to yourself. Make us witnesses who tell simply what you have done for us. Stay with us, Lord, so that we may hear you for ourselves. Father, you are at work in us, giving us both the will and the strength to do your pleasure: keep us from murmuring, and let us shine like stars, holding fast to the word of life. Glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and for ever. Amen.
altar: The Samaritans asked Jesus to stay with them, and he stayed. In every Holy Qurbana he comes to stay with us, not two days but in our very bodies; let us receive him as our guest and go out to tell others, as the woman did, what he has done for us.

2027-06-03.title: Third Thursday of the Apostles
2027-06-03.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: You are God's field, God's building
The seed is the word of God
2027-06-03.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), from Pentecost to the beginning of the Season of Summer (Kaitha): the Church remembers the apostles who, filled with the Holy Spirit, preached Christ and founded the Churches, among them the Church of India founded by Mar Thoma. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed at the three hours of the day. In the Latin calendar today is the memorial of St Charles Lwanga and his companions, the Martyrs of Uganda.
2027-06-03.verse: But as for that in the good soil, these are the ones who, when they hear the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patient endurance.
theo: In the first days of June the southwest monsoon reaches Kerala, and across the paddy fields of Palakkad and Kuttanad, in the hill farms of Idukki and Wayanad, farmers prepare the ground and sow. Today's Gospel could have been told in a Kerala village. “A sower went out to sow his seed; and as he sowed, some fell on the path and was trampled on, and the birds of the air ate it up. Some fell on the rock; and as it grew up, it withered for lack of moisture. Some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew with it and choked it. Some fell into good soil, and when it grew, it produced a hundredfold.” The first surprise is the sower himself. He throws seed generously, even where it seems wasted: on the beaten path, on the thin soil over rock, among the thorns. God does not ration his word to those who seem likely to receive it. Every person, even the hardest, hears the word at least once. Then Jesus cries out, “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!” The parable is not only a description; it is an appeal.

Jesus himself explains it: “Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.” The path is the heart where “the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved”: we hear on Sunday and have forgotten by the time we reach the church gate. The rock is the heart that receives the word with joy but has no root: a retreat, a feast, a moment of fervour, and then in the time of testing the faith falls away. The thorns are the heart that hears, but “as they go on their way, they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.” Notice the three thorns: cares, riches and pleasures. Worry and wealth and comfort are not obviously sins, but they can quietly choke the word. And the good soil: “these are the ones who, when they hear the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patient endurance.” Hold it fast, and wait. A farmer does not dig up his seed every morning to see if it has sprouted. He keeps the field, clears the weeds and trusts the rain. Fruit in the spiritual life takes the same patience.

Paul's letter shows what happens when a community is still poor soil. “I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for solid food. Even now you are still not ready, for you are still of the flesh. For as long as there is jealousy and quarreling among you, are you not of the flesh?” The sign of spiritual infancy in Corinth was not a lack of gifts; it was faction. “For when one says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ and another, ‘I belong to Apollos,’ are you not merely human?” Paul refuses to be the head of a party: “What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, as the Lord assigned to each. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” Parishes and dioceses can still divide around personalities, preferences and old grievances, and every such quarrel keeps a community on milk. The cure Paul offers is to look away from the servants to the Lord of the harvest: “For we are God’s servants, working together; you are God’s field, God’s building.” The Church is not the property of any preacher or group. She is God's field, sown by the apostles, watered by their successors, and made to grow by God alone.

The Latin Church today remembers the Martyrs of Uganda, St Charles Lwanga and his companions. Missionaries had arrived in Buganda only in 1879. Within a few years young men at the court of King Mwanga II, many of them royal pages, had received the word with joy and held it fast. When the king demanded what their faith forbade, they refused. On 3 June 1886, at Namugongo, Charles Lwanga and a group of companions were burned to death; others were killed in the months before and after, the youngest, Kizito, still a boy of about fourteen. Anglican Christians died with them. Pope Paul VI canonised the twenty-two Catholic martyrs in 1964 and in 1969 became the first Pope to visit Africa, going to Namugongo. Today Uganda's Church is one of the most vigorous in the world. The seed that fell on that good soil bore fruit a hundredfold, exactly as the parable says, with patient endurance.
outline: Opening
The monsoon arrives and the farmers sow: the parable told in a Kerala field.
Point 1 · A generous sower
God sows his word everywhere; let anyone with ears listen.
Point 2 · Path, rock and thorns
The devil, the time of testing, and the cares, riches and pleasures of life.
Point 3 · God gave the growth
Factions keep a community on milk; we are God's field, God's building.
Point 4 · Patient endurance
The Martyrs of Uganda, seed that bore fruit a hundredfold.
Take-home line
“Hold it fast in an honest and good heart.”
live: Keep the word (Luke 8:12)
After Sunday's Qurbana this week, write down one sentence from the Gospel and read it every morning until the next Sunday.
Clear the thorns (Luke 8:14)
Name the worry, the possession or the pleasure that most chokes your prayer, and give it to God in confession or in a concrete sacrifice.
Refuse the factions (1 Corinthians 3:4)
Do not join any talk that divides your parish into parties; speak instead of what unites.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)

The good soil brings forth fruit through patience, because nothing we do is good unless we bear patiently the wrongs of our neighbours. The higher a person climbs, the more he finds in this world to endure; the fruit is not lost if it is guarded by patience.
Tertullian (in substance)
The more often you mow us down, the more numerous we grow: the blood of Christians is seed.
magis: Catechism 543
The word of the Lord is compared to a seed sown in a field; those who hear it with faith and are numbered among the little flock of Christ have truly received the kingdom.
Catechism 820
Christ always gives his Church the gift of unity, but the Church must always pray and work to maintain, reinforce and perfect it.
Catechism 2473
Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith: a witness even unto death, bearing witness to Christ who died and rose.
saints: Today

Latin calendar: St Charles Lwanga and his twenty-one companions, Martyrs of Uganda, killed under King Mwanga II between 1885 and 1887 (Charles Lwanga at Namugongo on 3 June 1886); canonised by Pope Paul VI in 1964.
This week

1–6 June: the third and fourth weeks of the Season of the Apostles. Tue 1: St Justin, martyr. Thu 3: in the Latin calendar, St Charles Lwanga and his companions, the Martyrs of Uganda. Fri 4: the Feast of the Sacred Heart of Jesus (Third Friday of the Apostles), and First Friday. Sat 5: the Feast of the Immaculate Heart of Mary (Third Saturday of the Apostles); in the Latin calendar also St Boniface. Sun 6: Fourth Sunday of the Apostles. June is the month of the Sacred Heart in popular devotion; in Kerala it is also the month the schools reopen and the monsoon rains arrive.
2027-06-03.prayer: Lord God, Lord of the harvest, you sow your word in every heart, on the path, on the rock and among the thorns. Break up the hard ground in us, give our faith deep roots, and clear away the cares, riches and pleasures that choke your word. Keep us from jealousy and factions, for we are your field and your building, and you alone give the growth. By the prayers of the Martyrs of Uganda, give us honest and good hearts that hold your word fast and bear fruit with patient endurance. Through Christ our Lord, to whom with you and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: Every Holy Qurbana begins with the sowing of the word in the readings, and then the bread, fruit of the earth and of the patience of farmers, becomes the Body of the Lord. Let the word we hear and the Bread we receive find good soil in us.

2027-06-04.title: Third Friday of the Apostles: the Feast of the Sacred Heart of Jesus
2027-06-04.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Abram gives Lot the first choice
He was wounded for our transgressions
They will look on the one whom they have pierced
2027-06-04.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), from Pentecost to the beginning of the Season of Summer (Kaitha): the Church remembers the apostles who, filled with the Holy Spirit, preached Christ and founded the Churches, among them the Church of India founded by Mar Thoma. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed at the three hours of the day. The Feast of the Sacred Heart of Jesus is a Feast of Our Lord, and today is also the First Friday of June. The calendar notes the fuller passages: Romans 9:30–10:17, and for the Gospel Matthew 11:25–30 together with John 19:30–37. The Latin Church keeps the solemnity of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus on the same day, with the World Day of Prayer for the Sanctification of Priests (verify locally for adoration, confessions and the renewal of the consecration of families).
2027-06-04.verse: Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.
theo: Eight days after the Feast of the Body and Blood of Christ, on the First Friday of June, the Church turns to the source of that gift: the Heart of Jesus. In very many Syro-Malabar homes a picture of the Sacred Heart hangs above the family altar, with a small lamp burning before it, and the family has been consecrated to the Sacred Heart, often on the day the house was blessed. On First Fridays parishes hold adoration, confessions are heard, and many of the faithful come to the Holy Qurbana. June is the month of the Sacred Heart. The devotion is not a sentimental extra. In the Bible the heart is the centre of the person, the place where one thinks, decides, loves and meets God. To speak of the Heart of Jesus is to speak of the whole person of the Word made flesh, who loved the Father and loved us with a human heart. The Church found this devotion in the Gospel itself, in the pierced side of the Crucified; it was deepened by medieval mystics, spread through the revelations given to St Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial between 1673 and 1675, extended to the whole Church by Pope Pius IX in 1856, explained by Pius XII in the encyclical Haurietis Aquas (1956), and recommended anew by Pope Francis in Dilexit Nos (2024).

The first reading may seem at first to have little to do with the feast. Abram and his nephew Lot have both grown rich, and the land cannot support their flocks; their herders quarrel. Abram is the elder and the head of the clan; by right, the first choice is his. Instead he says: “Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herders and my herders; for we are kindred. Is not the whole land before you? Separate yourself from me. If you take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if you take the right hand, then I will go to the left.” Lot looks, and chooses with his eyes: “the plain of the Jordan was well watered everywhere like the garden of the Lord.” The text adds quietly that he moved his tent as far as Sodom, and “the people of Sodom were wicked, great sinners against the Lord.” Abram, who has given up the best land for the sake of peace, is not the loser. God speaks to him: “Raise your eyes now, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward; for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.” Abram builds an altar at Mamre. Here is a heart that prefers peace to rights, kinship to profit, and God's promise to what the eye can grasp. The Church reads it on this feast because it is a first sketch of the Heart of Christ, who did not hold on to what was his, and who says in the fuller Gospel of the day: “learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). In Kerala, where families are so often divided by quarrels over land and inheritance, Abram's words to Lot are a word for brothers and sisters today.

The second reading is the song of the suffering Servant, which the Church reads on Good Friday: “He was despised and rejected by others; a man of suffering and acquainted with infirmity… Surely he has borne our infirmities and carried our diseases… But he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have all turned to our own way, and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all.” The Heart of Jesus is not a heart that loves from a safe distance. It is a wounded heart, a heart that carries. In the Season of the Apostles we remember how the deacon Philip met an Ethiopian official on the road to Gaza who was reading this very passage, “like a sheep he was led to the slaughter”, and asked of whom the prophet spoke. “Then Philip began to speak, and starting with this scripture, he proclaimed to him the good news about Jesus” (Acts 8:35). The apostles preached the Servant song as the key to the Cross: the One who was pierced bore our sins out of love.

Paul's Epistle opens with Paul's own heart: “Brothers and sisters, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.” He is speaking of his own people, Israel, whom he loves and for whom, in the chapter before, he says he has great sorrow and unceasing anguish. This is not the language of contempt but of love, and Christians must always read it so, honouring the Jewish people to whom belong the covenants and the promises. Then Paul places faith exactly where today's feast places it, in the heart: “The word is near you, on your lips and in your heart (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim); because if you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For one believes with the heart and so is justified, and one confesses with the mouth and so is saved.” Devotion to the Sacred Heart is not a feeling to be enjoyed in private. It is faith in the risen Lord believed with the heart and confessed with the lips: at the family prayer, before meals in a restaurant, in the office, in the hospital ward.

The Gospel takes us to Calvary at the moment after death. “When Jesus had received the wine, he said, ‘It is finished.’ Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.” Because the next day was the great Sabbath of Passover, the bodies were not to remain on the crosses, and the soldiers came to break the legs of the crucified. “But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.” The evangelist, who stood there with the Mother of Jesus, solemnly testifies to what he saw, “so that you also may believe.” He sees two Scriptures fulfilled: “None of his bones shall be broken”, as with the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46), and “They will look on the one whom they have pierced” (Zechariah 12:10). The Fathers saw in the blood and water the sacraments of the Church, Baptism and the Eucharist, and they saw the Church herself born from the side of the new Adam asleep on the Cross, as Eve was formed from the side of the first Adam. And our own father in the faith comes into this mystery. Eight days after Easter the risen Lord said to Thomas, “Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe” (John 20:27). The apostle of India, invited to touch the wounded side of Christ, confessed, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). The Mar Thoma Christians received their faith from the one to whom the Lord showed his opened side. Today we look on the One whom we have pierced, not to stay in grief, but to drink from the spring of mercy, and to say with Thomas and with every First Friday pilgrim: Jesus, meek and humble of heart, make our hearts like yours.
conn: They will look on the one they pierced.

“when they look on the one whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child” (Zechariah 12:10); “On that day a fountain shall be opened for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, to cleanse them from sin and impurity” (Zechariah 13:1).
The struck rock.

“Strike the rock, and water will come out of it, so that the people may drink” (Exodus 17:6); “For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).
Water from the temple.
Ezekiel sees “water was flowing from below the threshold of the temple toward the east” (Ezekiel 47:1); Jesus spoke of “the temple of his body” (John 2:21).
Rivers of living water.
“Let anyone who is thirsty come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink” (John 7:37–38).
The Passover lamb.
“you shall not break any of its bones” (Exodus 12:46); “None of his bones shall be broken” (John 19:36).
Gentle and humble in heart.
“Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:28–29).
Thomas and the open side.
“Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe” (John 20:27).
Water and blood.
“This is the one who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ, not with the water only but with the water and the blood” (1 John 5:6).
altar: At the preparation of the gifts in the Holy Qurbana a little water is mingled with the wine in the chalice. The Church has long seen in it the blood and water that flowed from the side of Christ, and our humanity united with his divinity. What flowed from the pierced Heart on Calvary is given to us at the altar.

When we receive the Body and Blood of the Lord, we receive the whole Christ, his Heart included, truly present. On this First Friday let us receive him with a clean heart and ask him to make our hearts like his.
outline: Opening
A lamp before the Sacred Heart in a Kerala home: what the heart means in the Bible.
Point 1 · Let there be no strife
Abram yields the first choice for peace: a first sketch of the gentle and humble Heart.
Point 2 · Wounded for our transgressions
The suffering Servant, preached by Philip as the key to the Cross.
Point 3 · One believes with the heart
Paul's heart for his people, and faith believed in the heart and confessed with the lips.
Point 4 · Blood and water
The pierced side, the sacraments, the Church born from the Cross, and Thomas invited to the wounded side.
Closing image
A family kneeling before the picture of the Sacred Heart on the First Friday evening, renewing their consecration.
Take-home line
“They will look on the one whom they have pierced.”
live: Keep the First Friday
Go to confession this week if you can, receive the Holy Qurbana today or on Sunday, and spend some time in adoration.
Renew the family consecration
Gather the family before the Sacred Heart this evening, light the lamp, and renew your consecration with a simple prayer.
Let there be no strife (Genesis 13:8)
If there is a quarrel in your family over land, money or inheritance, take one step toward peace, even at a cost to yourself.
Confess with your lips (Romans 10:9)
Make the sign of the cross and say grace before meals this week, also when you eat outside the home.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The evangelist chose his word with care. He did not say that the soldier struck or wounded the side, but that he opened it, so that there, as it were, the door of life might be thrown open, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed out, without which no one enters the life that is true life.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Do not pass this mystery by lightly. Water and blood came from the side: the symbols of Baptism and of the holy mysteries. From these the Church is formed. As God made the woman from the side of Adam while he slept, so Christ gave us water and blood from his side after his death, and from them built the Church.
St Bonaventure (in substance)
The side of Christ was pierced so that through the visible wound we might see the invisible wound of love. Let us enter by that open door and dwell there, in the Heart that was wounded for us.
magis: Catechism 478

Jesus knew and loved us each and all during his life, his agony and his Passion; the Sacred Heart of Jesus, pierced by our sins and for our salvation, is rightly considered the chief sign and symbol of that love.
Catechism 766
The Church is born primarily of Christ's total self-giving; her origin and growth are symbolized by the blood and water that flowed from the open side of the crucified Jesus.
Catechism 2669

The prayer of the Church venerates and honours the Heart of Jesus, just as it invokes his most holy name; it adores the incarnate Word and his Heart which, out of love for us, he allowed to be pierced by our sins.
Catechism 2563
The heart is the place to which I withdraw, the place of decision, of truth and of encounter, the place of covenant.
Pius XII, Haurietis Aquas (1956) (in substance)

The Heart of the incarnate Word is the natural sign and symbol of his threefold love: the divine love he shares with the Father and the Spirit, and the human love, both spiritual and sensible, with which he loves us.
Pope Francis, Dilexit Nos (2024) (in substance)
In a world that risks losing its heart, the Heart of Christ shows us a love that gives itself; from it we learn to love others and to be healed.
saints: Today

The Feast of the Sacred Heart of Jesus (Syro-Malabar, Third Friday of the Apostles) and First Friday. The Latin Church keeps the solemnity of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus today, with the World Day of Prayer for the Sanctification of Priests.
This week

1–6 June: the third and fourth weeks of the Season of the Apostles. Tue 1: St Justin, martyr. Thu 3: in the Latin calendar, St Charles Lwanga and his companions, the Martyrs of Uganda. Fri 4: the Feast of the Sacred Heart of Jesus (Third Friday of the Apostles), and First Friday. Sat 5: the Feast of the Immaculate Heart of Mary (Third Saturday of the Apostles); in the Latin calendar also St Boniface. Sun 6: Fourth Sunday of the Apostles. June is the month of the Sacred Heart in popular devotion; in Kerala it is also the month the schools reopen and the monsoon rains arrive.
2027-06-04.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, gentle and humble of heart, your side was opened by the spear, and from your Heart flowed blood and water, the fountain of our salvation. Like Abram, teach us to choose peace over our rights; like the Servant, you bore our infirmities: heal us by your wounds. Give us hearts that believe and lips that confess that you are Lord. As you showed your side to Mar Thoma, show us your mercy, that we too may say, My Lord and my God. Make our families your dwelling, bless our priests, and make our hearts like your Heart. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory and honour for ever. Amen.

2027-06-05.title: Third Saturday of the Apostles: the Feast of the Immaculate Heart of Mary
2027-06-05.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Sarah shall give rise to nations
The Lord himself will give you a sign: Immanuel
Chosen in Christ to be holy and blameless
His mother treasured all these things in her heart
2027-06-05.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), from Pentecost to the beginning of the Season of Summer (Kaitha): the Church remembers the apostles who, filled with the Holy Spirit, preached Christ and founded the Churches, among them the Church of India founded by Mar Thoma. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed at the three hours of the day. The Immaculate Heart of Mary is listed in the First Set calendar as an important Marian feast; no seasonal readings are printed for the Third Saturday, so the feast's readings are the day's. In the Latin calendar the memorial of the Immaculate Heart falls this year on the same day as that of St Boniface, bishop and martyr, and both are optional. 5 June is also World Environment Day.
2027-06-05.verse: Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them. His mother treasured all these things in her heart.
theo: Yesterday the Church looked on the pierced Heart of Jesus; today she turns to the Heart of his Mother. The two belong together. When the infant Jesus was presented in the Temple, old Simeon said to Mary, “and a sword will pierce your own soul too” (Luke 2:35), and at the foot of the Cross that sword went through her heart as the spear went through his. The devotion to the Heart of Mary is old in the Church. St John Eudes in the seventeenth century gave it a liturgical form; at Fatima in 1917 the Mother of God spoke to three shepherd children of her Immaculate Heart; Pope Pius XII consecrated the world to the Immaculate Heart in 1942 and extended the feast to the whole Church in 1944, and Pope Francis renewed the consecration of humanity, and in particular of Russia and Ukraine, on 25 March 2022. The word Immaculate reminds us that this heart was never stained by sin. By a singular grace and in view of the merits of Christ, Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception. The word Heart reminds us of her inner life: the place where she received the word of God, kept it, pondered it and answered it with her whole self. In the Syro-Malabar calendar this is an important Marian feast, and it falls fittingly in the Season of the Apostles, for after the Ascension the apostles “were constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). The first Church was gathered around the heart of the Mother.

The first reading is God's promise to Abraham about his wife: “As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her Sarai, but Sarah shall be her name. I will bless her, and moreover I will give you a son by her. I will bless her, and she shall give rise to nations; kings of peoples shall come from her.” Abraham falls on his face and laughs: “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Can Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?” God holds to his word: Sarah will bear Isaac, and the everlasting covenant will pass through him. God does not forget Ishmael either: “As for Ishmael, I have heard you; I will bless him.” The Church reads this passage today because Sarah, the barren woman who becomes a mother of nations by God's power, is a figure of the Mother of the Messiah. What God began with Sarah's laughter he completed in Mary's faith. To her the angel said what was said to Abraham long before: “For nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). Mary became the mother not of one nation but of all, for from the Cross Jesus gave her to the beloved disciple and, through him, to the whole Church: “Here is your mother” (John 19:27).

In the second reading King Ahaz of Judah is terrified because two neighbouring kings have joined against him. The prophet Isaiah invites him to trust God and even to ask for a sign, as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven. Ahaz refuses with pious words, “I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test”, because he has already decided to trust in a foreign empire rather than in God. Isaiah answers: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Look, the young woman is with child and shall bear a son, and shall name him Immanuel.” The Hebrew word speaks of a young woman of marriageable age; the ancient Greek translation made by Jewish scholars before Christ rendered it “virgin”; and St Matthew, quoting that translation, sees the sign fulfilled in Mary: “Look, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall name him Emmanuel,” which means, “God is with us” (Matthew 1:23). The Church professes that Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit without the seed of man and remained a virgin for ever. And notice the contrast between two hearts. Ahaz's heart was closed by fear and calculation; he would not even ask. Mary's heart was open; she asked, “How can this be?”, and then said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).

The Epistle is the great blessing that opens the Letter to the Ephesians: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, just as he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love.” This is God's plan for the whole Church: to be holy and without blemish. What is promised to all of us, and will be completed only at the end, has already been accomplished in one person. Mary was chosen before the foundation of the world, and from the first moment of her existence she was holy and blameless before God in love. She too was redeemed; Paul's next words apply to her first of all: “In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace that he lavished on us.” She was redeemed, as the Church says, in a more exalted way: not by being washed from sin but by being preserved from it, through the blood her Son would shed. Her Immaculate Heart is the masterpiece of grace, “to the praise of his glorious grace.” That is why honouring Mary never takes anything from Christ; it praises what his grace can do.

The Gospel is the only story from the hidden years of Jesus. At twelve he goes up with Mary and Joseph to Jerusalem for the Passover and stays behind. For three days they search for him. When they find him in the Temple among the teachers, his mother speaks: “Child, why have you treated us like this? Look, your father and I have been searching for you in great anxiety.” Mary does not hide her pain, and she names Joseph first: your father and I. Jesus answers, “Why were you searching for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?” And Luke tells us honestly: “But they did not understand what he said to them.” The Immaculate Heart is not a heart that understood everything at once, nor a heart without anxiety. It is a heart that did not close itself in the dark. “Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them. His mother treasured all these things in her heart.” She kept what she did not yet understand, and turned it over in prayer until God gave the light. Parents who worry about children growing up and going their own way, mothers who have searched through a long night for a son or daughter, can bring their anxiety to her. And all of us can learn from her the way to hold God's word: not to throw it away when it is hard, but to treasure it, ponder it and wait.
conn: The woman and her offspring.

God promises enmity between the serpent and the woman, and between their offspring (Genesis 3:15); the Church sees in the woman the New Eve, and in her offspring Christ, who crushes the power of evil.
Full of grace.
“Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28): the greeting of the angel to one who was already filled with God's favour.
No flaw in you.
“You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you” (Song of Songs 4:7), applied by the Church's tradition to the Immaculate Mother.
Mary pondered.
“But Mary treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart” (Luke 2:19).
The sword.
“and a sword will pierce your own soul too” (Luke 2:35).
Here is your mother.
“Woman, here is your son… Here is your mother” (John 19:26–27).
With the apostles.
“All these were constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14).
The woman clothed with the sun.
“A great portent appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars” (Revelation 12:1).
altar: Mary's heart received the Word of God, and the Word became flesh in her womb. At every Holy Qurbana the same Word made flesh is placed on the altar and given to us. Let us receive him as she received him, with an open and believing heart.
The Mother who stood by the Cross stands by the altar where the sacrifice of the Cross is made present. In her company let us offer ourselves with Christ to the Father.
outline: Opening
The pierced Heart of the Son and the pierced heart of the Mother.
Point 1 · A mother of nations
Sarah's laughter and Mary's faith: nothing is impossible with God.
Point 2 · The Lord himself will give you a sign
Ahaz's closed heart and Mary's open heart; the virgin mother of Immanuel.
Point 3 · Holy and blameless
Chosen before the foundation of the world; preserved from sin by the blood of her Son.
Point 4 · She treasured all these things
Anxiety, searching, not understanding, and keeping the word in the heart.
Closing image
A mother praying the rosary late at night at the family altar, waiting for a child to come home.
Take-home line
“His mother treasured all these things in her heart.”
live: Treasure the word (Luke 2:51)
Each evening this week, before sleeping, recall one thing God has said or done that day, and keep it in your heart.
Consecrate yourself
Pray an act of consecration to the Immaculate Heart of Mary this week, alone or with your family.
Pray the rosary for the world
Pray one decade each day for peace, especially for countries at war, as the Mother of God asked at Fatima.
Bring your anxieties to her
If you are anxious about a child, a marriage or a decision, entrust it to Mary's heart and ask her to keep it with you.
fathers: St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)
You alone, Lord, and your Mother are beautiful in every way; for there is no blemish in you, and no stain in your Mother.
St Augustine (in substance)

Mary conceived Christ first in her heart by faith, and then in her womb. It was a greater thing for her to be his disciple than to be his mother; she is blessed because she heard the word of God and kept it.
St Bede the Venerable (in substance)

Mary kept all these words in her heart: whatever she heard of the Lord, or saw done by him, she laid up carefully in her memory, comparing it with what she had read in the prophets, so that she might ponder it and later hand it on.
magis: Catechism 491

Through the centuries the Church has become ever more aware that Mary, full of grace through God, was redeemed from the moment of her conception; in 1854 Pope Pius IX proclaimed the dogma of the Immaculate Conception.
Catechism 492

Mary is redeemed in a more exalted fashion, by reason of the merits of her Son; the Father blessed her more than any other created person in Christ, and chose her before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love.
Catechism 499
The Church confesses Mary's real and perpetual virginity, even in the act of giving birth to the Son of God made man.
Catechism 534

At the finding in the Temple Mary and Joseph did not understand his words, but they accepted them in faith, and Mary kept all these things in her heart during the years Jesus remained hidden in the silence of an ordinary life.
Catechism 2617
Mary's prayer is revealed at the dawning of the fullness of time; her prayer and that of the Church are marked by the generous offering of her whole being in faith.
Pius XII, Act of Consecration (1942) (in substance)
Queen of the most holy Rosary, help of Christians, refuge of the human race, we entrust and consecrate ourselves, the Church and the whole human race, to your Immaculate Heart.
saints: Today

The Feast of the Immaculate Heart of Mary (Syro-Malabar, an important Marian feast). Latin calendar: the Immaculate Heart and St Boniface (about 675–754), the English Benedictine monk who became the apostle of Germany and archbishop of Mainz, martyred at Dokkum in Frisia on 5 June 754 with his companions; both memorials optional this year.
This week

1–6 June: the third and fourth weeks of the Season of the Apostles. Tue 1: St Justin, martyr. Thu 3: in the Latin calendar, St Charles Lwanga and his companions, the Martyrs of Uganda. Fri 4: the Feast of the Sacred Heart of Jesus (Third Friday of the Apostles), and First Friday. Sat 5: the Feast of the Immaculate Heart of Mary (Third Saturday of the Apostles); in the Latin calendar also St Boniface. Sun 6: Fourth Sunday of the Apostles. June is the month of the Sacred Heart in popular devotion; in Kerala it is also the month the schools reopen and the monsoon rains arrive.
2027-06-05.prayer: God our Father, you prepared a worthy dwelling for your Son in the Immaculate Heart of the Virgin Mary, chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in love. As you gave Sarah a son and gave Ahaz a sign, you gave us Immanuel through the faith of Mary. Give us hearts like hers, open to your word, faithful in anxiety, and treasuring what we do not yet understand. Mother of God and Mother of the Church, as you prayed with the apostles in the Upper Room, pray with us now: keep our families in your heart, bring peace to the nations, and lead us to your Son. Through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with you and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-06-07.title: Fourth Monday of the Apostles
2027-06-07.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Daughter, your faith has made you well
2027-06-07.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. No saint is kept today in the First Set calendar; in the Latin calendar it is a weekday of the tenth week in Ordinary Time.
2027-06-07.verse: He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.”
theo: Today's Gospel is a story inside a story. Jesus is on his way to the house of Jairus, whose little daughter is dying, and a great crowd is pressing in on him. Into that crowd comes a woman nobody notices. Mark describes her in a few heavy lines: she “had been suffering from hemorrhages for twelve years. She had endured much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had; and she was no better, but rather grew worse.” Twelve years of bleeding meant twelve years of exhaustion, and, under the law of purity in Leviticus, twelve years of being kept at a distance from worship and from the touch of others. Her money is gone, her health is going, and her place in the community has quietly disappeared. She is the kind of person a crowd walks past. Yet she has heard about Jesus, and hearing has become hope: “If I but touch his clothes, I will be made well.” She does not ask for attention. She only reaches out from behind, in the crush of bodies, and touches the edge of his cloak.

“Immediately her hemorrhage stopped; and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease.” She could have slipped away, healed and unseen. But Jesus stops. “Immediately aware that power had gone forth from him, Jesus turned about in the crowd and said, ‘Who touched my clothes?’” The disciples find the question almost foolish: everyone is touching him. But there is a difference between the crowd that presses and the one who touches in faith. Many brush against Jesus; one person reaches for him. Jesus will not let her go home with a healed body and a hidden heart. He wants to meet her. And so she comes “in fear and trembling, fell down before him, and told him the whole truth.” Then comes the word that she will remember for the rest of her life: “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.” She came as a nameless case; she leaves as a daughter. The healing of her body is followed by the healing of her place among the people of God. This is what the Holy Qurbana is meant to be for us: not a crowd pressing in, but a touch of faith, and a word of peace that sends us home as sons and daughters.

Paul's letter opens with a blessing that could be the woman's song: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction with the consolation with which we ourselves are consoled by God.” Paul wrote these words after a time of great suffering in Asia, when he despaired even of life (2 Corinthians 1:8). He does not pretend that the apostles are spared trouble. He says rather that consolation is a gift that flows on: God consoles us so that we can console others. The comfort we receive is not meant to stop with us, any more than the woman's healing was meant to stay hidden. In this Season of the Apostles we remember that the Church was born among sufferings, and that the apostles became channels of a consolation greater than their own. Every Christian who has been comforted by God in grief, illness or failure has something to give to someone else who is now walking that same road.

June has come to Kerala with the monsoon and with the opening of schools. The rain beats on the roofs, children set out with new bags and old fears, parents count fees and worry about the year ahead. The Gospel today is a quiet encouragement for all who feel lost in the crowd: the sick who have tried many remedies, the families who have spent all they had on treatment, the student who feels invisible in a large class, the elderly who are seldom touched or visited. Jesus notices the one touch of faith in the crowd. He turns, he looks, he calls by name. And he sends his disciples, the apostles of every age, to be the same kind of presence: to notice, to stop, and to console with the consolation they themselves have received.
outline: Opening
A woman nobody notices, reaching out from behind in the crowd.
Point 1 · Twelve years in the shadows
Illness, poverty and exclusion; and the hope that comes from hearing about Jesus.
Point 2 · Who touched my clothes?
The crowd that presses and the one who touches in faith; Jesus turns to meet her.
Point 3 · Daughter, go in peace
Healing of the body and of her place among God's people.
Point 4 · The God of all consolation
Comforted in order to comfort others.
Take-home line
“Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.”
live: Reach out in faith (Mark 5:28)
At your next Holy Qurbana, make your communion a personal touch of faith: tell the Lord in one sentence what you need him to heal.
Pass on the consolation (2 Corinthians 1:4)
Think of a grief or illness the Lord helped you through, and this week contact one person who is going through the same thing now.
Notice the one in the crowd (Mark 5:30)
In the classroom, the office or the parish, look for one person who seems unseen, and speak to them by name.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)
The crowd presses, but only she touches. Flesh presses, faith touches. Many throng around the Lord's body in the Church, but few touch him with faith; let us be among those who touch.
St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)

The woman stretched out her hand to the hem of his garment, and the hidden power in him came to her openly. If the edge of his clothing gave her healing, what will his Body give to those who receive it with faith?
magis: Catechism 1504

Often Jesus asks the sick to believe. He makes use of signs to heal; and the sick try to touch him, ‘for power came forth from him and healed them all’. So in the sacraments Christ continues to touch us in order to heal us.
Catechism 2448
Human misery in all its forms, illness included, draws the compassion of Christ, who took it upon himself; it is the object of a preferential love on the part of the Church.
Catechism 1521
United to the passion of Christ, suffering acquires a new meaning: it becomes a participation in the saving work of Jesus.

2027-06-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you turned in the crowd to find the woman who touched your cloak in faith, and you sent her home as a daughter, healed and at peace. Look on all who are weary of illness, on families who have spent everything for treatment, and on those who feel unseen. Give us faith to reach out to you, especially in the Holy Qurbana. Father of mercies and God of all consolation, comfort us in every affliction, so that we may comfort others with the consolation we have received. Holy Spirit, make us apostles of consolation in our homes, schools and parishes. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: The woman touched only the edge of his cloak and power went out from him. At the Holy Qurbana we do not touch the hem of his garment: we receive the Lord himself, his Body and Blood. Let us come not as a crowd that presses, but as those who reach out in faith, and let us listen for his word: go in peace.

2027-06-08.title: Fourth Tuesday of the Apostles · St Mariam Thresia
2027-06-08.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Go from your country to the land that I will show you
When you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing
Crucified with Christ: Christ lives in me
Just as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me
2027-06-08.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. St Mariam Thresia is listed in the First Set calendar as an important feast, among the commemorations of martyrs and saints, with the readings above. Weekday readings of the Fourth Tuesday of the Apostles: Philippians 1:12–18; Luke 10:38–42. Follow the direction of the eparchy and parish on which readings are used (verify locally). Her shrine at Kuzhikattussery (Irinjalakuda eparchy) keeps the feast with great solemnity.
2027-06-08.verse: And the king will answer them, ‘Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me.’
theo: Today the Syro-Malabar Church keeps the feast of one of her own daughters, St Mariam Thresia, the saint of the families of Kerala. She was born on 26 April 1876 at Puthenchira, in the present district of Thrissur, into the Chiramel Mankidiyan family, an old Christian family that had fallen on hard times. She lost her mother while still a girl. From childhood she was drawn to prayer and penance, and she longed to give herself entirely to the Lord. But the path God opened for her was not the one she first imagined. She dreamed of a hidden life of prayer; God led her instead into the homes of her neighbours, to the sick, the dying, the poor and the troubled families of her village. She died on 8 June 1926 at Kuzhikattussery, was beatified by St John Paul II on 9 April 2000, and was canonised by Pope Francis on 13 October 2019. The readings chosen for her feast trace the shape of her life.

The first reading is the call of Abraham: “Now the Lord said to Abram, ‘Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you.’” Abram did not receive a map; he received a promise. “So Abram went, as the Lord had told him.” Mariam Thresia knew that kind of obedience. She did not leave her country, but she left the security of the ordinary road for a young woman of her time and place, and she stepped into a land God showed her one step at a time. With three companions she began to go from house to house, nursing the sick, washing the bodies of those who died alone, praying with families in trouble, bringing quarrelling relatives to reconciliation, and teaching children their prayers. Such a life was new and surprising in the villages around Puthenchira, and not everyone understood it. Like Abraham, she went out not knowing where she was going (Hebrews 11:8), and like Abraham she became a blessing: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” The words fit her well: through her, countless families have been blessed.

Sirach gives the second key: “My child, when you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing… For gold is tested in the fire, and those found acceptable, in the furnace of humiliation.” Her life was full of testing. She passed through long seasons of spiritual darkness and through fierce trials that she and her spiritual director, Fr Joseph Vithayathil, understood as attacks of the evil one. Her bishop, Mar John Menachery, Vicar Apostolic of Trichur, examined her experiences carefully and with prudence, as the Church must, and for a time she was misunderstood and doubted. She accepted all this with humility and obedience. Those who knew her also spoke of a deep union with the sufferings of Christ, which she asked the Lord to keep hidden. The Epistle puts words to that hidden centre of her life: “I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” Her many works were not the activity of a restless social worker. They flowed from a life hidden with Christ.

Then comes the Gospel of the last judgment, which reads like a description of her days: “I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me, I was naked and you gave me clothing, I was sick and you took care of me, I was in prison and you visited me.” She saw Christ in the poorest and the most neglected, and she served him there. On 14 May 1914, with the approval of Mar John Menachery, the community that had gathered around her was erected as the Congregation of the Holy Family (CHF), with Kuzhikattussery as its first home. Its charism is the one she lived: to serve families, especially families in difficulty, so that every home may become a Nazareth. Today her sisters serve in Kerala, in other parts of India and abroad, in homes, schools, hospitals, hostels and among the elderly and the sick.

The weekday Gospel of the Fourth Tuesday, the story of Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42), fits her feast as well. In Mariam Thresia the two sisters were joined. She sat at the Lord's feet for long hours of prayer, and she rose from prayer to serve in homes like Martha's. “Mary has chosen the better part”: she chose the Lord first, and that is why her service did not become anxious and distracted. In this Season of the Apostles she reminds us that the apostolate begins at home. The Holy Spirit who sent the Twelve to the nations sent this woman of Puthenchira to the family next door. As schools reopen and families are tested by money worries, illness, migration, addiction and quarrels, her feast is an invitation to pray for our homes and to visit the families around us who are carrying burdens alone.
conn: The call of Abraham.

“Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you” (Genesis 12:1); “By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called… and he set out, not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8).
Gold tested in the fire.
Sirach's image (Sirach 2:5) returns in Peter: the genuineness of faith, more precious than gold that is tested by fire (1 Peter 1:7).
Bring the homeless poor into your house.
Isaiah describes the fast the Lord chooses: “to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house” (Isaiah 58:7).
The home at Nazareth.
Jesus “went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them” (Luke 2:51): the Holy Family is the model of every Christian home and the name of her congregation.
Martha and Mary.
“Mary has chosen the better part” (Luke 10:42): prayer at the feet of the Lord and service in the home, united in one life.
Crucified with Christ.
Paul: “I carry the marks of Jesus branded on my body” (Galatians 6:17); the saints share the Cross in order to share the life of Christ.
altar: St Mariam Thresia served Christ in the hungry, the sick and the dying, because she first adored him in the Holy Qurbana and in long hours of prayer. At the altar the same Lord who said, “you did it to me”, gives himself to us. Let us receive him, and then go out to find him in the least of our brothers and sisters.
As the Holy Family lived around Jesus at Nazareth, may our families live around the Eucharist, so that every home becomes a little Nazareth.
outline: Opening
A young woman of Puthenchira who dreamed of a hidden life and was sent into the homes of her neighbours.
Point 1 · Go to the land I will show you
Abraham's obedience and hers: a new road, one step at a time.
Point 2 · Prepare yourself for testing
Darkness, misunderstanding and obedience; gold tested in fire.
Point 3 · Christ lives in me
The hidden centre of a life of service.
Point 4 · You did it to me
The works of mercy and the Congregation of the Holy Family.
Closing image
A woman with a lamp walking at night to a house where someone is dying alone.
Take-home line
“Just as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me.”
live: Visit a family (Matthew 25:36)
This week visit one family in your parish or neighbourhood that is carrying illness, grief or trouble, and pray with them if they wish.
Pray for your home (Luke 2:51)
Make the family prayer this week a prayer to the Holy Family, asking St Mariam Thresia to protect your home.
Accept the testing (Sirach 2:4)
Offer to the Lord one humiliation or misunderstanding you are carrying, without complaint.
Sit at his feet (Luke 10:39)
Before your work tomorrow, give ten quiet minutes to the Lord, as Mary of Bethany did.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Do you wish to honour the Body of Christ? Do not neglect him when he is naked. Do not honour him here in the church with silk while outside you leave him to perish of cold. He who said, This is my Body, also said, You saw me hungry and did not feed me.
St Augustine (in substance)

Christ is still in need here below. He is hungry in his poor, thirsty in his poor, naked in his poor, a stranger in his poor, sick in his poor, in prison in his poor. Whatever you give to them, you give to him.
St Gregory the Great (in substance)
The love of God gives birth to the love of neighbour, and the love of neighbour nourishes the love of God. One who neglects to love God does not know how to love the neighbour.
magis: Catechism 2447

The works of mercy are charitable actions by which we come to the aid of our neighbour in his spiritual and bodily necessities: feeding the hungry, sheltering the homeless, clothing the naked, visiting the sick and imprisoned, burying the dead.
Catechism 1657
It is in the family, the domestic church, that the father, the mother and the children exercise the priesthood of the baptised by prayer, the witness of a holy life, self-denial and active charity.
Catechism 2013
All Christians in any state or walk of life are called to the fullness of Christian life and to the perfection of charity.
Catechism 828
By canonising some of the faithful, the Church recognises the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.

2027-06-08.prayer: Lord God, you called St Mariam Thresia to leave the ordinary road and to serve your Son in the poor, the sick and the families of her people, and you made her strong in testing and hidden with Christ in prayer. Through her intercession bless our homes, so that each may become a Nazareth where Jesus, Mary and Joseph are welcome. Heal families wounded by illness, poverty, addiction and quarrels; comfort the dying who are alone; and give us eyes to see Christ in the least of our brothers and sisters and hands ready to serve him there. Through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-06-09.title: Fourth Wednesday of the Apostles · Mar Aprem (St Ephrem the Syrian)
2027-06-09.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: You shall be a people holy to the Lord your God
Moses, whose memory is blessed: the law of life and knowledge
God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit
You are the salt of the earth and the light of the world
2027-06-09.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. Mar Aprem (St Ephrem the Syrian) is listed in the First Set calendar as an important feast, with the readings above. Weekday readings of the Fourth Wednesday of the Apostles: 1 Corinthians 15:31–34; Matthew 14:22–33. In the Latin calendar St Ephrem, deacon and Doctor of the Church, is an optional memorial on the same day. Follow the direction of the eparchy and parish on which readings are used (verify locally).
2027-06-09.verse: You are the light of the world. A city built on a hill cannot be hid.
theo: Today our Church keeps the feast of Mar Aprem, St Ephrem the Syrian, whom the Syriac tradition calls “the Harp of the Spirit”. For the Syro-Malabar Church he is not a distant figure. He is one of the fathers of our own Syriac heritage: his hymns and his way of praying shaped the liturgy of the Church of the East, from which our Holy Qurbana, our Hours and our feasts have come down to us. Ephrem was born around the year 306 in Nisibis, a frontier city between the Roman and Persian empires, in what is now south-eastern Turkey. He grew up in the Christian community of that city, was formed by its bishop, Mar Jacob of Nisibis, and served the Church as a deacon and a teacher. When Nisibis was handed over to Persia in 363, Ephrem went with the Christians who left the city and settled in Edessa (Urhai), where he taught and wrote for the last ten years of his life. Tradition says that he died in 373, after spending himself in caring for the hungry and the sick during a famine. In 1920 Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the universal Church.

Ephrem was a theologian who sang. He wrote verse homilies (memre), commentaries on Scripture, and above all hundreds of madrashe, teaching hymns set to melodies that the people knew. He trained choirs of women to sing them in the church, so that the faith of Nicaea, the mystery of the Incarnation, the virginity of Mary and the gift of the sacraments would be carried in the memory and the heart of ordinary believers. He did not reduce God to definitions. He knew that God is beyond our grasp, and that the best way to speak of him is often through the symbols that God himself has placed in Scripture and in nature: the pearl, the light, the fire, the bread, the robe, the womb, the river. His hymns teach us to stand before the mystery with wonder rather than curiosity, with love rather than argument. That is why the Church calls him a Doctor: not only because he taught truly, but because he taught us how to adore.

The readings of his feast are well chosen. Sirach praises Moses, “whose memory is blessed”, whom the Lord “allowed to hear his voice, and led him into the dark cloud, and gave him the commandments face to face, the law of life and knowledge, so that he might teach Jacob the covenant, and Israel his decrees.” Ephrem too entered the cloud of the divine mystery and came back to teach. Deuteronomy calls Israel “a people holy to the Lord your God”, a treasured people set high “in praise and in fame and in honor”. Ephrem's hymns are one long effort to make the Church that holy, praising people. And Paul gives the source of it all: “hope does not disappoint us, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.” In this Season of the Apostles, after Pentecost, we see in Ephrem what the Spirit does when he is poured into a heart: he turns it into an instrument of praise, a harp on which the Spirit himself plays.

The Gospel is from the Sermon on the Mount: “You are the salt of the earth… You are the light of the world. A city built on a hill cannot be hid.” Jesus adds a word that fits a teacher of the Church: “whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” Ephrem did not only teach; he lived what he taught. He remained a deacon, a servant, all his life, and his last work was not a hymn but the care of the hungry in a time of famine. His light shone through good works, “so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.” His love for Mary was tender and strong; he sang of her as the one who carried the Fire that does not burn, and he could say to Christ that he and his Mother alone are entirely beautiful, without any stain (in substance). In his hymns on the Eucharist he marvels that the Spirit and the fire dwell in the bread and in the cup, and that we eat and drink the Lord himself.

The weekday readings add their own note. Paul says, “I die every day!”, and asks the Corinthians to come “to a sober and right mind”, because the dead will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:31–34). In the Gospel Jesus walks on the water, and Peter, sinking, cries out, “Lord, save me!” (Matthew 14:30). Ephrem's life, lived on a troubled frontier, through sieges, exile and famine, was a long walk on the water, held by the hand of Christ. He invites us today to sing our faith, to love the liturgy we have received, to teach it to our children, and to let the Holy Spirit make each of us a harp in the hands of God.
conn: Face to face, as with a friend.
“Thus the Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend” (Exodus 33:11); Sirach 45:5 recalls the dark cloud and the law of life.
Awake, O harp and lyre!
“Awake, my soul! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn” (Psalm 108:2): the psalmist's harp becomes Ephrem's name, the Harp of the Spirit.
Psalms, hymns and spiritual songs.
“Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; teach and admonish one another in all wisdom; and with gratitude in your hearts sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God” (Colossians 3:16).
The burning bush.
Moses saw a bush that burned without being consumed (Exodus 3:2); Ephrem and the Syriac tradition see in it Mary, who carried the divine Fire without being consumed.
Light of the world.
Jesus says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and to his disciples, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14): the saints shine with a borrowed light.
Mary treasured all these things.
“But Mary treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart” (Luke 2:19): Ephrem learned from her to ponder the mysteries and to sing them.
altar: Mar Aprem marvelled that in the bread of the Qurbana there dwells the Spirit who is not consumed, and in the cup the Fire that is not drunk (in substance). At this altar we receive the living Christ himself. Let us receive him with Ephrem's wonder, and let our thanksgiving become a hymn.
The Holy Qurbana we celebrate in the Syriac tradition carries the voices of Ephrem and of the fathers who prayed before us. Let us pray it with understanding and love, and hand it on to our children.
outline: Opening
A deacon of Nisibis and Edessa who taught the faith in song: the Harp of the Spirit.
Point 1 · God's love poured into our hearts
The Spirit turns a heart into a harp.
Point 2 · A teacher like Moses
Entering the cloud of mystery and coming back to teach the law of life.
Point 3 · Salt and light
A theology lived in service, to the last day of famine.
Point 4 · Our Syriac heritage
Mary, the Eucharist and the liturgy we have received.
Closing image
Women's voices in the church of Edessa singing the faith of Nicaea to a melody everyone knew.
Take-home line
“You are the light of the world.”
live: Sing your faith (Colossians 3:16)
Learn by heart one hymn of the Holy Qurbana or the Hours this week, and sing it at home.
Teach what you believe (Matthew 5:19)
Explain to a child or a young person one part of the Qurbana: why we stand, why we face the east, why we sing.
Let your light shine (Matthew 5:16)
Do one hidden good work this week for the hungry or the sick, as Ephrem did in the famine.
Ponder with Mary (Luke 2:19)
Spend five minutes each day this week pondering one mystery of the Rosary in silence.
fathers: Mar Aprem (in substance)
You alone, Lord, and your Mother are fair in every way; for in you there is no blemish, and in your Mother no stain.
Mar Aprem (in substance)
In your bread is hidden the Spirit who is not eaten; in your wine dwells the Fire that is not drunk. The Spirit in your bread, the Fire in your wine: a wonder, received by our lips.
Mar Aprem (in substance)

Lord, who can grasp even one of your words? We leave behind far more than we take from it, like thirsty people drinking from a spring. Let the thirsty one rejoice that he drank, and not grieve that he could not drink the spring dry.
Pope Benedict XVI (in substance)
St Ephrem shows that theology can be done in poetry; his hymns combine faith and beauty, and teach that the mystery of God is best approached through praise.
magis: Catechism 1156
The musical tradition of the universal Church is a treasure of inestimable value; song and music are integral to solemn liturgy.
Catechism 1157

Song and music fulfil their function as signs more significantly the more closely they are connected with the liturgical action: beauty expressive of prayer, the unanimous participation of the assembly, and the solemn character of the celebration.
Catechism 1203

The liturgical traditions or rites presently in use in the Church include the Latin, Byzantine, Alexandrian or Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Maronite and Chaldean rites; the Church holds all of them to be of equal right and dignity.
Catechism 2641
Address one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with all your heart: the hymns of the Church are an expression of the praise of God.

Wed 9: Mar Aprem, St Ephrem the Syrian, the Harp of the Spirit (an important feast; in the Latin calendar an optional memorial the same day). Thu 10: Fourth Thursday of the Apostles. Fri 11: St Barnabas, the Apostle (in the Latin calendar a memorial the same day). Sun 13: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles; St Antony of Padua, so dear to Kerala, gives way to the Sunday this year. 2027-06-09.prayer: Lord God, you poured your love into the heart of Mar Aprem through the Holy Spirit and made him a harp of praise, a teacher of the true faith and a servant of the hungry. By his prayers, give us hearts that sing your wonders, minds that ponder your mysteries with humility, and hands that serve the poor. Make our families and parishes love the holy liturgy we have received from our fathers; keep us faithful to the faith of the apostles; and with the Virgin Mary, whom he praised so tenderly, let us glorify you in the Church, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-06-10.title: Fourth Thursday of the Apostles
2027-06-10.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: There is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ
Even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs
2027-06-10.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. Today's readings are taken from the official First Set calendar of 2022-23 (the Fourth Thursday of the Apostles), because in the 2024-25 calendar from which this month is mapped the same day was the Dukhrana of St Thomas; verify locally. In the Latin calendar, a weekday of the tenth week in Ordinary Time.
2027-06-10.verse: But she answered him, “Sir, even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.”
theo: Today the Gospel takes Jesus out of Galilee. Mark says that “he set out and went away to the region of Tyre”, a Gentile coastal region on the Mediterranean, in what is now southern Lebanon. He enters a house and wants no one to know he is there, perhaps seeking rest with his disciples. “Yet he could not escape notice.” A woman hears of him and comes at once, because her little daughter is tormented by an unclean spirit. Mark is careful to tell us who she is: “the woman was a Gentile, of Syrophoenician origin.” She is outside the people of the covenant, a woman, a foreigner, without any claim on a Jewish teacher. She bows down at his feet and begs him to cast the demon out of her daughter. Every parent who has prayed at night for a sick or troubled child knows what was in her heart.

Jesus' answer sounds hard to our ears: “Let the children be fed first, for it is not fair to take the children's food and throw it to the dogs.” We should not soften it too quickly, but we should read it well. Jesus speaks of an order in God's plan: the promises were made first to Israel, the children of the household, and the Messiah came first to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. The word he uses can mean the little dogs of the house, not the wild dogs of the street. And the word “first” leaves a door open: if the children are fed first, then someone else is fed afterwards. The woman hears the open door and walks through it with faith and wit: “Sir, even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs.” She does not argue that she deserves the bread. She trusts that there is so much bread at this table that even the crumbs are enough for her daughter. She calls him “Sir”, or “Lord”, the only person in Mark's Gospel to address Jesus with that title. And Jesus answers, “For saying that, you may go; the demon has left your daughter.” She goes home and finds the child lying quietly on the bed, healed.

Mark places this story just after Jesus has declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and just before he feeds a crowd in Gentile territory (Mark 8:1–10). The bread of the children is about to overflow the table. In this Season of the Apostles the Church remembers how that happened: after the Resurrection and Pentecost the apostles carried the bread of the Gospel to the nations, and the household of God was opened to all. We, the Christians of India, are among those who were once outside the table. Through the apostle Thomas, as our tradition holds, the bread came to our shores. Every Holy Qurbana we celebrate is a sign that the Syrophoenician woman's hope was right: there is enough at the Lord's table for all.

Paul's letter speaks of a very practical question in Corinth: may Christians eat meat that has been offered in pagan temples? Some say, “all of us possess knowledge”: we know that idols are nothing, so we may eat anything. Paul agrees with the doctrine but corrects the attitude: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. Anyone who claims to know something does not yet have the necessary knowledge; but anyone who loves God is known by him.” Then he proclaims the heart of the faith in words that sound like an early creed: “yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.” This is the Shema of Israel, “Hear, O Israel: The Lord is our God, the Lord alone” (Deuteronomy 6:4), opened up to include Jesus within the one God. We say the same in the Creed every Sunday. But Paul's point is that right doctrine must be held with love. The one who knows the truth must use it to build up the weak, not to show off or to wound.

Both readings meet in a single lesson. The proud knowledge of the Corinthians puffed them up; the humble faith of a foreign mother won her daughter's healing. It is not always the one who knows most who receives most, but the one who trusts most and loves most. Today let us pray for parents who carry a child's illness or struggle to the Lord; for those who feel they have no claim on God; and for ourselves, that our knowledge of the faith may become love that builds up.
outline: Opening
A foreign mother at the feet of Jesus in the region of Tyre.
Point 1 · She could not be kept away
A parent's love and a Gentile's faith.
Point 2 · Even the dogs eat the crumbs
Humble, persistent, witty trust; the table that is enough for all.
Point 3 · One God, one Lord
The creed of Israel opened to Christ.
Point 4 · Knowledge puffs up, love builds up
Truth held with love.
Take-home line
“Even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs.”
live: Pray like this mother (Mark 7:25–26)
Name a child or young person you love who is struggling, and bring them to Jesus each day this week with persistent faith.
Build up, do not puff up (1 Corinthians 8:1)
In one conversation about faith this week, choose to encourage rather than to win the argument.
Say the Creed slowly (1 Corinthians 8:6)
At the next Holy Qurbana, pray the Creed slowly and mean each phrase about the one God and the one Lord.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

See the woman's wisdom: she does not contradict the Lord, nor is she grieved at being called a dog; she takes his very word and turns it into a plea. Her persistence is rewarded because it came from faith.
St Augustine (in substance)
Christ seemed to reject her so that her humility might be revealed; she accepted the lowly name and so received the high gift. Humility opened what pride would have kept closed.
magis: Catechism 2610

Just as Jesus prays to the Father and gives thanks before receiving his gifts, he teaches us filial boldness: everything is possible for one who believes. Jesus is moved by the faith of those who ask, like the Canaanite woman.
Catechism 543
Everyone is called to enter the kingdom. First announced to the children of Israel, this messianic kingdom is intended to accept people of all nations.
Catechism 228
Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord: faith in God leads us to turn to him alone as our first origin and our ultimate goal.
