2027-06-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you could not be hidden from the mother who came to you for her daughter, and you rejoiced in her humble and persistent faith. Look on the children we carry in our hearts: heal the sick, deliver those who are oppressed, and bring back those who have wandered. Teach us to trust that there is bread enough at your table for all. One God and Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we exist, keep us in the true faith and make our knowledge humble and our love strong, so that we may build up and not puff up. altar: The Syrophoenician woman asked only for crumbs. At the Holy Qurbana the Lord gives us not crumbs but the Bread itself, his own Body and Blood, at a table opened to all nations. Let us come with her humility and her trust, and let us remember those who still wait outside.

2027-06-11.title: Fourth Friday of the Apostles · St Barnabas, the Apostle (Mar Barnabas Shleeha)
2027-06-11.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Make known his deeds among the peoples
Barnabas at Antioch: a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith
The right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and Paul
I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves
2027-06-11.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. St Barnabas, the Apostle, is listed in the First Set calendar with the readings above; for the second reading the calendar adds the note “(11:1–3 + 21–26)”. Weekday readings of the Fourth Friday of the Apostles: Galatians 2:15–18; Mark 5:21–24, 35–43. In the Latin calendar St Barnabas is a memorial on the same day. Follow the direction of the eparchy and parish on which readings are used (verify locally).
2027-06-11.verse: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were brought to the Lord.
theo: Today the Church keeps the feast of St Barnabas, whom the Acts of the Apostles calls an apostle together with Paul (Acts 14:14), though he was not one of the Twelve. His real name was Joseph. He was a Levite from Cyprus, and the apostles gave him a new name, Barnabas, “which means ‘son of encouragement’” (Acts 4:36). We first meet him in the earliest days of the Church in Jerusalem, when he sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet. It is a small gesture, but it tells us who he is: a man who gives without holding back, and who trusts the community of the apostles. All through Acts he lives up to his name. Wherever Barnabas appears, someone is encouraged, welcomed, trusted, or given a second chance.

The clearest example is Saul. After his conversion on the road to Damascus, the disciples in Jerusalem were afraid of him; they remembered the persecutor and did not believe he had changed. “But Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles, and described for them how on the road he had seen the Lord” (Acts 9:27). Barnabas risked his own reputation to vouch for a former enemy. Without that act of trust, the Church might have kept at a distance the greatest missionary she has ever had. Today's reading shows him again in the same role. When the Gospel reaches Gentiles in Antioch, the church in Jerusalem sends Barnabas to see what is happening. “When he came and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast devotion; for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.” He does not come as an inspector looking for faults, but as a brother looking for grace, and when he finds it he rejoices. Then he does something humble and wise: he goes to Tarsus to look for Saul, and brings him to Antioch, and the two of them teach there for a whole year. “It was in Antioch that the disciples were first called ‘Christians.’”

From Antioch the Holy Spirit sends them out. “While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.’ Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off” (Acts 13:2–3). Barnabas and Paul go first to Cyprus, Barnabas' own island, and then into Asia Minor. In this Season of the Apostles we see the Church's mission born from worship, fasting and the laying on of hands: not from a human plan, but from the Spirit speaking in a praying community. The Epistle tells how, years later, Paul and Barnabas went up to Jerusalem to lay before the leaders the gospel they preached among the Gentiles, and how “James and Cephas and John, who were acknowledged pillars, recognized the grace that had been given to me, they gave to Barnabas and me the right hand of fellowship.” The unity of the Church, with Peter among the pillars, guarded the truth of the Gospel. And the leaders asked only one thing: “that we remember the poor.” Barnabas, who had sold his field for the poor, would not have needed reminding.

Barnabas was not without weakness. Paul tells that at Antioch “even Barnabas was led astray” for a time when some held back from eating with Gentile believers (Galatians 2:13). And Acts honestly records that Paul and Barnabas had a sharp disagreement over John Mark, who had left them in the middle of their first journey; “they parted company; Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus” (Acts 15:39). Barnabas gave Mark a second chance, as he had once given Saul a first one. Later Paul himself would write, “Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful in my ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11). The encourager had been right about his cousin. Tradition holds that Barnabas died a martyr in Cyprus, at Salamis.

The Gospel is the Lord's warning to those he sends: “See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.” The apostles will be handed over and hated, but they will not be alone: “it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.” And the psalm of the first reading gives the apostle's song: “O give thanks to the Lord, call on his name, make known his deeds among the peoples.” The weekday Gospel of this Fourth Friday, the raising of Jairus' daughter, adds a word that Barnabas lived: “Do not fear, only believe” (Mark 5:36). Every parish needs a Barnabas: someone who sees grace and rejoices, who welcomes the newcomer and the convert, who speaks for the person others are afraid of, and who gives a second chance to those who have failed. Today let us ask him to make us sons and daughters of encouragement.
conn: Son of encouragement.
“There was a Levite, a native of Cyprus, Joseph, to whom the apostles gave the name Barnabas (which means ‘son of encouragement’)” (Acts 4:36).
Strengthen the weak hands.
“Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees” (Isaiah 35:3): the prophet's task becomes Barnabas' way of life.
Here am I; send me!
Isaiah answers the Lord's call, “Whom shall I send?” (Isaiah 6:8); in Antioch the Spirit says, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul” (Acts 13:2).
Encourage one another.
“Therefore encourage one another and build up each other, as indeed you are doing” (1 Thessalonians 5:11).
A second chance for Mark.
Barnabas took Mark with him (Acts 15:39); later Paul writes, “Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful in my ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11).
The first Christians.
“It was in Antioch that the disciples were first called ‘Christians’” (Acts 11:26), in the church that Barnabas and Saul taught for a year.
altar: The church at Antioch was worshipping the Lord and fasting when the Holy Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul for the mission. Every mission begins at the altar. Here we receive the Lord who sends us, and the Spirit who speaks through us.
Barnabas laid his money at the apostles' feet. At the Holy Qurbana we too bring our gifts to the altar, and we go out to remember the poor, as the apostles asked.
outline: Opening
A Levite from Cyprus whom the apostles renamed: son of encouragement.
Point 1 · He took Saul and brought him to the apostles
Trusting the convert others feared.
Point 2 · He saw the grace of God and rejoiced
A good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.
Point 3 · Set apart for the work
Mission born in worship and fasting; the right hand of fellowship.
Point 4 · Sheep among wolves
Courage, weakness and a second chance for Mark.
Closing image
A man at the door of the church at Antioch, looking for grace rather than faults.
Take-home line
“He was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.”
live: Be a son or daughter of encouragement (Acts 4:36)
Each day this week, say one sincere word of encouragement to someone who is struggling.
Welcome the newcomer (Acts 9:27)
Greet and introduce yourself to someone new in your parish or workplace, especially someone others keep at a distance.
Look for grace (Acts 11:23)
When you see something new in the Church this week, look first for the grace of God in it before you look for faults.
Give a second chance (Acts 15:39)
Think of someone who has failed you, and offer them a concrete opportunity to begin again.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Barnabas was rightly called the son of encouragement, for he was gentle and kind. He did not envy Paul when Paul became the greater preacher; he went to look for him and brought him to the work, seeking the good of the Church and not his own glory.
St Bede the Venerable (in substance)
Barnabas went to Tarsus to seek Saul, because he knew that the harvest at Antioch was great and needed a strong labourer. Humility seeks helpers, and charity rejoices to share the work.
St Augustine (in substance)
The love of the brethren is the sure sign of the Spirit. Where a person rejoices in the grace given to another, there the Holy Spirit dwells.
magis: Catechism 857

The Church is apostolic because she is founded on the apostles, keeps and hands on their teaching with the help of the Spirit, and continues to be taught, sanctified and guided by the apostles through their successors.
Catechism 849
The missionary mandate: having been divinely sent to the nations, the Church strives to preach the Gospel to all.
Catechism 1556
To fulfil their exalted mission, the apostles were endowed by Christ with a special outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and they passed on this gift by the laying on of hands.
Catechism 2443
God blesses those who come to the aid of the poor; when we attend to the needs of those in want, we give them what is theirs.

2027-06-11.prayer: Lord God, you chose St Barnabas, a good man full of the Holy Spirit and of faith, to encourage the young Church, to welcome Saul, to rejoice in your grace among the Gentiles, and to carry the Gospel to the nations. By his prayers make us sons and daughters of encouragement: generous with the poor, welcoming to newcomers, quick to see your grace, slow to judge, and ready to give a second chance. Send labourers into your harvest, keep them wise and innocent among dangers, and let your Spirit speak through them. Through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-06-12.title: Fourth Saturday of the Apostles
2027-06-12.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: We are the aroma of Christ to God
Moved with pity, Jesus touched the leper: “I do choose. Be made clean!”
2027-06-12.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. No saint is kept today in the First Set calendar; in the Latin calendar it is a Saturday of the tenth week in Ordinary Time. Tomorrow is the Fifth Sunday of the Apostles; St Antony of Padua (13 June) gives way to the Sunday this year.
2027-06-12.verse: Moved with pity, Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, and said to him, “I do choose. Be made clean!”
theo: Today's Gospel brings us very close to Jesus, close enough to see his hand. “A leper came to him begging him, and kneeling he said to him, ‘If you choose, you can make me clean.’” To understand the courage of this man we must remember what leprosy meant in the world of the Bible. The law said that the person with a leprous disease must wear torn clothes, cover his upper lip, and cry out, “Unclean, unclean”; “He shall live alone; his dwelling shall be outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:45–46). He was cut off from his family, from worship and from every human touch. The man in the Gospel breaks that distance. He comes near, he kneels, and he makes a prayer that is at once humble and full of faith: “If you choose, you can make me clean.” He does not doubt the power of Jesus; he only leaves the decision to his will.

Mark tells us what happened in the heart of Jesus before he speaks: “Moved with pity, Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him.” The word Mark uses for pity speaks of being moved in one's very depths, a compassion felt in the body. And then comes the gesture that no one expected: he touched him. Jesus could have healed with a word, as he did at other times. He chooses to touch first. For a man who had perhaps not been touched for years, that touch was already a healing. By the law, touching a leper made a person unclean; here the opposite happens. The uncleanness does not pass to Jesus; the holiness of Jesus passes to the man. “I do choose. Be made clean!” The prayer “if you choose” receives its answer: Jesus wills our healing. “Immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean.”

Jesus then sends the man to the priest, to offer what Moses commanded “as a testimony to them”, so that he may be received back into the community and into worship. Healing in the Gospel is never only private; it restores people to the people of God. But the man cannot keep silent. He goes out and spreads the word everywhere, so that Jesus can no longer enter a town openly and stays out in the country. There is a quiet exchange here: the man who lived outside the town can now go in, and Jesus, who touched him, must now stay outside. It is a small picture of the whole Gospel. Christ takes our place outside the camp so that we may come home. The Letter to the Hebrews will say that Jesus “suffered outside the city gate” (Hebrews 13:12) to sanctify the people by his own blood.

Paul's letter adds a lovely image for the life of an apostle. He has come to Troas, where “a door was opened for me in the Lord”, but he is restless because he cannot find Titus. Then he breaks into thanksgiving: “But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads in every place the fragrance that comes from knowing him. For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing.” In a Roman triumph, incense was burned along the route. Paul says that the apostles are like that incense: wherever they go, the fragrance of Christ goes with them. We know this from experience. Some people carry the scent of Christ into a room: patience, kindness, purity, joy. Others carry the smell of gossip, anger or greed. Paul adds that the apostles are not “peddlers of God's word”, selling a diluted message for profit, but persons of sincerity, “sent from God and standing in his presence.”

On this Saturday at the end of the fourth week of the Season of the Apostles, the two readings meet. The leper, touched by Jesus, becomes a messenger who cannot stop speaking of what was done for him. The apostle, led in Christ's procession, spreads his fragrance everywhere. Our country has known the long work of doctors, sisters and lay volunteers among people with leprosy, many of them inspired by Christ who touched the leper. There are still people around us whom society keeps outside the camp: those with stigmatised illnesses, those with disabilities, those of low caste or no status, those whose families have abandoned them. Let us ask the Lord for his pity that moves the heart and for hands that are not afraid to touch, so that our lives may be the aroma of Christ in the places where we live.
outline: Opening
A man who lived outside the camp kneels before Jesus.
Point 1 · If you choose
A humble and confident prayer.
Point 2 · He touched him
Pity that moves the heart, and a touch that heals.
Point 3 · Jesus outside the town
The exchange of places: Christ outside so that we may come home.
Point 4 · The aroma of Christ
Apostles who carry the fragrance of knowing him.
Take-home line
“I do choose. Be made clean!”
live: Pray the leper's prayer (Mark 1:40)
Bring to Jesus one area of your life that feels unclean, and say simply, “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.” Then go to confession.
Touch the untouchable (Mark 1:41)
Visit, greet or help someone whom others avoid: a person with a disfiguring illness, a disability, or a broken past.
Carry the fragrance of Christ (2 Corinthians 2:15)
Choose one way this week to change the atmosphere at home or work: no gossip, a kind word, a patient answer.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Why does he touch the leper, when he could heal with a word? To show that he is not under the law but above it, and that to the pure nothing is unclean. His hand did not become leprous; the leprous body became clean.
St Jerome (in substance)
The leper said, If you will; the Lord answered, I will. The one asked with faith, the other gave with power. Let us also kneel and say, Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.
magis: Catechism 1503

Christ's compassion toward the sick and his many healings of every kind of infirmity are a resplendent sign that God has visited his people; his compassion goes so far that he identifies himself with them.
Catechism 1421

The Lord Jesus Christ, physician of our souls and bodies, who forgave sins and restored bodily health, has willed that his Church continue in the power of the Holy Spirit his work of healing and salvation.
Catechism 1935
The equality of all persons rests on their dignity as persons; every form of social or cultural discrimination is to be curbed and eradicated as incompatible with God's design.

2027-06-12.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, moved with pity you stretched out your hand and touched the leper, and said, I do choose; be made clean. Touch us where we are unclean and ashamed, and heal us by your mercy in the sacrament of Reconciliation. Give us your compassion for those whom the world keeps outside the camp, and hands that are not afraid to touch them. Lead us in your triumph, and make us the aroma of Christ in our homes, schools and workplaces, sincere and sent from God, standing in his presence. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: The hand that touched the leper is the hand that took bread and said, This is my body. At the Holy Qurbana Jesus still touches us and makes us clean. As the incense rises at the altar, let us ask that our lives too may become the aroma of Christ to God.

2027-06-14.title: Fifth Monday of the Apostles
2027-06-14.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Suffering was to make us rely on God
2027-06-14.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The Syro-Malankara calendar remembers the prophet Elisha today.
2027-06-14.verse: I have said this to you, so that in me you may have peace. In the world you face persecution. But take courage; I have conquered the world!”
theo: The Gospel takes us back to the Upper Room on the night before the Passion. Jesus has spoken at length to his disciples, and now he says, “I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will tell you plainly of the Father.” He promises a new closeness in prayer: “On that day you will ask in my name. I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf; for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.” Jesus does not stand between us and a distant, reluctant Father, persuading him to be kind; he brings us into the Father's own love. Then he sums up his whole mission in one sentence: “I came from the Father and have come into the world; again, I am leaving the world and am going to the Father.” The disciples are delighted: “Yes, now you are speaking plainly… by this we believe that you came from God.” But Jesus knows how fragile their certainty is: “Do you now believe? The hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each one to his home, and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone because the Father is with me.” Within hours they would run from Gethsemane. And yet his last word that night is not a reproach but a promise: “I have said this to you, so that in me you may have peace. In the world you face persecution. But take courage; I have conquered the world!” He announces the victory before the battle, on the eve of the Cross. In this Season of the Apostles we know how the story continued: the men who scattered that night were gathered again by the risen Lord, filled with the Spirit at Pentecost, and sent to the ends of the earth, where they did not run away again.

Paul's letter shows us one of those apostles in the thick of the world's persecution, and he is honest about it: “We do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters, of the affliction we experienced in Asia; for we were so utterly, unbearably crushed that we despaired of life itself.” We do not know exactly what happened in the Roman province of Asia, whether it was the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19), an imprisonment or a severe illness. What we do know is that a great apostle reached the point where he could not go on. Holiness does not mean having no breaking point. Paul tells us what he learned there: “Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death so that we would rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.” The faith of Easter is not only for the end of life; it is for the hospital corridor, the failed examination, the business that collapsed, the marriage that seems dead. The God who raised Jesus from the tomb can raise us from what crushes us. Paul's hope then stretches across time: “He who rescued us from so deadly a peril will continue to rescue us; on him we have set our hope that he will rescue us again.” Past rescue becomes the ground of future trust.

Then Paul adds something that every parish should hear: “as you also join in helping us by your prayers, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.” The apostle who founded Churches asks the Churches to carry him in prayer. Prayer for one another is not a pious extra; it is real help, and when God answers, the thanksgiving too becomes common. So Jesus was not alone, because the Father was with him; and Paul was not alone, because the Church was praying. Neither are we. Our evening family prayer, the intentions of the family unit, the names read out in the parish, the Karozutha of the Holy Qurbana in which the deacon lifts up the sick and the suffering: all these are the prayers of many through which God keeps rescuing his people. Whoever is crushed today should be able to say, with Paul, I am not carrying this alone.
outline: Opening
Ask: when was I last crushed beyond my strength, and who prayed for me?
Point 1 · Crushed, so as to rely on God
Paul's affliction in Asia; the God who raises the dead.
Point 2 · The prayers of many
Helping one another by prayer; thanksgiving made in common.
Point 3 · Take courage, I have conquered the world
The scattered disciples, the Father who is with Jesus, peace in him.
Take-home line
“In me you may have peace.”
live: Rely on God who raises the dead (2 Corinthians 1:9)
Name the thing that crushes you most right now and pray each day this week: Lord, raise me up from this.
Help by your prayers (2 Corinthians 1:11)
Write down the names of three people who are suffering and pray for them each evening at family prayer this week; send one of them a message that you are praying.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The Father loves you, Jesus says, because you have loved me. But did we love first? No: he loved us so that we might love him. Our love for Christ is itself the Father's gift, and when he crowns our love he crowns his own gifts.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

See how Paul, great as he was, asks the prayers of the faithful. He teaches us that the prayers of many, even of the lowly, obtain great things from God; and he wants the thanksgiving to be made by many too, so that the favour given to one becomes a feast of praise for all.
magis: Catechism 272

Faith in God the Father almighty can be put to the test by the experience of evil and suffering; but God revealed his almighty power in the most mysterious way in the voluntary humiliation and the Resurrection of his Son, by which he conquered evil.
Catechism 2635
Intercession is a prayer of petition which leads us to pray as Jesus did; in the time of the Church, Christian intercession participates in Christ's, as an expression of the communion of saints.
Catechism 1521
Suffering, a consequence of original sin, acquires a new meaning when it is united to the saving Passion of Jesus; it becomes a participation in his saving work.

Wed 16: in the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius are listed in the calendar. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles.
