2027-06-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, on the night before you suffered you told your disciples that they would scatter and leave you alone, and still you promised them peace. Father, you were with your Son in his loneliness, and you raised him from the dead. When we are crushed beyond our strength, teach us to rely not on ourselves but on you, who raise the dead. Make us a people who carry one another in prayer, and who give thanks together for every rescue. Take courage in us, Lord, for you have conquered the world. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we celebrate the victory that Jesus announced on the eve of his Passion. The Body that was broken and the Blood that was poured out are the proof that he has conquered the world.
The whole Church prays here together, the living and the saints, so that whoever comes crushed may go out in peace.

2027-06-15.title: Fifth Tuesday of the Apostles
2027-06-15.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me
2027-06-15.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven.
2027-06-15.verse: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news brought to them.
theo: Today's Gospel opens with a sentence that fits this Season of the Apostles: “Now when Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and proclaim his message in their cities.” Matthew has just given us the great missionary discourse of chapter 10, in which Jesus sends the Twelve to proclaim the kingdom. The one who sends is himself the first missionary. Then the scene shifts to a prison. John the Baptist, who had prepared the way, is in Herod's fortress; the Jewish historian Josephus names it as Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. From his cell John hears “what the Messiah was doing,” and he sends his disciples with a question: “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?” It is a startling question from the man who had pointed to Jesus at the Jordan. John had announced an axe at the root of the trees and a fire that would burn the chaff (Matthew 3:10–12). Now he hears of a Messiah who heals, forgives and eats with sinners, while the prophet himself sits in chains. Some of the Fathers thought John asked for the sake of his disciples, so that they might go to Jesus themselves; others saw in the question the real night of a faithful man. Either way, the question is ours too, whenever God does not act as we expected.

Jesus does not answer with a title. He answers with what is happening: “Go and tell John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news brought to them.” Every phrase echoes the prophet Isaiah, who had promised that in the day of salvation “the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped” (Isaiah 35:5), and that the Anointed One would “bring good news to the oppressed” (Isaiah 61:1). John knew these Scriptures well; he would understand. The list ends not with the most spectacular sign, the raising of the dead, but with the poor hearing good news. That is the sign by which the kingdom can always be recognised, in every age and in every parish. Then comes a beatitude that is also a warning: “And blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.” The word means to stumble over something in the road. Many stumble over Jesus: over his mercy to sinners, his silence before power, his Cross, and later over the weakness of his Church. Blessed is the one who keeps walking.

Paul's letter to the Colossians deals with a different stumbling block. Some teachers in Colossae were offering a religion of rules about food and festivals, of fear of “the elemental spirits of the universe,” and of special visions. Paul says: “If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the universe, why do you live as if you still belonged to the world? Why do you submit to regulations, ‘Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch’?” Such rules “refer to things that perish with use; they are simply human commands and teachings.” They have “an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-imposed piety, humility, and severe treatment of the body, but they are of no value in checking self-indulgence.” Paul is not condemning fasting or discipline. The Church has always fasted, as our Syro-Malankara brothers and sisters begin to do tomorrow in the Apostles' Fast, and as our own Church does in the Great Fast and on Wednesdays and Fridays. What Paul rejects is discipline cut off from Christ: rules that make us proud, rituals kept out of fear of unseen powers, practices that look holy but leave the heart unchanged. A Christian who has died and risen with Christ in Baptism does not need to fear auspicious hours or the evil eye, nor to buy God's favour by human regulations. Fasting in Christ is love that trains the heart; fasting without Christ is only hunger. John's question and Paul's warning meet here: the centre of our faith is not a system of rules or a Messiah of our own design, but the person of Jesus, seen in his works of mercy and followed without stumbling.
outline: Opening
Ask: when has God not acted as I expected, and did I stumble?
Point 1 · Are you the one?
John in prison, the night of a faithful man.
Point 2 · Go and tell what you hear and see
Isaiah's signs fulfilled; the poor hear good news.
Point 3 · Died with Christ
Rules without Christ, discipline in Christ.
Take-home line
“Blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.”
live: Look for the signs (Matthew 11:4–5)
When God seems silent this week, look for one place where the poor are hearing good news, and thank God for it; better still, become that place for someone.
Discipline in Christ (Colossians 2:20–23)
Choose one small fast this week, from food, screens or complaints, and offer it consciously in union with Christ, not out of fear or for show.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

John was not ignorant of who Jesus was; but his disciples were jealous for their master and suspicious of Jesus. So John, about to die, sent them to Jesus, so that seeing his works with their own eyes they might believe and follow him. Like a good teacher, he handed his disciples on to Christ.
St Gregory the Great (in substance)

Many admired Christ's miracles but stumbled at his death. When they saw him humbled, mocked and crucified, they lost faith. Therefore he says, blessed is the one who is not scandalised in me: blessed is the one who, seeing my lowliness, still believes in my glory.
magis: Catechism 547–549

Jesus accompanied his words with mighty works, wonders and signs, which show that the kingdom is present in him and attest that he is the promised Messiah; by his signs he did not come to abolish all evils here below, but to deliver us from the greatest slavery, sin.
Catechism 2111

Superstition is the deviation of religious feeling and of the practices it imposes; it can even affect true worship, as when one attributes an importance in some way magical to certain practices, otherwise lawful, apart from the interior dispositions they demand.
Catechism 2015

The way of perfection passes by way of the Cross; there is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle; spiritual progress entails the ascesis and mortification that gradually lead to living in the peace and joy of the Beatitudes.
saints: Today

No saint's memorial is kept in the Syro-Malabar or the Latin calendar today. The Syro-Malankara calendar recalls the founding of the first church dedicated to the Holy Mother of God; tomorrow that Church begins the Apostles' Fast.
This week

13–18 June: the fifth week of the Season of the Apostles. Sun 13: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles (in the Latin calendar the memorial of St Antony of Padua gives way to the Sunday). Wed 16: in the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius are listed in the calendar. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Ahead: Thu 24 June, the Birth of John the Baptist; Tue 29 June, Sts Peter and Paul, a day of obligation.
2027-06-15.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you sent your apostles to proclaim the kingdom and you went ahead of them to teach and to heal. When we sit in the prisons of doubt and disappointment, as John did, send us your answer: open our eyes to see the blind receiving sight and the poor hearing good news. Keep us from stumbling over your humility and your Cross. You have made us die and rise with you in Baptism: take away every fear of unseen powers and every pride in our own practices, and let our fasting and prayer flow from love of you. Blessed are we if we take no offense at you. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord answers John's question again: here the One who is to come is present, humble under the signs of bread and wine. Blessed are those who do not stumble at his lowliness, but kneel and receive him.
This is the true discipline of the Christian: not human regulations, but communion with Christ who died and rose, and who changes the heart from within.

2027-06-16.title: Fifth Wednesday of the Apostles
2027-06-16.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-06-16.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. Today the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church begins the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu).
2027-06-16.verse: But law came in, with the result that the trespass multiplied; but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more,
theo: In the fifth chapter of Romans Paul sets the whole of human history between two men. “Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death came through sin, and so death spread to all because all have sinned…” The one man is Adam. Through his disobedience sin entered our race like a poison entering the bloodstream, and with sin came death, the separation that God never willed. The Church reads in this passage the revealed basis of her teaching on original sin: we are born into a wounded humanity, deprived of the holiness in which Adam was created, and every personal sin adds to the wound. But Paul's purpose is not to frighten us with Adam; it is to dazzle us with Christ. Adam, he says, “is a type of the one who was to come.” He is like a rough sketch of the true Man. And the comparison is not equal. Again and again Paul writes “much more”: if many died through one man's trespass, “much more surely have the grace of God” and his gift “abounded for the many.” Then the great parallel: “Therefore just as one man’s trespass led to condemnation for all, so one man’s act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all. For just as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous.” Adam reached for the fruit of the tree to become like God; Christ, who is God, stretched out his arms on the tree of the Cross in obedience. Our own Mar Aprem, whom we remembered last week, loved to sing of the two trees, the tree of Eden and the tree of Golgotha, and of the Second Adam who opened again the gate of Paradise.

Then Paul writes one of the most consoling sentences in the Bible: “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.” God's grace is not a small repair that barely covers the damage. It overflows. No sin of ours, no history of a family, no darkness of a nation is deeper than the grace of Christ. Paul will immediately warn that this is no excuse to go on sinning (Romans 6:1–2); grace that abounds is grace that changes us. But it means that no one in the parish, in the prison or in the hospital bed is beyond hope.

The Gospel tells the same story as a parable. Jesus speaks in the Temple, in the last days before his Passion, to the chief priests, the scribes and the elders who had questioned his authority (Mark 11:27). “A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a pit for the wine press, and built a watchtower; then he leased it to tenants and went to another country.” His hearers knew Isaiah's song of the vineyard, in which the vineyard is God's people (Isaiah 5:1–7). The owner sends servant after servant to collect his share of the fruit; they are beaten, insulted, killed. The patience of the owner is almost foolish. “He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’” The word “beloved” is the word the Father spoke over Jesus at the Jordan and on the mountain (Mark 1:11; 9:7). But the tenants reason: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” Jesus is telling his own story, and he knows how it will end. Yet he ends with the psalm: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is amazing in our eyes.” The greatest sin ever committed, the rejection and killing of the Son, became the cornerstone of our salvation. Here is Paul's “where sin increased, grace abounded” in the shape of a story. The parable was spoken to particular leaders at a particular hour, and Mark says that the crowd was on Jesus' side; the Church has always refused to turn it into a verdict on the Jewish people, then or now (Nostra Aetate 4). It is addressed to us, the tenants of the vineyard today. Our parish, our family, our own life are leased to us by the Owner, who still sends his messengers looking for fruit. As our Syro-Malankara brothers and sisters begin the Apostles' Fast today, the question is for all of us: what fruit will the Owner find?
outline: Opening
Ask: what fruit is the Owner of the vineyard looking for in my life?
Point 1 · Through one man
Adam's disobedience, sin and death spread to all.
Point 2 · Much more, grace abounded
The obedience of Christ, the Second Adam.
Point 3 · The beloved son and the rejected stone
God's patience, the Son killed, the cornerstone.
Take-home line
“Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.”
live: Grace abounding (Romans 5:20)
If a sin has weighed on you for a long time, bring it this week to the sacrament of Reconciliation and believe that grace is greater.
Give the Owner his fruit (Mark 12:2)
Choose one fruit to give God this week: an hour of prayer, a reconciliation, an alms, or a visit to someone alone.
fathers: St Irenaeus of Lyons (in substance)

As through the disobedience of one man, formed from untilled earth, the many were made sinners and lost life, so through the obedience of one Man, born of the Virgin, the many are justified and receive salvation. The Word recapitulated Adam in himself, so that what we had lost in Adam we might recover in Christ Jesus.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Christ did not only pay what we owed; he gave far more. It is as if someone found a man in prison for a small debt, paid it, and then not only set him at liberty but gave him a great fortune, made him his own son and seated him on a royal throne. Such is the grace that abounds where sin abounded.
magis: Catechism 402–404

All men are implicated in Adam's sin, as St Paul affirms (Romans 5:12, 19); original sin is a deprivation of original holiness and justice, transmitted with human nature, and it is called sin only in an analogical sense: it is contracted, not committed.
Catechism 412

Why did God not prevent the first man from sinning? St Leo the Great answers: Christ's inexpressible grace gave us blessings better than those the demon's envy had taken away. Nothing prevents human nature being raised to something greater after sin, as St Paul says: where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.
Catechism 597–598

The historical complexity of Jesus' trial must be respected; neither all Jews indiscriminately at that time, nor Jews today, can be charged with the crimes committed during his Passion. The Church teaches that sinners were the authors of Christ's sufferings, and that Christians bear the gravest responsibility.
saints: Today

No saint's memorial is kept in the Syro-Malabar or the Latin calendar today. In the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins today and ends on the feast of Sts Peter and Paul (29 June).
This week

13–18 June: the fifth week of the Season of the Apostles. Sun 13: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles (in the Latin calendar the memorial of St Antony of Padua gives way to the Sunday). Wed 16: in the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius are listed in the calendar. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Ahead: Thu 24 June, the Birth of John the Baptist; Tue 29 June, Sts Peter and Paul, a day of obligation.
2027-06-16.prayer: Lord God, through one man's disobedience sin and death entered the world, and through the obedience of your Son, the Second Adam, grace and life have abounded for all. You planted your vineyard with love and sent your servants and at last your beloved Son, whom we rejected; yet you made the rejected stone the cornerstone of our salvation. Where sin has increased in our lives, let your grace abound all the more. Make us faithful tenants of your vineyard, giving you the fruit you seek. Bless our Syro-Malankara brothers and sisters in their fast. Glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The beloved Son, thrown out of the vineyard and killed, is present on the altar as the cornerstone of the Church. The Blood that the tenants shed has become the cup of salvation.
At every Holy Qurbana the obedience of the Second Adam is offered for the many, and grace abounds where sin increased.

2027-06-17.title: Fifth Thursday of the Apostles
2027-06-17.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Called to share the glory of Christ
2027-06-17.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven.
2027-06-17.verse: It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh is useless. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.
theo: The Second Letter of Peter opens with one of the boldest sentences in the New Testament: “His divine power has given us everything needed for life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and goodness. Thus he has given us, through these things, his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may escape from the corruption that is in the world because of lust, and may become participants of the divine nature.” Participants of the divine nature: the Christian vocation is not only to be forgiven, nor only to be good, but to share in the very life of God. The Eastern Churches, our own among them, have always loved this verse. The Fathers summed it up in a famous phrase (in substance): the Son of God became what we are so that we might become what he is, not by nature but by grace. We do not cease to be creatures; we are taken up into the communion of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, as iron placed in the fire glows with the fire's heat while remaining iron. This happens first in Baptism, grows through the sacraments, above all the Holy Qurbana, and will be complete in glory.

Because God has given so much, Peter says, our response must be wholehearted: “For this very reason, you must make every effort to support your faith with goodness, and goodness with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with endurance, and endurance with godliness, and godliness with mutual affection, and mutual affection with love.” It is like a ladder, or like a chain in which each link holds the next. It begins with faith, the gift we received at the font, and it ends with love, the greatest gift. Between them stand the ordinary virtues of a Christian life: goodness in conduct, knowledge of the faith, self-control of tongue and appetite, endurance in trouble, godliness in prayer, the warm affection of brothers and sisters, and finally love that reaches even enemies. Grace and effort are not rivals here. God gives everything needed, and we must “make every effort.” Where these virtues are growing, Peter says, they “keep you from being ineffective and unfruitful.” And the one who lacks them “is short-sighted and blind, and is forgetful of the cleansing of past sins.” To forget our Baptism is to forget who we are.

The Gospel brings us to the end of the discourse on the bread of life. Jesus has said, “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood have eternal life” (John 6:54), and many of his disciples are shaken: “This teaching is difficult; who can accept it?” Jesus does not soften his words. He asks, “Does this offend you? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?” and adds, “It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh is useless. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” He is not taking back what he said about his flesh as true food. He is answering a crude, merely human way of hearing it, as if he meant pieces of meat. The flesh he gives is the flesh of the Son of Man who will ascend to the Father, filled with the life-giving Spirit. On its own, human understanding profits nothing here; only the Spirit opens the mystery. That is why, in the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, the priest prays that the Holy Spirit may come and rest upon the offering. Many disciples turned back that day (John 6:66), but Peter answered for the Twelve: “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:68). Here the two readings meet. We become participants of the divine nature above all by receiving, in the Spirit, the Body and Blood of the Son of God, and each Communion is meant to lift us one rung higher on Peter's ladder, from faith toward love.
outline: Opening
Ask: do I know that I am called to share the life of God himself?
Point 1 · Participants of the divine nature
God's power gives everything needed; becoming by grace what he is by nature.
Point 2 · From faith to love, rung by rung
Peter's ladder of virtues; grace and every effort.
Point 3 · The spirit gives life
A hard teaching, the flesh of the Son of Man, Peter's answer.
Take-home line
“The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.”
live: Make every effort (2 Peter 1:5–7)
Choose the rung of Peter's ladder where you are weakest, perhaps self-control or endurance, and practise it consciously each day this week.
Spirit and life (John 6:63)
Before your next Holy Qurbana, spend five quiet minutes asking the Holy Spirit to open your heart to the mystery you will receive.
fathers: St Athanasius of Alexandria (in substance)

The Word of God became man so that we might be made God: he showed himself through a body so that we might come to know the unseen Father, and he endured the insults of men so that we might inherit immortality. What he is by nature, we become by grace.
St Augustine (in substance)

They understood his flesh as flesh is cut up in a corpse or sold in the market, not as it is quickened by the Spirit. The flesh profits nothing, he says, but only when it is alone; let the Spirit come to the flesh, as love comes to knowledge, and it profits very much. Otherwise the Word would not have become flesh to dwell among us.
magis: Catechism 460

The Word became flesh to make us partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4); as St Athanasius says, the Son of God became man so that we might become God, and St Thomas Aquinas: the only-begotten Son, wanting to make us sharers in his divinity, assumed our nature, so that he, made man, might make men gods.
Catechism 1336

The first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the announcement of the Passion scandalised them: this is a hard saying; who can listen to it? The Eucharist and the Cross are stumbling blocks, and the question, will you also go away?, echoes through the ages as a loving invitation to discover that only he has the words of eternal life.
Catechism 1803–1804

A virtue is a habitual and firm disposition to do the good; the human virtues, acquired by effort and purified and elevated by divine grace, make possible ease, self-mastery and joy in leading a morally good life.
saints: Today
No saint's memorial is kept in the Syro-Malabar or the Latin calendar today. In the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church it is the second day of the Apostles' Fast.
This week

13–18 June: the fifth week of the Season of the Apostles. Sun 13: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles (in the Latin calendar the memorial of St Antony of Padua gives way to the Sunday). Wed 16: in the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius are listed in the calendar. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Ahead: Thu 24 June, the Birth of John the Baptist; Tue 29 June, Sts Peter and Paul, a day of obligation.
2027-06-17.prayer: Father, by your divine power you have given us everything needed for life and godliness, and you have called us to share your own divine nature. Holy Spirit, who gives life, open our hearts to the words of Jesus, which are spirit and life, and come upon the offering of our Holy Qurbana. Lord Jesus, when your teaching is hard, keep us from turning back, and let us say with Peter: to whom can we go? Help us to make every effort to add to our faith goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, mutual affection and love. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar the Spirit who gives life comes upon the bread and wine, and they become the Body and Blood of the Son of Man who ascended to the Father. Receiving him, we become partakers of the divine nature.
The words of the anaphora are spirit and life. Whoever listens to them with faith and receives the Lord with love climbs, Sunday by Sunday and day by day, from faith to love.

2027-06-18.title: Fifth Friday of the Apostles
2027-06-18.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Put to death in the flesh, made alive in the spirit
2027-06-18.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The Syro-Malankara calendar keeps the memory of Mar Aprem (St Ephrem) today; the Syro-Malabar Church remembered him on 9 June.
2027-06-18.verse: but in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be ready to make your defense to anyone who demands from you an accounting for the hope that is in you;
theo: The First Letter of Peter was written to small Christian communities scattered across Asia Minor, people who were misunderstood, slandered and sometimes mistreated by their neighbours. Peter does not tell them to hit back, nor to hide. He writes: “But even if you do suffer for doing what is right, you are blessed. Do not fear what they fear, and do not be intimidated, but in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord.” The answer to fear is to enthrone Christ in the heart. Then comes the sentence that has shaped Christian witness ever since: “Always be ready to make your defense to anyone who demands from you an accounting for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and reverence.” The word for defense gives us the word apologetics, but Peter's apologetics is not a debate to be won. It is an account of hope, given with gentleness toward the questioner and reverence toward God. Christians in India know this situation well. We are a small flock among neighbours of many faiths, and most of our neighbours are friends; yet sometimes we are asked hard questions, and in some places Christians are misunderstood or falsely accused. Peter's counsel holds: know why you hope, answer when asked, and answer kindly. “Keep your conscience clear, so that, when you are maligned, those who abuse you for your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame.” A good life is the most persuasive defense.

Peter grounds all this in the Cross, which we remember on every Friday: “For it is better to suffer for doing good, if suffering should be God’s will, than to suffer for doing evil. For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, in order to bring you to God. He was put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit.” Once for all: the sacrifice of Calvary needs no repetition, and the Holy Qurbana does not repeat it; it makes that one sacrifice present, so that we may enter into it. The righteous for the unrighteous: the innocent One suffered in place of the guilty. In order to bring you to God: the whole purpose of the Passion is reconciliation. When a Christian suffers unjustly and does not return evil for evil, he is drawn into the same pattern, and his patience becomes a quiet preaching of the Cross.

The Gospel shows us the same patience from God's side. A householder sows good seed in his field, “but while everybody was asleep, an enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and then went away.” The weed Jesus means was probably darnel, which in its early growth looks almost exactly like wheat; farmers in Kuttanad know such weeds in the young paddy. Only at heading time can the difference be seen. The servants are scandalised: “Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? Where, then, did these weeds come from?” The answer is plain: “An enemy has done this.” Evil is not God's sowing. But when they offer to pull up the weeds, the master says: “No; for in gathering the weeds you would uproot the wheat along with them. Let both of them grow together until the harvest.” Later, in the house, Jesus explains: the field is the world, the good seed the children of the kingdom, the weeds the children of the evil one, the harvest the end of the age, the reapers the angels. The judgement is real, and it is serious; but it belongs to God and to his time. Until then the Church is a field where wheat and weeds grow side by side, and the line between them runs through every human heart, including our own. The parable forbids two things: despair when we see evil in the Church and the world, and violence in the name of purity, whether by persecuting those we judge to be weeds or by cutting off brothers and sisters we have given up on. As the Fathers loved to say (in substance), today's weed may by grace become tomorrow's wheat. And it gives one great promise: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Let anyone with ears listen!”
outline: Opening
Ask: how do I respond when I am misunderstood for my faith, and when I see evil in the field?
Point 1 · Blessed when you suffer for doing right
Sanctify Christ as Lord; do not fear.
Point 2 · An account of hope, with gentleness
Peter's apologetics; Christ who suffered once for all.
Point 3 · Let both grow until the harvest
God's patience, the mixed field, the righteous who will shine.
Take-home line
“Always be ready to make your defense… yet do it with gentleness and reverence.”
live: An account of your hope (1 Peter 3:15)
Write down in three or four sentences why you are a Christian and what you hope for, so that you are ready if someone asks; then pray for that person by name.
Let both grow (Matthew 13:30)
Think of someone you have written off as a weed, in the family, the parish or at work, and pray for them each day this week instead of judging them.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

There are weeds that become wheat, and wheat that falls away. Therefore let no one who is wheat be proud, and let no one despair of anyone who seems a weed; while the field is still growing, the Lord gives time for conversion. Those who are evil today may be good tomorrow.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

By these words the Lord forbids us to take up the sword against those in error. If you were to kill them, you would fill the world with war, and many of the saints would be uprooted with them; and many who are now weeds may change and become wheat. He does not forbid us to restrain evil or to correct it, but he forbids the destruction of persons.
magis: Catechism 827

Christ, holy, innocent and undefiled, knew nothing of sin; but the Church, clasping sinners to her bosom, is at once holy and always in need of purification. All members of the Church, including her ministers, must acknowledge that they are sinners; in everyone the weeds of sin will still be mixed with the good wheat of the Gospel until the end of time.
Catechism 2472

The duty of Christians to take part in the life of the Church impels them to act as witnesses of the Gospel by word and deed; witness is an act of justice that establishes the truth or makes it known.
Catechism 1366–1367

The Eucharist is a sacrifice because it re-presents the sacrifice of the Cross; the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice: only the manner of offering is different.
saints: Today

No saint's memorial is kept in the Syro-Malabar or the Latin calendar today. The Syro-Malankara calendar remembers Mar Aprem, the deacon and teacher of Nisibis and Edessa, whom our Church honoured on 9 June. Tomorrow: Sts Gervasius and Protasius.
This week

13–18 June: the fifth week of the Season of the Apostles. Sun 13: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles (in the Latin calendar the memorial of St Antony of Padua gives way to the Sunday). Wed 16: in the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius are listed in the calendar. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Ahead: Thu 24 June, the Birth of John the Baptist; Tue 29 June, Sts Peter and Paul, a day of obligation.
2027-06-18.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. When we are misunderstood or mistreated for doing what is right, keep us from fear, and let us sanctify you as Lord in our hearts. Make us ready to give an account of our hope to anyone who asks, always with gentleness and reverence. Lord of the harvest, you are patient with the field of the world and with the field of our hearts: keep us from despair and from violence, let your grace turn weeds into wheat, and on the last day let us shine like the sun in the kingdom of your Father. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: On this Friday the one sacrifice of Christ, offered once for all on the Cross, is made present on the altar. He was put to death in the flesh and made alive in the spirit, and he comes to bring us to God.
The Lord of the harvest feeds the wheat of his field with his own Body, so that even now we may begin to shine with the light of the kingdom.

2027-06-19.title: Fifth Saturday of the Apostles · Sts Gervasius and Protasius
2027-06-19.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The law is holy, but sin seized its opportunity
2027-06-19.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations and founded the Churches. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed in place of the Queen of Heaven. Sts Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs of Milan, are listed in the First Set calendar for today without proper readings; the readings are those of the day. In the Latin calendar today is the optional memorial of St Romuald, abbot.
2027-06-19.verse: Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the treasury.
theo: Saint Paul is never more honest than in the seventh chapter of his letter to the Romans. He has just said that Christians have died to the law through the body of Christ, and he knows the objection that will come at once: is the law then something bad? “What then should we say? That the law is sin? By no means!” The law is not the enemy. It is a lamp that shows what is in the room. “If it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, ‘You shall not covet.’” Paul chooses the last of the Ten Commandments, the only one that concerns the heart rather than the hand. No court can see covetousness; only God and conscience can. And here Paul describes something every one of us has felt: “sin, seizing an opportunity in the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness.” Tell a child not to open a box, and the box becomes the most interesting thing in the house. Sin is a parasite. It has no life of its own; it lives on what is good and twists it. The same commandment that “promised life proved to be death to me,” not because the commandment was bad, but because “sin, seizing an opportunity in the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.” The word “deceived” takes us back to the garden, where the serpent used God's own command to plant suspicion in Eve's heart. Paul's verdict stands firm: “So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good.” What is wrong is not the law but the heart that cannot keep it.

Why does this matter in the Season of the Apostles? Because the law can show us the right road but cannot give us legs to walk on it. In later Jewish tradition the feast of Weeks, Pentecost, came to be remembered as the day the Law was given at Sinai. Fifty days after the Resurrection, God gave his people something the tablets of stone could not give: the Holy Spirit, writing the law of love on human hearts, as Jeremiah and Ezekiel had promised. St Augustine summed it up in a famous sentence (in substance): the law was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the law might be fulfilled. The apostles went out after Pentecost not with a longer list of rules but with the power to keep the commandments from within. The tenth commandment still stands, and it is still hard: in a world of advertisements, comparison and endless scrolling, covetousness is the air we breathe. But the Spirit who came at Pentecost is stronger than the desire that grows in the dark. Paul will cry out a few verses later, “Who will rescue me from this body of death?” and answer at once, “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:24–25).

The Gospel puts a living picture beside Paul's teaching. Jesus is in the Temple in the last days before his Passion. He warns against the scribes “who like to walk around in long robes, and to be greeted with respect in the marketplaces, and to have the best seats in the synagogues and places of honor at banquets!” We must read this carefully. Jesus is not condemning all scribes; only a few verses earlier he told a scribe who answered wisely, “You are not far from the kingdom of God” (Mark 12:34). He is warning against a temptation that lives in every religious person in every age, in priests and lay leaders, in parish committees and prayer groups: the love of being seen. Then Jesus sits down “opposite the treasury, and watched the crowd putting money into the treasury.” He watches. The rich put in large sums, and no doubt the sound of their coins was loud. “A poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which are worth a penny.” Jesus calls his disciples, as if to give them a lesson for their whole apostolic life: “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the treasury. For all of them have contributed out of their abundance; but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.” The covetous heart of Romans 7 grasps; the widow's heart lets go. She is the opposite of the scribes who “devour widows’ houses”: they take, she gives. And she gives not out of what is left over, but out of her whole life. Within a few days the Lord who watched her will give everything he has, his own body and blood, for the life of the world. The widow is the last person Jesus praises in Mark's account of his public ministry, and she is a picture of him.

Today the First Set calendar also lists Sts Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs of the early Church in Milan. Little is known of their lives. In 386, during a hard struggle between St Ambrose and the imperial court, the bishop found their bodies and laid them beneath the altar of his new basilica in Milan, saying (in substance) that the victorious victims should rest in the place where Christ is the victim. St Augustine, who was in Milan at the time and not yet baptised, recalls in his Confessions the joy of the people and the healing of a blind man. Every altar stone with relics, and every Holy Qurbana offered over the bones of the saints, recalls that day: the martyrs, like the widow, gave everything, and their offering is joined to the one sacrifice of Christ.
outline: Opening
Two pictures: a commandment that shows sin, and a widow who gives everything.
Point 1 · The law is holy
The tenth commandment and the heart that covets.
Point 2 · Grace to fulfil the law
Pentecost writes the law on the heart.
Point 3 · All she had to live on
The love of being seen, and the love that gives its whole life.
Take-home line
“She out of her poverty has put in everything she had.”
live: You shall not covet (Romans 7:7)
Name one thing you have been wanting because someone else has it. Give thanks today for three things you already have.
All she had to live on (Mark 12:44)
Give something this week that you will actually miss: time, money or comfort, quietly and without being seen.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The law was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the law might be fulfilled. It was not the fault of the law that it was not kept, but the fault of the proud mind that trusted itself.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

The widow gave two small coins, yet she was preferred to the rich, because God does not look at the amount but at the heart and the means of the giver. Let no one say, I am poor and have nothing to give: she was poorer than you, and she gave all.
magis: Catechism 1963

According to Christian tradition, the Law is holy, spiritual and good, yet still imperfect: like a tutor it shows what must be done, but does not of itself give the strength, the grace of the Spirit, to fulfil it.
Catechism 2544
Jesus enjoins his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone; the example of the poor widow of Jerusalem, who gave out of her poverty all that she had to live on, is put before them.
Catechism 2534–2535
The tenth commandment forbids greed and the desire to amass earthly goods without limit; the sensitive appetite leads us to desire what we do not have, and disordered desire must be governed.
saints: Today

Sts Gervasius and Protasius, early martyrs of Milan, whose relics St Ambrose discovered in 386 and placed beneath the altar of his basilica (listed in the First Set calendar without proper readings). Latin calendar: St Romuald (about 952–1027), abbot, founder of the Camaldolese monks, who joined the hermit's life with the common life of monks.
This week

19–24 June: the end of the fifth week and the sixth week of the Season of the Apostles. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs, are listed in the First Set calendar without proper readings; in the Latin calendar, St Romuald. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Mon 21: St Aloysius Gonzaga is listed without proper readings (in the Latin calendar an obligatory memorial). Tue 22: Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, martyrs, with proper readings. Thu 24: the Birth of John the Baptist. Then Sun 27: Seventh Sunday of the Apostles, the last Sunday of the season; Tue 29: Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles, an important feast and a day of obligation.
2027-06-19.prayer: Holy Father, your law is holy and just and good, but our hearts are weak and easily deceived. Send us the Holy Spirit whom you poured out at Pentecost, to write your commandments on our hearts and to heal the desire that grasps at what is not ours. Lord Jesus, you watched the poor widow give everything she had, and you gave your whole life for us: teach us to give without being seen and to trust you with all we have. With Sts Gervasius and Protasius and all your martyrs, may we offer ourselves with you on the altar. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: The widow put her whole life into the treasury; at the Holy Qurbana Christ places his whole life, his Body and Blood, on the altar for us. When we bring our gifts and ourselves to the altar, he does not count the coins; he looks at the heart and joins our small offering to his great one.

2027-06-21.title: Sixth Monday of the Apostles · St Aloysius Gonzaga
2027-06-21.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: How unsearchable are the ways of God
The tree is known by its fruit
2027-06-21.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations and founded the Churches. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed in place of the Queen of Heaven. St Aloysius Gonzaga is listed in the First Set calendar for today without proper readings; the readings are those of the day. In the Latin calendar today is the obligatory memorial of St Aloysius Gonzaga, religious.
2027-06-21.verse: For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.
theo: For three chapters of his letter to the Romans Paul has been wrestling with a question that pained him deeply: why had so many of his own people, the Jewish people, not accepted Jesus as the Messiah, while Gentiles were coming to faith in great numbers? He does not answer with contempt. He has just written that his people remain “beloved, for the sake of their ancestors; for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:28–29). The Second Vatican Council quoted these very words in Nostra Aetate when it taught that the Jews remain most dear to God and must never be presented as rejected or accursed. Now Paul sees the whole of history as a single story of mercy: “Just as you were once disobedient to God but have now received mercy because of their disobedience, so they have now been disobedient in order that, by the mercy shown to you, they too may now receive mercy. For God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all.” No one is saved by merit, Gentile or Jew; all are saved by mercy. And having reached that point, Paul stops arguing and begins to sing: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!”

This hymn is a lesson in humility for every believer. Paul, the greatest theologian of the apostolic Church, ends his most difficult argument not with a neat solution but with wonder: “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” “Or who has given a gift to him, to receive a gift in return?” We cannot put God in our debt, and we cannot fit his ways into our small calculations. The next verse, which closes the chapter, gives the reason: “For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory forever. Amen.” When we do not understand why a prayer seems unanswered, why a child has wandered from the faith, why a good person suffers, we are in Paul's company. The apostle does not pretend to know everything. He knows enough to trust. In the Season of the Apostles we remember that the mission to the nations was not a human plan; it was the unsearchable wisdom of God working through disobedience, persecution and scattering, until the Gospel reached even our own shores.

The Gospel brings us from the depths of God to the depths of the human heart. Some Pharisees had just said that Jesus cast out demons by the power of Beelzebul (Matthew 12:24). Jesus answers with an image every Kerala farmer understands: “Either make the tree good, and its fruit good; or make the tree bad, and its fruit bad; for the tree is known by its fruit.” A jackfruit tree does not produce bitter gourds. What comes out of us shows what is inside us. Then he speaks with the same severity as John the Baptist (Matthew 3:7): “You brood of vipers! How can you speak good things, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” Our words are fruit; the heart is the root. “The good person brings good things out of a good treasure, and the evil person brings evil things out of an evil treasure.” Then comes a sentence that should make every one of us pause: “I tell you, on the day of judgment you will have to give an account for every careless word you utter; for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” Every careless word: the gossip after the Qurbana in the church courtyard, the cruel joke about a classmate, the forwarded message we did not check, the comment typed in anger at midnight. Words are never only words. They build up or destroy reputations, families and parishes. But the remedy Jesus offers is not only to guard the tongue; it is to change the treasure of the heart. Fill the heart with the word of God, with prayer, with gratitude, and the mouth will speak from that abundance.

Today the First Set calendar lists St Aloysius Gonzaga (1568–1591), whom the Latin Church keeps as an obligatory memorial. Born the eldest son of an Italian marquis, he gave up his inheritance to his brother and entered the Society of Jesus in Rome at seventeen. During an epidemic in 1591 he carried the sick to hospital and nursed them himself; he caught the disease and died on 21 June, at twenty-three. His spiritual director was St Robert Bellarmine. A saying attributed to him sums up his life: what is this in the light of eternity? The Church has made him patron of Christian youth. In June, as schools and colleges reopen across Kerala, his short life is a good fruit from a good tree: a young man whose pure heart overflowed in service of the sick.
outline: Opening
From the depths of God to the depths of the heart.
Point 1 · O the depth
Mercy for all, and the irrevocable call of God's people.
Point 2 · The tree is known by its fruit
The heart is the root; words and deeds are the fruit.
Point 3 · Every careless word
Gossip, cruelty and forwarded messages; filling the heart's treasure.
Take-home line
“For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”
live: To him be the glory (Romans 11:36)
When something you cannot understand troubles you today, pray Paul's words: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!”
Every careless word (Matthew 12:36)
For one day, speak no word about an absent person that you would not say in their presence, and forward no message you have not checked.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Love, and do what you will. If you keep silence, keep silence out of love; if you speak, speak out of love; if you correct, correct out of love. Let the root of love be within, for from that root nothing can spring but what is good.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

The tongue is a member given to us to praise God and to build up our neighbour. If we use it for slander and for abuse, we turn the instrument of praise into a weapon, and the Lord will ask us to account for it.
magis: Catechism 314

We firmly believe that God is master of the world and of its history; but the ways of his providence are often unknown to us. Only at the end, when we see God face to face, will we fully know the ways by which he has guided creation.
Catechism 839

The relationship of the Church to the Jewish people: unlike other non-Christian religions, the Jewish faith is already a response to God's revelation in the Old Covenant; to them belong the sonship, the glory, the covenants, for the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable.
Catechism 2477–2479
Respect for the reputation of persons forbids rash judgment, detraction and calumny; everyone should be careful to interpret the thoughts, words and deeds of the neighbour in a favourable way.
saints: Today

St Aloysius Gonzaga (1568–1591), religious of the Society of Jesus, who died at twenty-three after nursing the sick in Rome; patron of Christian youth (listed in the First Set calendar without proper readings; an obligatory memorial in the Latin calendar).
This week

19–24 June: the end of the fifth week and the sixth week of the Season of the Apostles. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs, are listed in the First Set calendar without proper readings; in the Latin calendar, St Romuald. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Mon 21: St Aloysius Gonzaga is listed without proper readings (in the Latin calendar an obligatory memorial). Tue 22: Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, martyrs, with proper readings. Thu 24: the Birth of John the Baptist. Then Sun 27: Seventh Sunday of the Apostles, the last Sunday of the season; Tue 29: Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles, an important feast and a day of obligation.
2027-06-21.prayer: O God, how deep are your riches and wisdom and knowledge, how unsearchable your judgments and how inscrutable your ways! You have shown mercy to all, and your gifts and calling are irrevocable. Teach us to trust you where we cannot understand. Lord Jesus, you know the heart from which our words come: make the tree good, so that its fruit may be good; fill the treasure of our hearts with your word, and keep our tongues from careless and wounding speech. Through the prayers of St Aloysius Gonzaga, give our young people pure hearts and generous hands. For from you and through you and to you are all things: to you be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Word of God is placed on our tongues. The same mouth that receives the Body of Christ is called to speak words of blessing; may the abundance of the heart he fills overflow today in words that heal.

2027-06-22.title: Sixth Tuesday of the Apostles · Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, Martyrs
2027-06-22.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: We have a house eternal in the heavens
The lamp is not put under a basket
Epistle (Sts John Fisher and Thomas More)
If you suffer as a Christian, glorify God
Gospel (Sts John Fisher and Thomas More)
The one who endures to the end will be saved
2027-06-22.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations and founded the Churches. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed in place of the Queen of Heaven. The First Set calendar lists Sts John Fisher and Thomas More (the calendar prints “Moore”) with the proper readings given above, besides the readings of the Sixth Tuesday of the Apostles. In the Latin calendar they are an optional memorial today, together with St Paulinus of Nola. Follow the direction of the eparchy and parish on which readings are used (verify locally).
2027-06-22.verse: Yet if any of you suffers as a Christian, do not consider it a disgrace, but glorify God because you bear this name.
theo: Saint Paul knew about tents. Luke tells us that in Corinth he lodged with Aquila and Priscilla, “and they worked together, by trade they were tentmakers” (Acts 18:3). So when he writes to the same Corinthians about death and eternal life, he reaches for the image he knew best: “For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.” A tent is good, but it is temporary; it is pitched for a journey and folded at the end. Our bodies are such tents. They grow tired, they are wounded, and one day they are taken down. Paul does not despise the tent; he groans in it, “longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling”, not to be stripped bare but to be “further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.” This is the Christian hope: not escape from the body but its transformation in the resurrection. And the pledge of it is already given: “He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.” The Greek word means a first instalment, the advance payment that promises the rest. The Spirit poured out at Pentecost is God's down payment on our eternal home. Therefore, says Paul, “we are always confident… for we walk by faith, not by sight.”

The Gospel turns to a lamp. “Is a lamp brought in to be put under the bushel basket, or under the bed, and not on the lampstand?” Every Kerala home once had its nilavilakku, lit at dusk, set high in the front room so that its light would reach every corner. No one lights a lamp to hide it. The faith given to us at baptism, when a lighted candle was placed in our parents' hands, is not meant to be hidden under the bed of private feeling. “For there is nothing hidden, except to be disclosed; nor is anything secret, except to come to light.” Jesus adds a warning about how we listen: “Pay attention to what you hear; the measure you give will be the measure you get, and still more will be given you.” Those who give themselves generously to the word receive more light; those who hold back find even the little they have growing dim.

Today the First Set calendar honours two men who would not put their lamp under a basket, though it cost them their lives: St John Fisher and St Thomas More, martyrs of England in 1535. When King Henry VIII broke with Rome and had himself declared Supreme Head of the Church in England, the oath that was demanded of his subjects touched both his second marriage and the authority of the Pope. John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, a learned and austere pastor, refused it; he was the only bishop of England to stand firm. While he lay in the Tower of London, Pope Paul III named him a cardinal. He was beheaded on 22 June 1535. It is told that on the way to execution he opened his New Testament and his eyes fell on the words, “And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Thomas More was a layman: a lawyer, a scholar, a loving husband and father, the friend of the king and once his Lord Chancellor, famous for his wit and for his book Utopia. He did not seek martyrdom. For more than a year in the Tower he kept silent and used every honest means the law allowed. But he would not swear against his conscience, and he was condemned for treason on false testimony and beheaded on 6 July 1535, declaring, according to the reports of the time, that he died the king's good servant, but God's first. Pope Pius XI canonised them together in 1935, and in 2000 St John Paul II named Thomas More patron of statesmen and politicians.

The readings of their commemoration describe their road. Peter writes to Christians facing hostility: “Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal that is taking place among you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you are sharing Christ’s sufferings”. He draws a sharp line: let none of you suffer as a criminal, “Yet if any of you suffers as a Christian, do not consider it a disgrace, but glorify God because you bear this name.” Fisher and More were not rebels; they honoured the king in everything that was the king's. They suffered only for the name. And Jesus had warned the Twelve: “See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves… you will be dragged before governors and kings because of me”. More was wise as a serpent in his careful silence and innocent as a dove in his refusal to lie. Both found that the promise held: “what you are to say will be given to you at that time; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.” In our own time, Christians in many lands, and in some places in our own country, pay a price for their faith; Christians in public life in India face daily pressures to bend their conscience. Today's martyrs remind them, and us, that a well-formed conscience is a lamp that must not be hidden, and that the earthly tent may be taken down, but the house from God is eternal. “The one who endures to the end will be saved.”
outline: Opening
A tentmaker writes about tents; two martyrs who did not hide their lamp.
Point 1 · A house not made with hands
The tent of the body, the groan of hope, the Spirit as guarantee.
Point 2 · The lamp on the lampstand
Faith is not hidden; the measure we give.
Point 3 · The king's good servant, but God's first
Fisher and More: conscience, courage and the Spirit who speaks.
Take-home line
“If any of you suffers as a Christian… glorify God because you bear this name.”
live: Walk by faith (2 Corinthians 5:7)
When fear of illness or death troubles you today, pray: “Lord, you have given me the Spirit as a guarantee.”
Put the lamp on the lampstand (Mark 4:21)
Do not hide your faith this week: make the sign of the cross before a meal in public, or speak up kindly for what is right at work or school.
fathers: St Ignatius of Antioch (in substance)

I am writing to all the Churches that I die willingly for God, unless you hinder me. Let me be food for the wild beasts, through whom I may reach God. I am the wheat of God, and I am ground by the teeth of the beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ.
Tertullian (in substance)
Your cruelty does not succeed. It is rather an attraction to our religion. The more you mow us down, the more we grow: the blood of Christians is seed.
magis: Catechism 2473
Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith: it means bearing witness even unto death. The martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity.
Catechism 2242

The citizen is obliged in conscience not to follow the directives of civil authorities when they are contrary to the demands of the moral order, to the fundamental rights of persons or the teachings of the Gospel: “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (Acts 5:29).
Catechism 1776

Deep within his conscience man discovers a law which he has not laid upon himself but which he must obey; conscience is man's most secret core and sanctuary, where he is alone with God, whose voice echoes in his depths.
saints: Today

Sts John Fisher (1469–1535), Bishop of Rochester and cardinal, and Thomas More (1478–1535), layman, husband and father, Lord Chancellor of England, martyrs, canonised together in 1935; St Thomas More is patron of statesmen and politicians (First Set calendar, with proper readings).
