2027-06-22.prayer: Lord God, you have given us the Holy Spirit as the guarantee of an eternal home not made with hands. While we live in this tent of the body, teach us to walk by faith and not by sight. Lord Jesus, you sent your apostles like sheep among wolves and promised them your Spirit when they stood before governors and kings: as you gave St John Fisher and St Thomas More the courage to keep faith and conscience even unto death, give us the grace to set our lamp on the lampstand, to serve our country faithfully and you above all. Strengthen those who suffer for your name today, and bring us all to the house of the Father. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: Every Holy Qurbana is offered in communion with the martyrs, who gave their bodies as Christ gave his. The Body we receive is the pledge of the house not made with hands; nourished by it, the martyrs walked to the scaffold, and we walk by faith through our own trials.

2027-06-23.title: Sixth Wednesday of the Apostles
2027-06-23.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The parable of the lost coin
2027-06-23.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations and founded the Churches. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed in place of the Queen of Heaven. Tomorrow the Church celebrates the Birth of John the Baptist; in the Latin Church the Vigil Mass of the solemnity is celebrated this evening.
2027-06-23.verse: Just so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.
theo: Paul had promised to visit Corinth, and then changed his plans. Some in the community seized on it: here is a man who says yes and no in the same breath; how can we trust his gospel? The opening of his second letter is his answer, and it is a lesson in integrity for every pastor and every Christian. “Indeed, this is our boast, the testimony of our conscience: we have behaved in the world with frankness and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and all the more toward you.” Paul's boast is not his eloquence, his miracles or the number of his converts. It is a clear conscience. The word translated ‘sincerity’ is sometimes explained as something held up to the sunlight and found without a flaw. Paul has nothing to hide: “For we write you nothing other than what you can read and also understand”. No double meanings, no hidden agenda, no smooth words that say one thing and intend another. And this integrity is not his own achievement; it comes “by the grace of God.”

Then Paul says something tender about the bond between an apostle and his people: “on the day of the Lord Jesus we are your boast even as you are our boast.” On the last day, a pastor will not be proud of his buildings or his projects but of his people, and a people will be proud of a pastor who was honest with them. In this Season of the Apostles we pray for our priests and bishops, that they may be able to say with Paul that they have behaved among us with frankness and godly sincerity; and we pray for ourselves as a parish, that we may be their joy on that day. Integrity is also asked of every lay Christian: in the account books of a shop, in the marks of an examination, in the promises of a marriage. A yes that is truly yes is the beginning of holiness.

The Gospel is the second of the three parables of the lost in Luke 15. They are told because “the tax collectors and sinners were coming near to listen to him. And the Pharisees and the scribes were grumbling and saying, ‘This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them.’” Luke also shows Jesus eating in the homes of Pharisees (Luke 14:1); he is not against them. But he wants every listener, in every age, to see the heart of God. “Or what woman having ten silver coins, if she loses one of them, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?” Think of a village house in the old days, with small windows and an earthen floor, and a woman on her knees with a lamp and a broom, moving every mat and pot, refusing to rest until she hears the clink of the coin. A silver coin was about a day's wage for a labourer; for a poor woman, one coin in ten mattered greatly. Jesus dares to compare God to this woman. God is not only the shepherd who goes out into the hills; he is also the housewife who searches the corners of her own home. Some of the lost are far away in the wilderness; others are lost inside the house, inside the parish, inside the family, unnoticed in a dark corner. The coin cannot search for itself; it can only be found. And when it is found, she does not keep her joy private: “she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’ Just so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”

The Fathers noticed that the coin bears the image of the king. St Gregory the Great saw in it the image of God stamped on every human being; sin covers the image with dust, but does not erase it. Tomorrow the Church celebrates the Birth of John the Baptist, whose whole mission was to call people to repentance and to prepare the way for the One who came to seek and to save the lost. On the eve of his feast, let us light a lamp in our own house: examine our conscience, sweep away what hides the image of God in us, and go to the sacrament of Reconciliation, where heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents.
outline: Opening
A man accused of saying yes and no; a woman who will not stop searching.
Point 1 · The testimony of our conscience
Frankness, godly sincerity, and grace.
Point 2 · You are our boast
The bond of pastors and people on the day of the Lord.
Point 3 · She lights a lamp and searches
God who searches the corners of his house; the coin that bears the king's image.
Take-home line
“There is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”
live: Godly sincerity (2 Corinthians 1:12)
Check one area of your life today, money, studies or work, and correct one thing that would not bear the sunlight.
Search carefully (Luke 15:8)
Think of someone who has drifted from the Church or from your family. Call, visit or write to them this week, without reproach.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)

The woman who has ten coins is the Wisdom of God. She lost one when man, created in God's image, went astray. She lit a lamp when Wisdom appeared in our flesh, for a lamp is light in an earthen vessel. She swept the house when the conscience of sinners was stirred. And the coin is found when the image of the Creator is restored in us.
St Ambrose (in substance)
Who are this father, this shepherd and this woman? Are they not God the Father, Christ and the Church? Christ carries you on his own shoulders; the Church searches for you; the Father receives you.
magis: Catechism 545

Jesus invites sinners to the table of the kingdom: “For I have come to call not the righteous but sinners” (Matthew 9:13). He invites them to that conversion without which one cannot enter the kingdom, and shows them in word and deed his Father's boundless mercy for them and the vast joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.
Catechism 1778

Conscience is a judgment of reason whereby the human person recognises the moral quality of a concrete act; in all he says and does, man is obliged to follow faithfully what he knows to be just and right.
Catechism 1439

The process of conversion and repentance was described by Jesus in the parables of mercy: the fascination of an illusory liberty, the realisation of what has been lost, the decision to return, and the generous welcome of the Father, with the festive joy of the household.
saints: Today
Sixth Wednesday of the Apostles. In the Latin Church, the Vigil Mass of the Nativity of St John the Baptist is celebrated this evening.
This week

19–24 June: the end of the fifth week and the sixth week of the Season of the Apostles. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs, are listed in the First Set calendar without proper readings; in the Latin calendar, St Romuald. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Mon 21: St Aloysius Gonzaga is listed without proper readings (in the Latin calendar an obligatory memorial). Tue 22: Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, martyrs, with proper readings. Thu 24: the Birth of John the Baptist. Then Sun 27: Seventh Sunday of the Apostles, the last Sunday of the season; Tue 29: Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles, an important feast and a day of obligation.
2027-06-23.prayer: Lord God, you search for every one of your children as a woman searches her house for a lost coin, and you rejoice with all your angels over one sinner who repents. Light the lamp of your Word in us, sweep away the dust that hides your image in our souls, and bring back to you all who are lost, near or far. Give our pastors and our people frankness and godly sincerity, so that on the day of the Lord Jesus we may be each other's joy. On the eve of the birth of John the Baptist, prepare our hearts for conversion. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: The Holy Qurbana is the feast of the household that has found what was lost. When the priest raises the Body of Christ, heaven and earth rejoice together; every communion received with a contrite heart is a share in the joy of the angels over one sinner who repents.

2027-06-24.title: Sixth Thursday of the Apostles · The Birth of John the Baptist
2027-06-24.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Nathan says to David: You are the man
Before I formed you in the womb I knew you
When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son
The birth and naming of John
2027-06-24.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations and founded the Churches. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed in place of the Queen of Heaven. The Birth of John the Baptist is listed in the First Set calendar with the four readings above. Weekday readings of the Sixth Thursday of the Apostles: Romans 11:1–10 (a remnant chosen by grace); Mark 10:46–52 (Jesus heals Bartimaeus). The Latin Church keeps the Nativity of St John the Baptist today as a solemnity. Follow the direction of the eparchy and parish on which readings are used (verify locally).
2027-06-24.verse: All who heard them pondered them and said, “What then will this child become?” For, indeed, the hand of the Lord was with him.
theo: The Church keeps the birthdays of very few people. Of most saints she celebrates the day of their death, their birth into heaven. But she celebrates the birth of the Lord at Christmas, the birth of his Mother, and, from the earliest centuries, the birth of John the Baptist. St Augustine already remarked on it: the Church celebrates the birth of no prophet, patriarch or apostle, except this one. The reason is in the Gospel itself. The angel had told Zechariah, “many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great in the sight of the Lord… even before his birth he will be filled with the Holy Spirit” (Luke 1:14–15). John's birth is already part of the Gospel. Six months before Christmas, in the season when the days in the northern lands begin to grow shorter, we keep the birth of the one who said of Christ, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). The Syriac tradition calls him Yohannan Mamdana, John the Baptiser, and our Church honours him among the greatest of the saints: Jesus himself said, “among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:11).

Luke tells the birth simply and joyfully: “Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown his great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.” An old woman who had borne the shame of childlessness for a lifetime now holds her son, and the whole village of the hill country shares her joy. Mary had stayed with her about three months (Luke 1:56); the two mothers had already rejoiced together when the unborn John leaped at the sound of Mary's greeting. Then comes the naming. On the eighth day the relatives want to call the child Zechariah after his father, as custom expected. Elizabeth says, “No; he is to be called John.” They object: “None of your relatives has this name.” Zechariah, who had been mute since he doubted the angel's word, “asked for a writing tablet and wrote, ‘His name is John.’ And all of them were amazed.” The name means ‘the Lord has been gracious’. The child does not belong to the family's plans or traditions; he belongs to God's plan. And the moment Zechariah obeys, “Immediately his mouth was opened… and he began to speak, praising God.” Doubt had silenced him; obedience gives him back his voice. Fear and wonder spread through the hill country, and everyone asks the question that every parent asks over a cradle: “What then will this child become?” Luke answers: “For, indeed, the hand of the Lord was with him.”

The reading from Jeremiah shows that John's vocation began before his birth: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations.” These words, spoken to Jeremiah, fit John perfectly, and they speak to every human life. Each child in the womb is already known and loved by God; this is why the Church defends human life from conception. Jeremiah protests, “Truly I do not know how to speak, for I am only a boy.” God answers by touching his mouth: “Now I have put my words in your mouth.” John will be “the voice of one crying out in the wilderness” (John 1:23). And God gives the young prophet strength for the struggle ahead: “I for my part have made you today a fortified city, an iron pillar, and a bronze wall… They will fight against you; but they shall not prevail against you, for I am with you, says the Lord, to deliver you.” John needed that strength when he stood before Herod.

That is why the First Set places beside the feast the story of Nathan and David. King David has taken Uriah's wife and arranged Uriah's death. God sends the prophet Nathan, who tells a story of a rich man with many flocks who takes the one little lamb of a poor man, the lamb that “used to eat of his meager fare, and drink from his cup, and lie in his bosom, and it was like a daughter to him.” David burns with anger: the man deserves to die! “Nathan said to David, ‘You are the man!’” A prophet does not flatter kings. A thousand years later John would tell another king, Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6:18), and it would cost him his head. There is another link: Nathan's parable turns on a stolen lamb; John's great word will be to point to the Lamb who is not stolen but given of his own will: “Here is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). David repented when he heard the truth; Herod imprisoned the one who told it. The feast asks us which we will be when the voice of conscience says, ‘You are the man.’

Paul's letter to the Galatians places John at the hinge of history. Heirs who are minors are “no better than slaves… they remain under guardians and trustees until the date set by the father.” Then: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as children.” John is the last of the guardians, the greatest of the prophets standing at the door of the fullness of time: “The law and the prophets were in effect until John came” (Luke 16:16). He does not keep the people for himself; he hands them over to the Bridegroom. Through the Son born of the Virgin Mary, and through the Spirit who cries “Abba! Father!” in our hearts, we are no longer slaves but children and heirs. The weekday readings, which the parish may also hear, fit the feast: Paul speaks of “a remnant, chosen by grace” (Romans 11:5), and in Mark blind Bartimaeus hears the call, “Take heart; get up, he is calling you” (Mark 10:49), throws off his cloak and follows Jesus on the way. That is what John lived for: to prepare a people, open their eyes, and send them after Jesus. In this Season of the Apostles, John reminds every apostle, bishop, priest, catechist and parent: point to Christ, then step aside.
conn: Filled with the Spirit before birth.
The angel said of John, “even before his birth he will be filled with the Holy Spirit” (Luke 1:15); at Mary's greeting “the child leaped in her womb” (Luke 1:41).
Named before birth.
“The Lord called me before I was born, while I was in my mother’s womb he named me” (Isaiah 49:1); the angel: “you will name him John” (Luke 1:13).
The spirit of Elijah.
“Lo, I will send you the prophet Elijah before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes” (Malachi 4:5); John will go before the Lord “With the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17).
You are the man.
As Nathan rebuked David, John rebuked Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6:18).
The lamb.
Nathan's parable of the poor man's lamb finds its fulfilment when John points to Jesus: “Here is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29).
The voice.
“A voice cries out: ‘In the wilderness prepare the way of the Lord’” (Isaiah 40:3); John: “I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness” (John 1:23).
He must decrease.
“He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).
altar: Zechariah's mouth was opened and he blessed God; at the Holy Qurbana the Church opens her mouth in the great thanksgiving, and the Lord whom John announced comes among us.

Before communion we hear, in the words of John, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. The prophet who pointed to the Lamb by the Jordan points us still to the altar, where the Lamb is given for the life of the world.
outline: Opening
A birthday the Church celebrates: John, the one who must decrease.
Point 1 · Before I formed you in the womb
Known, consecrated and named by God before birth.
Point 2 · His name is John
Not the family's plan but God's grace; obedience opens Zechariah's mouth.
Point 3 · You are the man
The prophet who speaks truth to kings, and the Lamb he points to.
Point 4 · The fullness of time
The last of the prophets hands us over to the Son; we become children and heirs.
Closing image
An old man with a writing tablet, his tongue loosened, singing God's praise over a cradle.
Take-home line
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
live: Known before birth (Jeremiah 1:5)
Pray today for expectant mothers, for unborn children and for those tempted to end a pregnancy; support a family expecting a child.
His name is John (Luke 1:63)
Learn the meaning of your own baptismal name and the life of your patron saint, and thank God for calling you by name.
You are the man (2 Samuel 12:7)
When your conscience speaks this week, do not argue with it; go to confession.
Point to Christ (John 1:29)
In one conversation this week, speak of Jesus rather than yourself.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The Church celebrates the birth of no prophet, no patriarch, no apostle, except two: the birth of John and the birth of Christ. John was born when the days begin to shorten, Christ when they begin to lengthen, as John said: He must increase, but I must decrease. John was the voice; Christ was the Word. The voice passes; the Word remains.
St Ambrose (in substance)

The birth of a saint brings joy to many, for it is a common good. Righteousness is a virtue for all; and so at the birth of a righteous man a sign of his future life is given, and the neighbours rejoice.
St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)
The barren woman gave birth to the voice, and the Virgin to the Word. The voice went before to prepare the way, and the Word followed to fill the world with life.
magis: Catechism 523

St John the Baptist is the Lord's immediate precursor, sent to prepare his way. Prophet of the Most High, he surpasses all the prophets, of whom he is the last; he inaugurates the Gospel, already from his mother's womb welcomes the coming of Christ, and rejoices in being the friend of the bridegroom.
Catechism 719

John the Baptist is more than a prophet. In him the Holy Spirit concludes his speaking through the prophets; John completes the cycle of prophets begun by Elijah and proclaims the imminence of the consolation of Israel.
Catechism 2270
Human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you.”
Catechism 2158
God calls each one by name. Everyone's name is sacred. The name is the icon of the person and demands respect as a sign of the dignity of the one who bears it.
saints: Today
The Birth of John the Baptist (Yohannan Mamdana), listed in the First Set calendar with proper readings; in the Latin calendar the solemnity of the Nativity of St John the Baptist.
Next days
Sun 27: Seventh Sunday of the Apostles, the last Sunday of the season (Kaitha begins on 4 July). Tue 29: Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles, an important feast and a day of obligation.
2027-06-24.prayer: Lord God, before John was formed in the womb you knew him, before he was born you consecrated him, and you filled him with the Holy Spirit to prepare a people for your Son. On this day of his birth we rejoice with Elizabeth and Zechariah and all their neighbours, for you have shown your great mercy. Open our mouths, as you opened the mouth of Zechariah, to bless you; give us the courage of John to speak the truth to the great and the small; and teach us to point to the Lamb of God and to decrease, so that he may increase in us. Protect every child in the womb, bless every name given in baptism, and make us your children and heirs through the Spirit who cries “Abba, Father” in our hearts. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.

2027-06-25.title: Sixth Friday of the Apostles
2027-06-25.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Give to the emperor what is the emperor's, and to God what is God's
2027-06-25.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar's own headings: “All powers are from God”; “Give to Caesar what is to him”.
2027-06-25.verse: They answered, “The emperor’s.” Then he said to them, “Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
theo: In the last week of the Season of the Apostles the readings turn to a question that every disciple faces in the street, in the office and at the ballot box: how does a Christian live under earthly government? The Gospel begins with a trap. “Then the Pharisees went and plotted to entrap him in what he said.” They send their disciples together with the Herodians, the party that supported the house of Herod and therefore Roman rule. The two groups did not normally agree, but they agree now against Jesus. They begin with flattery: “Teacher, we know that you are sincere, and teach the way of God in accordance with truth, and show deference to no one.” Then the question: “Is it lawful to pay taxes to the emperor, or not?” If Jesus says yes, he loses the crowds who hate the Roman tax; if he says no, the Herodians can report him to the governor as a rebel. Jesus, “aware of their malice”, asks for the coin used for the tax. They produce a denarius. The detail matters: they carry Caesar's coin, with Caesar's image and an inscription calling him a son of a god, even into the precincts of the Temple. “Whose head is this, and whose title?” “The emperor’s.” “Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

The answer is not a clever escape. It draws a line through every human life. The coin bears the emperor's image, so give it back to him: pay what is due, take part in the life of the city, respect the law. But the human person bears another image. “So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them” (Genesis 1:27). If the coin belongs to the one whose image it carries, then you belong wholly to God, whose image you carry. Caesar may ask for taxes; he may not ask for your soul. The early Christians lived exactly this way. They paid taxes and prayed for the emperors, but they refused to offer incense before the emperor's statue, and many died for that refusal. Peter and the apostles, who will be honoured on Tuesday, had already said it before the council in Jerusalem: “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (Acts 5:29).

Paul's letter to the Romans, written to Christians living in the capital of the empire, gives the other side of the teaching. “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities; for there is no authority except from God, and those authorities that exist have been instituted by God.” Paul is not praising Nero, nor saying that every ruler is good. He is saying that order in society, law, courts and public service are part of God's providence for human life; without them the weak are devoured by the strong. The ruler is “God’s servant for your good”. That phrase is both an honour and a judgment: authority exists for the good of the people, and it will answer to God for how it serves. Then comes a very ordinary instruction: “For the same reason you also pay taxes, for the authorities are God’s servants, busy with this very thing.” Honest taxes, honest bills, no bribe to the officer and no bribe taken from the citizen: these are part of Christian holiness. Paul adds that we obey “not only because of wrath but also because of conscience”. A Christian is honest not only when a camera is watching but because God sees.

For Christians in India this teaching is very practical. We live in a great democracy, among neighbours of many faiths. We are called to be good citizens: to vote with a formed conscience, to pay our taxes, to keep the traffic rules, to refuse the small corruption that has become normal, and to serve in public office with clean hands. At the same time we pray for those in authority, as Paul asked Timothy to pray “for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and dignity” (1 Timothy 2:2). And when a law or an order commands what God forbids, the Christian answers with Peter and with the martyrs: God first. On this Friday of the Season of the Apostles let us give back to Caesar the coin, and give back to God ourselves.
outline: Opening
A coin in the hand: whose image is on it, and whose image is on me?
Point 1 · All authority is from God
Order and law as God's providence; the ruler as God's servant for the good of the people.
Point 2 · Give to God what is God's
We bear God's image: we belong wholly to him.
Point 3 · Conscience and its limits
Honest citizens, praying for rulers, and God first when a law commands sin.
Take-home line
“Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
live: Pay what is due (Romans 13:6–7)
Check one area this week where you may be cutting corners: a tax, a bill, a ticket, a small bribe. Put it right.
Give yourself to God (Matthew 22:21)
Before sleep each night this week, offer the whole day back to God in a short prayer: “All that I am is yours.”
fathers: St Justin Martyr (in substance)

We pay the taxes and contributions to those appointed by you before all others, as Christ taught us. We worship God alone, but in other things we gladly serve you, acknowledging you as rulers and praying that with royal power you may also be found to have sound judgment.
St Augustine (in substance)

Caesar looks for his image on the coin; God looks for his image in you. As Caesar demands his coin back, so God demands back the soul he has stamped with his likeness. Give Caesar his money; give God yourself.
magis: Catechism 2238

Those subject to authority should regard those in authority as representatives of God; their loyal collaboration includes the right, and at times the duty, to voice their just criticisms of what seems harmful to the dignity of persons and the good of the community.
Catechism 2240
Submission to authority and co-responsibility for the common good make it morally obligatory to pay taxes, to exercise the right to vote and to defend one's country.
Catechism 2242

The citizen is obliged in conscience not to follow the directives of civil authorities when they are contrary to the demands of the moral order, to the fundamental rights of persons or the teachings of the Gospel: we must obey God rather than men.
saints: Today
Sixth Friday of the Apostles. June is the month of the Sacred Heart in popular devotion; many families pray the litany of the Sacred Heart in the evening prayer this month.
This week

25–30 June: sixth and seventh weeks of the Season of the Apostles. Sun 27: Seventh Sunday of the Apostles, the last Sunday of the season. 2027-06-25.prayer: Lord God, you are the source of all authority, and every human being bears your image. Bless our country and all who govern it, from the village panchayat to the Parliament; give them wisdom, honesty and a care for the poor. Make us good citizens, honest in our taxes and duties and faithful to our conscience. Keep us from every form of corruption, and give us courage, like your apostles and martyrs, to obey you first when the world asks what you forbid. We give back to you ourselves, made in your image, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with you and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, for ever. Amen.

2027-06-26.title: Sixth Saturday of the Apostles
2027-06-26.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: I promised you in marriage to one husband, Christ
2027-06-26.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar's own headings: “You are betrothed to Christ”; “Do not judge by appearances”. Saturday is kept in many homes as Mary's day.
2027-06-26.verse: Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.
theo: Paul writes to the Corinthians like a father who has arranged his daughter's marriage and now fears for her. “I feel a divine jealousy for you, for I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” In the customs of the time, the friend of the bridegroom arranged the betrothal and watched over the bride until the wedding day. Paul sees himself in that role: by his preaching he betrothed the Church of Corinth to Christ, and he longs to present her pure on the day of the Lord's coming. His jealousy is “divine”, the jealousy of God himself, who in the prophets calls Israel his bride: “I will take you for my wife forever; I will take you for my wife in righteousness and in justice, in steadfast love, and in mercy” (Hosea 2:19). The Church is not a club of the like-minded; she is a bride, loved and promised to one Husband. Our Syro-Malabar liturgy speaks often of the Church as the bride of Christ, and the crowning of bride and groom at a wedding is a living picture of that mystery.

Then comes the fear: “But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.” The danger is not that the Corinthians will abandon religion; it is that they will accept “another Jesus”, “a different spirit”, “a different gospel”, and hardly notice. Certain preachers, whom Paul calls with irony “these super-apostles”, had arrived with fine speech and impressive letters. They offered a Jesus without the Cross, a spirit without humility, a gospel of success. Paul admits, “I may be untrained in speech, but not in knowledge.” The question is never how eloquent the preacher is, but whether the Jesus he preaches is the Jesus of the apostles. In this last week of the Season of the Apostles the warning is timely. Our phones bring us a new preacher every hour; some promise wealth and healing as a reward for money, some mock the Church and the sacraments, some offer a Jesus who never asks for repentance. The bride keeps her devotion sincere and pure by staying with the faith of the apostles, handed down in the Church.

The Gospel takes us to Jerusalem at the Festival of Booths. Jesus goes up to the Temple and teaches, and those who hear him are astonished: “How does this man have such learning, when he has never been taught?” He had not studied under a famous rabbi. In John's Gospel the phrase “the Jews” often refers to the religious authorities of Jerusalem who opposed Jesus; it never condemns the Jewish people as a whole, to whom Jesus, his Mother and all the apostles belonged. Jesus answers: “My teaching is not mine but his who sent me.” Here is the test of every true teacher. “Those who speak on their own seek their own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true.” Jesus himself, the eternal Word, does not present his teaching as his own invention; it is the Father's. How much more must every preacher, priest and catechist in the Church hand on what was received, and not his own opinions.

Then Jesus speaks of the healing he had done on a sabbath (John 5), which had caused such anger. He reasons with them from their own practice: if a boy may be circumcised on the sabbath so that the law of Moses is kept, why be angry that he made a man's whole body well on the sabbath? And he ends with the line that is today's word: “Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.” The crowd judged by appearances: the man had no degree, so he could not be a teacher; the healing happened on the wrong day, so it could not be from God. We do the same when we judge people by colour, caste, accent, dress, bank balance or the size of their house, or when we decide about a marriage proposal by a photograph. The Lord said to Samuel, “they look on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). On this Saturday we look to Mary, the Virgin who was wholly devoted to Christ, whose humble appearance in Nazareth hid the purest heart of any creature. She teaches the Church to be the chaste bride Paul longed for, and to see others as God sees them.

The Church as the bride of Christ; Paul's divine jealousy.
Point 2 · Another Jesus, another gospel
Fine speech and a false Christ; staying with the faith of the apostles.
Point 3 · Not by appearances

“Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.”

Before you share or follow any religious video this week, ask: is this the Jesus of the apostles, the Jesus of the Church and the Gospel?
Judge rightly (John 7:24)
Notice one person this week whom you have judged by appearance, caste, colour or wealth, and do one kind thing for them.
fathers: St Cyprian of Carthage (in substance)
The bride of Christ cannot be made an adulteress; she is undefiled and chaste. She knows one home and guards with chaste modesty the holiness of one bedchamber. She keeps us for God.
St Augustine (in substance)

My teaching is not mine: what is so much yours as yourself, and what is so little yours as yourself? The teaching of the Son is the Word of the Father; so it is his, and yet not his, because he himself is the Word of the One who sent him.
magis: Catechism 796

The unity of Christ and the Church, head and members of one Body, also implies the distinction of the two within a personal relationship: the Church is the Bride of Christ, whom he loved and for whom he handed himself over.

The Magisterium is not superior to the Word of God, but is its servant: it teaches only what has been handed on, listening to it devoutly, guarding it scrupulously and explaining it faithfully.

To avoid rash judgment, everyone should be careful to interpret insofar as possible his neighbour's thoughts, words and deeds in a favourable way.

At once virgin and mother, Mary is the symbol and the most perfect realisation of the Church.

2027-06-26.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Bridegroom of the Church, you loved her and gave yourself up for her. Keep us, your bride, in a sincere and pure devotion to you. Guard us from every other Jesus, every other spirit and every other gospel, and keep us faithful to the teaching of your apostles. You did not seek your own glory but the glory of the Father who sent you: make us seek his glory, not ours. Give us eyes that do not judge by appearances but see the heart as you see it. Through the prayers of the Blessed Virgin Mary, wholly devoted to you, make us holy and blameless for the day of your coming. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Bridegroom gives himself to his bride. The Church receives the Body of her Lord, and her love is made sincere and pure again. Under the humble appearance of bread and wine, the eyes of faith judge with right judgment and see the Lord himself.

2027-06-28.title: Seventh Monday of the Apostles · Saint Irenaeus, Bishop and Martyr
2027-06-28.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Aaron bears the names of Israel on his heart
The lips of a priest should guard knowledge
Continue in what you have learned; all scripture is inspired by God
The Holy Spirit will teach you everything
2027-06-28.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar gives the weekday readings of the Seventh Monday of the Apostles and the readings of the commemoration of Saint Irenaeus; both sets are shown here (verify locally which are read). The Latin Church keeps the memorial of St Irenaeus today, and in the evening celebrates the Vigil Mass of Sts Peter and Paul.
2027-06-28.verse: But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything, and remind you of all that I have said to you.
theo: On the eve of the feast of Peter and Paul the Church remembers a bishop who loved the apostles' teaching more than his own life, and who handed it on so faithfully that he is called today the Doctor of Unity. Irenaeus was born in Asia Minor, probably at Smyrna, in the first half of the second century. As a boy he listened to Polycarp, the bishop of Smyrna, who had known the apostle John. Many years later Irenaeus wrote to a friend that he could still remember the place where Polycarp sat when he taught, how he went in and out, and how he spoke of his conversations with John and with others who had seen the Lord. That is a chain of only three links between Irenaeus and Jesus: the Lord, the beloved disciple, Polycarp, Irenaeus. He went to Gaul, served as a priest in Lyons, and after the persecution of 177, in which the old bishop Pothinus died in prison, he became bishop of that Church. He wrote five books against the false teachings of his day, usually called Against Heresies, and a shorter work, the Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching. When a dispute about the date of Easter threatened to divide the Church of Rome from the Churches of Asia, he wrote to Pope Victor asking for patience and peace; the historian Eusebius says that he lived up to his name, which means peacemaker. He died around the year 200 and has long been honoured as a martyr, though the details of his death are not known. In 2022 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church, with the title Doctor of Unity.

The readings chosen for him speak of the priest and the teacher. In Exodus the high priest Aaron wears the breastpiece engraved with the names of the twelve tribes: “So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart when he goes into the holy place, for a continual remembrance before the Lord.” A true shepherd carries his people on his heart into the presence of God. Malachi recalls God's covenant with Levi and describes the priest as God wanted him: “True instruction was in his mouth, and no wrong was found on his lips. He walked with me in integrity and uprightness, and he turned many from iniquity. For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts.” Irenaeus was such a priest: he guarded knowledge, not secret knowledge for a few, but the public faith of the whole Church.

Paul's words to Timothy could be Irenaeus' own motto: “But as for you, continue in what you have learned and firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it.” The Gnostic teachers of the second century claimed to possess secret knowledge passed down privately, and they despised the body, the created world and the God of the Old Testament. Irenaeus answered that the apostles had hidden nothing: their teaching is public, kept in the Churches they founded, and handed on by the bishops who succeeded them. He listed the bishops of Rome, “the very great, very ancient and universally known Church founded and organised at Rome by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul” (in substance), and said that every Church must agree with it because of its preeminent authority. So tomorrow's feast and today's saint belong together. He defended the goodness of creation and of the flesh, which the Son of God took from the Virgin Mary; he saw Mary as the new Eve, whose obedience untied the knot of Eve's disobedience; he taught that Christ sums up and renews the whole of human history in himself. And he gave us the sentence that sums up his joy: the glory of God is the human being fully alive, and the life of the human being is the vision of God. He knew that the Spirit was the guarantee of this teaching, as Jesus promised in today's Gospel: “the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything, and remind you of all that I have said to you.” All scripture, Paul adds, “is inspired by God and is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness.”

The weekday readings fit the peacemaker well. Paul writes about a member of the Corinthian Church who had caused great pain and been punished by the community. Now Paul asks for mercy: “so now instead you should forgive and console him, so that he may not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. So I urge you to reaffirm your love for him.” Discipline in the Church is never meant to crush, only to heal; and an unforgiving community gives the devil an opening: “we do this so that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.” In the Gospel the scribes and Pharisees ask Jesus for a sign. He gives them only the sign of Jonah, three days in the belly of the sea monster, a sign of his own death and resurrection, and he reminds them that the people of Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching and that the queen of the South came “from the ends of the earth to listen to the wisdom of Solomon, and see, something greater than Solomon is here!” Irenaeus, who carried the Gospel from Asia to the far west of the empire, and we in India, who received it from Mar Thoma at the eastern edge of the known world, know what it means to come from the ends of the earth to hear the One who is greater than Solomon. Let us listen, repent, forgive, and continue in what we have learned.
outline: Opening
A chain of three links: Jesus, John, Polycarp, Irenaeus; and the chain that reaches us.
Point 1 · Names on the heart
The priest who carries his people before God, and whose lips guard knowledge.
Point 2 · Continue in what you have learned
Public tradition against secret knowledge; the Churches of the apostles; the Spirit who reminds.
Point 3 · Forgive and console
The peacemaker; discipline that heals; something greater than Jonah.
Take-home line
“Continue in what you have learned and firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it.”
live: Know from whom you learned (2 Timothy 3:14)
Thank God today by name for the people who handed on the faith to you: parents, grandparents, catechism teachers, priests; if one is living, call or visit them this week.
Reaffirm your love (2 Corinthians 2:8)
Think of one person who has hurt you or the community and has been made to feel it. Find a way this week to console them and show that they are still loved.
fathers: St Irenaeus of Lyons (in substance)

The tradition of the apostles, made known in the whole world, can be seen in every Church by all who wish to see the truth. We can name those whom the apostles appointed as bishops in the Churches, and their successors down to our own time. The apostles, like a rich man depositing money in a bank, placed in the Church in fullness everything that belongs to the truth.
St Irenaeus of Lyons (in substance)

The glory of God is the human being fully alive, and the life of the human being is the vision of God. If the revelation of God through creation gives life to all who live on earth, much more does the manifestation of the Father through the Word give life to those who see God.
Eusebius of Caesarea, historian (in substance)

When Victor, bishop of Rome, wished to cut off the Churches of Asia over the date of Easter, Irenaeus wrote to him on behalf of the brethren in Gaul, urging him to keep peace with those who held to an ancient custom. So he lived up to his name, a peacemaker in name and in deed.
magis: Catechism 77
In order that the full and living Gospel might always be preserved in the Church, the apostles left bishops as their successors, handing over to them their own position of teaching authority.
Catechism 294

The glory of God consists in the realisation of his manifestation and communication of his goodness; as St Irenaeus says, the glory of God is man fully alive, and the life of man is the vision of God.
Catechism 494
As St Irenaeus says, being obedient Mary became the cause of salvation for herself and the whole human race; the knot of Eve's disobedience was untied by Mary's obedience.
Catechism 1327
The Eucharist is the sum and summary of our faith: our way of thinking is attuned to the Eucharist, and the Eucharist in turn confirms our way of thinking (St Irenaeus).

2027-06-28.prayer: Lord God, you gave your Church the bishop Saint Irenaeus to guard the faith of the apostles and to make peace among your people. Through his prayers keep us faithful to what we have learned and firmly believed, and grateful to those from whom we learned it. Give our bishops and priests the heart of Aaron, to carry your people before you, and the lips of a true priest, to guard knowledge and to teach. Send us the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, to teach us everything and to remind us of all that your Son has said. Make us quick to forgive and console, so that Satan may not outwit us, and let us live fully, for your glory, until we see you face to face. Through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with you and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

Here the glory of God makes us fully alive.

2027-06-30.title: Seventh Wednesday of the Apostles
2027-06-30.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Lead the life to which God called you
You cannot serve God and wealth
2027-06-30.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar's own headings: “The life according to the call”; “You cannot serve two masters”. In the Latin calendar today is the optional memorial of the First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church. On Saturday 3 July, the Dukhrana of St Thomas; on Sunday 4 July, the Season of Kaitha begins.
2027-06-30.verse: Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much; and whoever is dishonest in a very little is dishonest also in much.
theo: On the last day of June, and among the last days of the Season of the Apostles, Paul speaks to Christians who wondered whether becoming a disciple meant changing everything in their outward lives. Should a married convert leave an unbelieving spouse? Should a Jewish Christian hide the marks of circumcision, or a Gentile Christian receive it? Should a slave run away? Paul's rule is calm and deep: “let each of you lead the life that the Lord has assigned, to which God called you. This is my rule in all the churches.” Holiness is not found by escaping our situation but by living it with God. “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing; but obeying the commandments of God is everything.” Three times he repeats it: remain in the condition in which you were called, and the last time he adds two words that change everything: “there remain with God.” The farmer in Wayanad, the nurse in a hospital in the Gulf, the autorickshaw driver, the mother at home with small children, the student in a hostel in Bengaluru, the old man in the parish who can no longer walk: each has a calling, and each can become a saint exactly there. The Second Vatican Council taught that the lay faithful seek the kingdom of God precisely by engaging in ordinary work and family life and ordering them according to God.

Paul's words to slaves need careful reading. In the Roman world slavery was a legal institution, and the small Christian communities had no power to abolish it. Paul does not bless it. The verse on slaves is read in two ways: Paul tells them not to be troubled by their state, and the Malayalam Bible reads that they may take their liberty when it is offered. He puts master and slave on the same level before Christ: “For whoever was called in the Lord as a slave is a freed person belonging to the Lord, just as whoever was free when called is a slave of Christ.” In his letter to Philemon he sends back the runaway Onesimus “no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). That seed grew, slowly, until the Church taught clearly that the enslavement of human beings is a sin against their dignity (Catechism 2414). And Paul gives a word for every age: “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human masters.” A Christian, bought by the Blood of Christ, must not sell himself again: not to the opinion of others, not to a political party, not to a caste prejudice, not to a bank loan taken for show, not to an addiction.

The Gospel continues the teaching that follows the parable of the dishonest manager, who used his master's money to make friends before he lost his post. Jesus draws the lesson: “make friends for yourselves by means of dishonest wealth so that when it is gone, they may welcome you into the eternal homes.” Money, which so easily becomes unjust, can be turned into friendship with the poor, and the poor will be the ones who welcome us into heaven. Then: “Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much; and whoever is dishonest in a very little is dishonest also in much.” Character is built in small things: the correct change returned, the exam without copying, the honest weighing in the shop, the hour of work actually worked. “If then you have not been faithful with the dishonest wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches?” And the decisive sentence: “No slave can serve two masters; for a slave will either hate the one and love the other, or be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.” Some of the Pharisees who heard him, Luke says, were lovers of money and ridiculed him. Jesus answers them, and us: “You are those who justify yourselves in the sight of others; but God knows your hearts; for what is prized by human beings is an abomination in the sight of God.” The warning is not for one group of long ago; it is for every heart that has learned to admire what God despises.

Our society knows this temptation well. Gold for weddings counted in sovereigns, dowry demands that crush families, houses built bigger than needed with loans that cannot be repaid, the quiet competition of parish feasts and family functions: wealth has many ways of becoming a master. Jesus does not ask us to despise money; he asks us to make it a servant, a means of friendship with the poor. Today the Latin calendar remembers the First Martyrs of the Church of Rome, the many unnamed Christians put to death under Nero after the great fire of the year 64; the Roman historian Tacitus records that a great multitude died in cruel ways. They had learned to be faithful in very little, and so they were faithful in much, even unto death; they could not serve two masters. Yesterday we honoured Peter and Paul; today we remember the ordinary believers who died in the same persecution. On Saturday we will keep the Dukhrana of Mar Thoma, and on Sunday the Season of Kaitha begins. Let us close the Season of the Apostles by asking whom we really serve, and by making one concrete choice for God over wealth.
outline: Opening
A calling in every condition of life: holiness where we are.
Point 1 · Lead the life to which God called you
Remain with God in your situation; the lay vocation in daily work.
Point 2 · Bought with a price
Not slaves of human masters; the seed of human dignity that grew.
Point 3 · You cannot serve God and wealth
Faithful in little; making friends with money; what God sees in the heart.
Take-home line
“Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.”
live: Remain with God (1 Corinthians 7:24)
Offer your ordinary work tomorrow morning to God before you begin, and do one part of it with special care for his sake.
Make friends with your money (Luke 16:9)
Use some money this week for someone who cannot repay you, and resist one expense that is only for show.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Make friends with your money: the poor are the porters who carry your goods from earth to heaven. What you keep here you will lose; what you give through them you will find there, and they will welcome you into the eternal dwellings.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Are you a slave? Do not be troubled. The one who is truly a slave is the one who serves sin; and the truly noble is the one who is ruled by none of the passions. Christ does not ask where you stand in the world, but whether you serve him there.
St Clement of Alexandria (in substance)

Riches are not to be thrown away; they are instruments, and an instrument used with skill serves well. The Lord does not command us to destroy our possessions but to banish from the soul the passion for them, so that we may use them rightly for our neighbour.
magis: Catechism 898
By reason of their special vocation it belongs to the laity to seek the kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs and directing them according to God's will.
Catechism 2414
The seventh commandment forbids acts or enterprises that lead to the enslavement of human beings, to their being bought, sold and exchanged like merchandise, in disregard for their personal dignity.
Catechism 2113
Idolatry consists in divinising what is not God, for example power, pleasure, race, ancestors, the state or money. Jesus says, You cannot serve God and mammon.
Catechism 2443
God blesses those who come to the aid of the poor and rebukes those who turn away from them; the love of the poor is incompatible with immoderate love of riches or their selfish use.

2027-06-30.prayer: Lord God, you call each of us in the place and condition where we stand, and you ask us to remain there with you. Make our ordinary work, our families and our studies a path of holiness. You bought us with the precious Blood of your Son: do not let us become slaves of any human master, of opinion, of money or of any habit. Teach us to be faithful in very little, so that you may entrust to us the true riches. Loosen the hold of wealth on our hearts, and help us to make friends of the poor, who will welcome us into the eternal homes. With the first martyrs of Rome and the apostles Peter and Paul, may we serve you alone. Through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with you and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we bring to the altar the work of our hands in our own condition of life, and the Lord who bought us with a price gives himself to us. Fed by the true riches, we go out to be faithful in small things and to make friends of the poor with what we have.

quick: Deuteronomy: give a fair hearing to citizen and resident alien; hear the small and the great alike, for the judgment is God's.
Isaiah: God rejects worship with unjust hands; wash yourselves, learn to do good, and though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be like snow.
Paul: I have become all things to all people; run so as to win the imperishable wreath.

2027-06-06.action: Pray each day this week by name for someone who has hurt you, and pay every worker you employ fairly and on time.
2027-06-06.question: Is there someone I need to forgive before I come to the altar?
kidsaint: St Maria Goretti

Maria was an eleven-year-old girl from a poor farming family in Italy. In 1902 a young man named Alessandro attacked her, and when she refused to sin, he stabbed her. Before she died the next day, she said that she forgave him and wanted him to be with her in heaven. Years later, in prison, Alessandro changed his life. When Pope Pius XII declared Maria a saint in 1950, Alessandro was there, and Maria's mother had already forgiven him too. Lesson: forgiving someone who hurt us is the bravest kind of love!
2027-06-06.special: Fourth Sunday of the Apostles. Latin Church: Tenth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
term: Mar Thoma Margam

The Way of Thomas: the name the St Thomas Christians gave to their faith and their whole Christian tradition, received from the apostle Thomas and lived for centuries within Indian culture. It has been summed up in the phrase “Christian in faith, Indian in culture and Oriental in worship”, a living example of Paul's “all things to all people” without any change in the Gospel. Malayalam: മാർത്തോമ്മാമാർഗം.

family.explain: Jesus asks something very hard: to love even the people who are unkind to us. When someone hurts us, we want to hurt them back. Jesus says: do good to them, say good words about them, and pray for them. He also gives us a golden rule: treat others the way you want them to treat you. God is kind even to people who are ungrateful, and Jesus wants us to be like our Father in heaven.
family.intention: We pray for someone who has hurt us, and for people who suffer injustice.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there someone our family needs to forgive?”

illus: An illustration

On 25 February 1995 Sister Rani Maria Vattalil, a Franciscan Clarist sister from Pulluvazhy near Perumbavoor, who worked among poor villagers in Madhya Pradesh, was stabbed to death on a bus near Indore by a man named Samundar Singh. Some time later her younger sister, Sister Selmy Paul, also a religious sister, visited him in prison. On the feast of Raksha Bandhan she tied a rakhi on his wrist and called him her brother. The man wept. He later asked forgiveness of the family, and after his release he visited them in Kerala, where Rani Maria's mother and relatives received him. In 2017 the Church beatified Sister Rani Maria as a martyr at Indore, and Samundar Singh was among those present. The man who had been an enemy had become a brother because a family loved as Jesus asked.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you taught your apostles to love their enemies and to be merciful as the Father is merciful. Wash our hearts, make us just, and fill us with your mercy as we pray together. Amen.
share: Hear out the small and the great alike (Deuteronomy 1:17). Do I treat the poor and the powerful the same?
Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean (Isaiah 1:16). What must be washed from my hands before I pray?
I have become all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9:22). What would I change in myself for the sake of the Gospel?
Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you (Luke 6:27). Whom do I find hardest to love?
pm.resp: Lord, make us merciful as the Father is merciful.
interc: For the Church in this Season of the Apostles, that she may be just in her structures and merciful to all.
For judges, lawyers, police and all in public office, that they may hear the small and the great alike.
For migrant workers in Kerala and for Keralites working abroad, that they may be treated with justice and dignity.
For those who carry deep wounds caused by others, that they may receive the grace to forgive.
For students and young athletes at the start of a new year, that they may run the race of life with discipline and faith.
pm.close: Father, you are kind to the ungrateful and the wicked, and you call us to be your children. Make us just in judgment, clean of heart, disciplined in spirit and merciful as you are merciful. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Deuteronomy: keep the Lord's commandments so that you may live; no other nation has a god so near.
Isaiah: all the nations shall stream to the mountain of the Lord; swords shall become ploughshares.
Paul: not all things build up; seek the good of the other; do everything for the glory of God.
Luke: the suffering of others is not a judgment on them but a call to us: unless you repent, you will all perish.
2027-06-20.action: Take one concrete step towards peace with someone this week, and plan your confession before 29 June.
2027-06-20.question: Do I treat the suffering of others as a judgment on them, or as a call to my own conversion?
catechism: The commandments as a response of love.
Charity and the conscience of the neighbour.
kidsaint: St Dominic Savio

Dominic was an Italian boy who studied at the school of St John Bosco in Turin. On the day of his First Holy Communion, when he was seven, he wrote a promise: “Death rather than sin.” He was cheerful, he played games, he helped younger boys and he stopped fights between his friends. He did ordinary things for the glory of God. He died when he was only fourteen. Lesson: you can make everything you do, eating, playing and studying, a gift to God!
2027-06-20.special: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Latin Church: Twelfth Sunday in Ordinary Time. Father's Day in many countries.
term: Metanoia (repentance)

The Greek word used in the Gospels for repentance, as in Luke 13:3. It means more than feeling sorry: it is a change of mind and heart, a turning of the whole life back to God. Malayalam: മാനസാന്തരം, അനുതാപം.

family.explain: Isaiah saw a beautiful picture: people from every country walking up a mountain to learn God's ways. They were so full of God's peace that they melted their swords and made them into farming tools. Saint Paul says that whatever we do, eating, drinking, playing or studying, we can do it for the glory of God. And Jesus tells us to turn back to God every day. Today many families also thank God for their fathers.
family.intention: We pray for our fathers and grandfathers, living and dead, and for children starting the new school year.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one thing we can do together this week for the glory of God?”

illus: An illustration

Two families in a village in Idukki had quarrelled for years over a strip of land between their houses, hardly three feet wide. The case went to court, and lawyers' fees mounted on both sides. One Sunday the elder of the two men heard the homily on the Gospel: “on the way make an effort to settle the case.” On the way home from the Qurbana he passed his neighbour's gate and, without planning it, stopped. ‘We are both getting old,’ he said. ‘Our sons will inherit this quarrel and nothing else.’ They sat on the veranda and talked until the tea went cold. A month later both families withdrew the case and planted a row of plantains on the disputed strip, to be shared. The parish priest blessed the plants at the next house blessing. ‘Isaiah said swords would become ploughs,’ he told them. ‘Here a court case has become a plantain grove.’

pm.open: Lord God, there is no people with a God as near as you are to us. Draw us now to the mountain of your house, teach us your ways, and send your Holy Spirit to turn our hearts back to you. Amen.
share: What other great nation has a god so near to it? (Deuteronomy 4:7). When have I felt God near?
They shall beat their swords into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4). Which sword in my life needs to become a plough?
Do everything for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). What ordinary task can I offer to God this week?
Unless you repent, you will all perish (Luke 13:3). What is God calling me to turn away from?
pm.resp: Lord, teach us your ways.
interc: For the Church in this Season of the Apostles, that from every altar the word of the Lord may go out to the nations.
For peace in the world and in our land, that swords may become ploughshares and enemies may be reconciled.
For parents and catechists beginning the new year of faith formation, that they may hand on the faith with joy.
For our fathers, living and dead, and for those who have no father to care for them.
For victims of floods, landslides and accidents in this monsoon season, and for all who help them.
pm.close: Father, you are near to all who call upon you. Make us a wise and discerning people, who live by your word, build up one another and do everything for your glory, and who turn back to you while there is still time. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Deuteronomy: at Horeb you heard the sound of words but saw no form; learn to fear the Lord and teach your children.
Isaiah: woe to those who join field to field, who chase strong drink, who call evil good; the Holy God shows himself holy by righteousness.
Paul: put aside something on the first day of every week; keep alert, stand firm, be strong; let all that you do be done in love.
Luke: strive to enter through the narrow door; people will come from east and west to the feast of the kingdom.
2027-06-27.action: Set up a small box for the poor beside your family altar and put something in it every Sunday.
2027-06-27.question: Am I striving to enter the narrow door, or only standing near it?
catechism: The Lord's Day from apostolic times.
kidsaint: St Kuriakose Elias Chavara

Father Chavara was a priest in Kerala about two hundred years ago. He loved God and he loved children. He started a school at Mannanam and asked that every parish should have a school beside the church, so that all children, rich or poor, could learn to read and write and learn about Jesus. He also began a religious congregation of priests and one of sisters. Pope Francis declared him a saint in 2014. Lesson: when school begins, thank God for your teachers, and learn well for Jesus!
2027-06-27.special: Seventh Sunday of the Apostles, the last Sunday of the season. Kaitha begins on Sunday 4 July.
term: Kaitha (Qaita)

The East Syriac liturgical season that follows the Season of the Apostles. Qaita means summer, the time of fruit: after the apostles have sown the Gospel, the Church contemplates its growth and fruit in the saints and martyrs. In 2027 it begins on Sunday 4 July, the day after the Dukhrana of St Thomas. Malayalam: കൈത്താക്കാലം.

family.explain: Someone asked Jesus: will only a few people be saved? Jesus said: try hard to go in through the narrow door. A narrow door means we cannot carry everything with us: we leave behind selfishness, lies and bad habits. But Jesus also said that people from east and west, north and south will come and sit at God's table. God wants everyone to come in!
family.intention: We pray for children starting a new school year, for their teachers, and for children who cannot go to school.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one thing our family needs to leave outside so that we can go in through the narrow door?”

illus: An illustration

In a house near Pala (a story told to illustrate the reading) an old grandmother kept a small tin box beside the family altar, under the picture of the Sacred Heart. Every Sunday after the Holy Qurbana, she asked each grandchild to put in one coin from their own pocket money, and the adults put in what they could. Nobody opened the box during the year. In June, when the schools reopened, the grandmother called the family together and opened it, and they counted the money on the dining table. It was enough to pay the school fees, uniforms and books for a child in a poor family of the parish. The children were allowed to choose the colour of the umbrella for the monsoon. ‘Saint Paul told the Corinthians to put something aside on the first day of every week,’ the grandmother used to say. ‘The box is small, but love fills it.’ Years later, one of those grandchildren, now working abroad, still keeps a tin box beside his own family altar.

pm.open: Holy Spirit, who spoke from the fire and came upon the apostles, gather us at the end of this Season of the Apostles. Keep us alert, firm and strong, and let all that we do be done in love. Amen.
share: You heard the sound of words but saw no form (Deuteronomy 4:12). How do I listen to God's word?
Ah, you who call evil good and good evil (Isaiah 5:20). Where have I renamed sin to make it comfortable?
Let all that you do be done in love (1 Corinthians 16:14). What do I do without love?
Strive to enter through the narrow door (Luke 13:24). What must I leave behind to enter?
pm.resp: Lord, open to us the door of your kingdom.
interc: For the Church at the close of the Season of the Apostles, that she may be alert, firm in faith and courageous in mission.
For children and teachers at the beginning of the school year, and for those who teach the faith in our parishes.
For families harmed by alcohol, greed and quarrels over land, that they may find healing and peace.
For the poor and the missions, that our Sunday giving may be generous.
For all peoples of east and west, north and south, that they may come to the table of the kingdom.
pm.close: Father, you spoke from the fire and made your face known in your Son. As this Season of the Apostles closes, keep us faithful to the faith they handed on, generous in love, and striving to enter the narrow door, until we sit at your table with all your saints. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Feast of St Peter and St Paul, the two pillars of the Church, martyred in Rome; a day of obligation.
Elisha raises the Shunammite's son; Peter raises Tabitha: the apostle's hand lifts up the dead as Jesus did.
Paul boasts only of his sufferings and his weakness, and of his daily anxiety for all the Churches.
Jesus asks Peter three times, “Do you love me?” and entrusts him with his whole flock: feed my sheep.
2027-06-29.action: Answer Jesus tonight in your own words, “Lord, you know that I love you,” and pray every day this week for the Pope.
2027-06-29.question: If Jesus asked me today, “Do you love me?”, what would my life answer?
kidsaint: St Peter

Peter was a fisherman with big rough hands and a big loud voice. Jesus called him to fish for people. Peter loved Jesus, but one night he was afraid and said three times that he did not know him. Afterwards he cried. When Jesus rose from the dead, he asked Peter three times: “Do you love me?” Peter said, “Lord, you know that I love you!” Jesus forgave him and made him the shepherd of all his people. Lesson: when we fall, Jesus does not give up on us; he asks us to love him again!
2027-06-29.special: St Peter and St Paul, the Apostles: an important feast and a day of obligation.
term: Petrine ministry

The service of unity that Christ entrusted to Peter (Matthew 16:18–19; Luke 22:32; John 21:15–17) and that the Catholic Church believes continues in the Bishop of Rome, the Pope. It is a ministry of strengthening the faith of the brethren and of keeping all the Churches, of East and West, in one communion. Malayalam: പത്രോസിന്റെ ശുശ്രൂഷ.

family.explain: After Jesus rose from the dead, he made breakfast for his friends by the lake. Then he asked Peter three times: “Do you love me?” Peter had said three times that he did not know Jesus. Now he said three times, “Lord, you know that I love you.” Each time Jesus said: “Feed my sheep.” Jesus forgave Peter and gave him the job of looking after all his people. Today we also remember Saint Paul, who travelled far and suffered much to tell people about Jesus.
family.intention: We pray for Pope Leo, for our bishops and priests, and for Christians who suffer for their faith.
family.ask: Ask: “How can each of us show Jesus this week that we love him?”

illus: An illustration

In a fishing parish on the coast near Alappuzha (a story told to illustrate the reading) the church sacristan was an old fisherman named Pathrose, after St Peter. As a young man he had been given the keys of the church, but one year, after a bitter quarrel with some parishioners, he threw the keys on the vicar's table and stopped coming to church. For many months he went out to sea and drank on the shore. One evening the old vicar came down to the beach, sat by his fire of coconut husks, and asked him three times, slowly, ‘Pathrose, do you still love the Lord?’ The third time the fisherman wept and said, ‘Achen, you know that I do.’ The vicar took the keys out of his pocket and put them in his hand. ‘Then open the church tomorrow for the morning Qurbana.’ Pathrose kept those keys for forty more years. At his funeral the parish placed a small key on his coffin.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you asked Peter, “Do you love me?” and called Paul on the road to Damascus. Gather us now with your apostles; renew our love and our zeal, and keep us one with your whole Church. Amen.
share: Simon son of John, do you love me? (John 21:17). What is my answer today?
Tabitha, get up (Acts 9:40). Whom does Jesus want me to lift up by the hand?
I will boast of the things that show my weakness (2 Corinthians 11:30). Can I offer my weakness to God?
You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church (Matthew 16:18). How do I live my communion with the Pope and the whole Church?
pm.resp: Lord, you know that we love you.
interc: For Pope Leo XIV, successor of Peter, that the Lord may strengthen him to confirm his brothers and sisters in faith.
For our Major Archbishop, our bishops and the Synod of our Church, that they may feed the flock with love.
For persecuted Christians, that they may stand firm like Peter and Paul.
For the unity of all Christians, that East and West may be one.
For those who have denied or left the Lord, that they may hear again his question, “Do you love me?”
pm.close: Father, you gave your Church the two pillars Peter and Paul. Through their prayers keep us one in faith around the successor of Peter, make us shepherds of one another in love, and lead us to share their crown. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Deuteronomy: at Kadesh Israel first refused to go up in fear, then went up without God in presumption; Caleb followed the Lord wholeheartedly.
Isaiah: the faithful city forgot the orphan and the widow; God will smelt away its dross and make it again the city of righteousness.
Paul: pursue love and strive for the gifts that build up the Church.
Luke: do not worry; consider the ravens and the lilies; do not be afraid, little flock; where your treasure is, there your heart will be.
2027-06-13.action: Write down your greatest worry, give it to the Father in prayer tonight, and give one alms this week that you had not planned.
2027-06-13.question: Where is my treasure, and so where is my heart?
catechism: Charisms for building up the Church.
kidsaint: St Kuriakose Elias Chavara

Father Chavara was a priest in Kerala more than one hundred and fifty years ago. He wanted every child, rich or poor, to learn to read and write, and he asked that a school be started beside every church. He began religious congregations of priests and of sisters, a printing press and a home for the poor, and he often had very little money for all this. He trusted that God the Father would provide, and God did. Lesson: as you go back to school this June, thank God for your school, study well, and trust your Father in heaven with your worries!
2027-06-13.special: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles. Latin calendar: Eleventh Sunday in Ordinary Time (St Antony of Padua omitted this year).
term: Karozutha

The litany of intercession sung or said by the deacon (or the priest) in the Holy Qurbana and in the Hours, to which the people answer with a short prayer. The word comes from the Syriac for proclamation. In the Karozutha the whole Church lays its needs before the Father, for the Church and her pastors, the sick, travellers and the departed: Jesus' teaching on not worrying becomes a prayer. Malayalam: കാറോസൂസ.

family.explain: Jesus told his friends not to worry so much about food and clothes. He said: look at the crows. They do not plant rice or keep it in a store room, but God feeds them. Look at the flowers. They do not sew dresses, but they are more beautiful than a king's robes. You are worth much more than birds and flowers! God is our Father and he knows what we need. So we work and study, but we do not worry; we pray and trust him.
family.intention: We pray for families who do not have enough food, and for children starting a new school year.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one thing we are worried about? Let us give it to God together now.”

illus: An illustration

In a hill village in Idukki a widow ran a small tea shop to pay for her two children's education. Every June, when the schools reopened and fees, books and uniforms all fell due in the same week of heavy rain, she would lie awake counting. One year a neighbour found her at the shop at five in the morning, saying her rosary over the account book. ‘You look worried,’ he said. ‘I was,’ she answered, ‘until I remembered that I am not the father of this family; God is. My job is to do my work and keep my heart in the right place.’ That morning, as every morning, she set aside a glass of tea and a bun for an old man who slept at the bus stop. Her children both finished their studies. Her son says now: ‘We never had much money, but we never once saw our mother give up giving.’

pm.open: Father in heaven, you feed the ravens and clothe the lilies. We are your little flock, gathered in the Spirit of Pentecost. Take away our fear, build us up in love, and make our hearts rest where our treasure is, in you. Amen.
share: The Lord your God goes before you on the way (Deuteronomy 1:33). Where have I refused to follow because I was afraid?
