For those in power, that they may listen to the voice of conscience as David did.
For all named John, and for all baptised, that they may live by the name given them by God.
pm.close: Father, at the fullness of time you sent your Son, and before him you sent John to prepare his way. Make us your children, give us John's courage and humility, and let Christ increase in us. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Matthew: the Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus with a question about the tax to the emperor.
Jesus: give to the emperor what bears his image, and to God what bears God's image, that is, yourself.
Paul: all authority is from God; the ruler is God's servant for your good; pay taxes, not only from fear but for conscience.
2027-06-25.action: Put right one small dishonesty in your dealings with the government or the public this week, and pray for those who govern.
2027-06-25.question: Have I given to God what bears his image, my whole self?

family.explain: Some people wanted to trick Jesus with a question about money for the king. Jesus asked to see a coin. It had the king's picture on it. Jesus said: give the king what has his picture on it, and give God what belongs to God. What has God's picture on it? We do! God made each of us in his image. So we give our whole selves to God, and we are also good and honest citizens of our country.
family.intention: We pray for our country, for those who lead it, and for police officers, judges and all who serve the public.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one way our family can be honest and helpful to our town or village this week?”

illus: An illustration

A village officer in central Kerala (a story told to illustrate the reading) was known in his office as the man who would not take anything extra. One day a contractor left an envelope on his table with a file. The officer pushed it back and said quietly, ‘The government already pays me for this.’ The man was annoyed: ‘Everyone takes it. You will gain nothing.’ The officer kept a small picture of the Sacred Heart in his drawer, and that evening he told his wife, ‘The coin has the government's stamp, but my hands have God's.’ Years later, when he retired, many people from the village came to the small function, among them that same contractor, who said in his speech, ‘He was the only officer whose signature I never had to buy.’

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you saw through every trap and spoke the truth with love. Gather us now, made in the image of God; teach us to give to God what is God's. Amen.
share: Whose head is this, and whose title? (Matthew 22:20). Whose image do I carry, and whom do I serve first?
Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s (Matthew 22:21). Am I honest in what I owe to the state and the public?
There is no authority except from God (Romans 13:1). How do I pray for and speak about those in authority?
Not only because of wrath but also because of conscience (Romans 13:5). Do I do right only when someone is watching?
pm.resp: Lord, all that we are is yours.
interc: For our country and all who govern it, that they may serve the common good with honesty and wisdom.
For civil servants, police officers and judges, that they may resist corruption and protect the weak.
For Christians who suffer for refusing to deny their faith, that they may stand firm like the apostles.
For young people preparing for public service and politics, that they may enter it with clean hands.
For ourselves, that we may be honest citizens and faithful children of God.
pm.close: Father, every person bears your image and belongs to you. Make us faithful in our duties to the earthly city and wholly yours in heart, until we reach the city that is to come. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Paul: I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
He fears that clever preachers will bring another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel.
Jesus: my teaching is not mine but his who sent me; do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.
2027-06-26.action: Do one kind act this week for someone you have judged by appearance, and test every new preacher by the faith of the apostles.
2027-06-26.question: Whom have I judged by appearance this week?

family.explain: Some people in Jerusalem were surprised that Jesus could teach so well, because he had not studied in a famous school. They judged him by how he looked. Jesus said: my teaching comes from my Father. And he told them: do not judge by appearances. God looks at the heart. We should not decide that someone is good or bad because of their clothes, their colour, their house or the way they talk.
family.intention: We pray for children who are teased because of how they look, and for those who feel left out.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there someone at school or in our street whom we have judged too quickly? How can we be kind to them?”

illus: An illustration

A mother in Thrissur (a story told to illustrate the reading) was searching for a bride for her son, and she rejected one proposal after another by looking at the photographs: too dark, too short, family not well off. Her son was quiet about it. One evening her own mother, an old woman who had buried her husband young and raised five children on a teacher's salary, asked to see the photographs. She picked one that had been put aside and said, ‘Do you know this girl? She comes every Saturday to the palliative care unit at the parish and washes the old people's feet. I have seen her.’ Then she quoted the word of the Lord to Samuel: ‘The Lord looks on the heart.’ The mother went to meet the girl's family. A year later, at the wedding, it was the grandmother who placed the crown on the bride's head with the greatest joy.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, Bridegroom of the Church, gather us as your bride. Keep our love for you sincere and pure, and open our eyes to see as you see. Amen.
share: I promised you in marriage to one husband (2 Corinthians 11:2). Is my love for Christ undivided?
Another Jesus… a different gospel (2 Corinthians 11:4). Which voices draw me away from the faith of the apostles?
My teaching is not mine but his who sent me (John 7:16). Do I seek God's glory or my own when I speak of him?
Do not judge by appearances (John 7:24). Whom have I judged unfairly?
pm.resp: Lord, keep us faithful to you.
interc: For the Church, bride of Christ, that she may remain pure in faith and generous in love.
For preachers, priests and catechists, that they may hand on the faith of the apostles and not their own opinions.
For those confused by false teachers and new sects, that they may find their way back to the fullness of the truth.
For all who suffer discrimination because of colour, caste, appearance or poverty.
For young people seeking a partner in marriage, that they and their families may look at the heart.
pm.close: Father, your Son did not seek his own glory but yours. Keep us faithful to his Gospel as the apostles handed it on, keep us from every rash judgment, and make your Church a pure bride for her Bridegroom. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: St Irenaeus, who heard Polycarp, the disciple of John, guarded the public faith of the apostles and made peace in the Church; he is the Doctor of Unity.
His readings: the priest bears the names of Israel on his heart; the lips of a priest guard knowledge; continue in what you have learned; the Spirit will remind you of all that Jesus said.
Weekday: Paul asks the Corinthians to forgive and console the offender; Jesus offers the sign of Jonah, for something greater than Jonah is here.
2027-06-28.action: Thank God by name for those who handed on the faith to you, and console someone who needs to know they are still loved.
2027-06-28.question: Do I continue in what I have learned, or do I chase new and secret teachings?
kidsaint: St Irenaeus

When Irenaeus was a boy, he listened to an old bishop called Polycarp, who had known Saint John, the friend of Jesus. So Irenaeus heard about Jesus from someone who had heard it from Jesus' own friend! He became a bishop in France and wrote books to protect the true faith, and he helped people who were quarrelling to make peace. His name means peaceful. Lesson: listen to those who teach you about Jesus, and be a peacemaker!
term: Apostolic succession

The handing on of the apostles' mission and authority through the bishops, from the apostles to the present day, by the laying on of hands. St Irenaeus pointed to the lists of bishops in the Churches founded by the apostles as a guarantee that the Church teaches what the apostles taught.

family.explain: Saint Paul told Timothy: keep what you learned, and remember who taught you. Timothy had learned the Bible as a child from his grandmother and mother. Saint Irenaeus learned about Jesus from Polycarp, who learned from Saint John, who knew Jesus. The faith comes to us through a long chain of people who love Jesus, and the Holy Spirit helps us remember everything Jesus said.
family.intention: We pray for our grandparents, parents, catechism teachers and priests, who taught us the faith.
family.ask: Ask: “Who taught each of us to pray? Let us thank God for them by name.”

illus: An illustration

In a parish in Kuttanad (a story told to illustrate the reading) an old catechism teacher was asked by a sharp boy in her class, ‘Teacher, how do we know that what you teach is really what Jesus said?’ She did not answer at once. The next Sunday she brought a long paper chain and hung it across the classroom. On the first link she had written her own name. On the next, the name of the priest who had taught her; then the bishop who had ordained him; then, link by link, the bishops of the Church back through the centuries, until the last links read ‘the Apostles’ and ‘Jesus’. ‘I did not invent this faith,’ she said. ‘I received it, and now I give it to you. One day you will add your link.’ Many years later, that boy, now a priest, told the story at her funeral and said, ‘She taught me what St Irenaeus taught: continue in what you have learned, knowing from whom you learned it.’

pm.open: Holy Spirit, Advocate sent by the Father, you teach us everything and remind us of all that Jesus said. With St Irenaeus we gather to listen; keep us in the faith of the apostles and make us peacemakers. Amen.
share: So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel… on his heart (Exodus 28:29). Whom do I carry on my heart before God?
The lips of a priest should guard knowledge (Malachi 2:7). How do I pray for and support our priests?
Continue in what you have learned… knowing from whom you learned it (2 Timothy 3:14). Who handed on the faith to me?
You should forgive and console him (2 Corinthians 2:7). Whom do I need to forgive and comfort?
pm.resp: Holy Spirit, remind us of all that Jesus said.
interc: For the Church, that she may remain one in the faith of the apostles, through the prayers of St Irenaeus, Doctor of Unity.
For our bishops and priests, that they may carry their people on their hearts and teach the faith with integrity.
For catechism teachers and parents, who hand on the faith to the next generation.
For those who have been hurt in the Church and those who have caused hurt, that forgiveness and consolation may heal them.
For Christians separated from one another, that they may be reconciled in truth and love.
pm.close: Father, through St Irenaeus you kept your Church faithful to the teaching of the apostles. Keep us in that faith, make us peacemakers, and let us live fully for your glory until we see you. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Paul: let each lead the life to which God called him; remain with God in that condition; you were bought with a price, do not become slaves of human masters.
Jesus: make friends with your wealth; whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.
No slave can serve two masters: you cannot serve God and wealth; God knows your hearts.
2027-06-30.action: Give something this week to someone who cannot repay you, and refuse one expense that is only for show.
2027-06-30.question: Is money my servant or my master?

family.explain: Jesus says that if we are honest in small things, we will be honest in big things too. Returning the extra change in the shop, telling the truth about homework, sharing our snacks: these small things matter to God. Jesus also says we cannot have two bosses. If money becomes our boss, we forget God. Money is good when we use it to help others.
family.intention: We pray for families who are in debt, and for children whose families cannot pay for school.
family.ask: Ask: “What small thing can each of us do honestly and faithfully this week?”

illus: An illustration

A young couple from a parish near Changanassery (a story told to illustrate the reading), both nurses who had worked for years in the Gulf, came home to get married. The relatives expected a grand wedding: a large hall, many guests, and the bride covered in gold. The two had saved carefully. One evening they sat with their parish priest and said, ‘We do not want to begin our marriage by serving two masters.’ They had a simple wedding after the Holy Qurbana, with lunch in the parish hall, and the bride wore a little of her mother's gold. With what they saved, they paid for the roof of a house for a widow in the parish whose old roof leaked every monsoon. Some relatives grumbled. But on the day the widow moved in under the new roof, she held the bride's hands and blessed them, and the young wife said later that it was the best wedding gift they ever received.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you call us where we are and ask us to serve you alone. Gather us now; deliver our hearts from every other master, and make us faithful in small things. Amen.
share: Let each of you lead the life that the Lord has assigned (1 Corinthians 7:17). Do I believe that God has called me in my present situation?
You were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 7:23). To what human master have I sold myself?
Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10). In which small things am I unfaithful?
You cannot serve God and wealth (Luke 16:13). Is money my servant or my master?
pm.resp: Lord, you alone are our Master.
interc: For all who work in ordinary jobs, at home and abroad, that they may find God in their daily labour.
For victims of modern slavery and human trafficking, and for those who work to set them at liberty.
For families crushed by debt, dowry demands and the pressure of display.
For the persecuted Church, in memory of the first martyrs of Rome.
For ourselves, that we may be faithful in small things and generous to the poor.
pm.close: Father, you bought us with the Blood of your Son and called us to serve you alone. Make us faithful in little things and wise in the use of wealth, so that the poor may welcome us into the eternal homes. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today's readings take our faith out of the church and into daily life. Moses tells the judges of Israel: give a fair hearing to the citizen and the stranger; hear out the small and the great alike; do not be afraid of anyone, for the judgment is God's (Deuteronomy 1:16–17).

Each of us judges others: parents, teachers, employers, officers, committee members. Do we give the poor man the same hearing as the rich man? Do we pay the migrant worker on our building site the full wage on time? Justice is the first form of love.

Through Isaiah God says something shocking: I cannot bear your feasts and prayers when your hands are full of injustice. Wash yourselves; learn to do good; defend the orphan and the widow. Then he says: come, let us argue it out; though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be like snow (Isaiah 1:18). God's door is always open to the one who repents.

Saint Paul says: I have become all things to all people, that I might save some (1 Corinthians 9:22). He compares the Christian to an athlete who trains hard for a prize. Athletes discipline themselves for a medal that fades; we run for a crown that lasts for ever. Let us bring that same discipline to prayer, fasting and self-control.

And in the Gospel Jesus tells his apostles: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you (Luke 6:27–28). It is easy to love those who love us. Jesus asks more: be merciful, just as your Father is merciful (Luke 6:36).

Blessed Rani Maria's family forgave the man who killed her, and he became like a brother to them. Mercy changed him. This week let us name in prayer someone who has hurt us, and ask God to bless them. Then we will truly be children of the Most High. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says: love even those who are unkind to you, and pray for them. That is hard! But Jesus helps us.
Remember the golden rule: treat others the way you want them to treat you. Today, say a little prayer for someone who was not nice to you.

homily: Dear friends, on this Sixth Sunday of the Apostles, Moses asks a beautiful question: “what other great nation has a god so near to it as the Lord our God is whenever we call to him?” (Deuteronomy 4:7). God gave his commandments not to burden us but so that we might live. And he asks us to make them known to our children and our children's children.

This month our children have gone back to school and the catechism classes have begun again. Parents, you are the first teachers of the faith. Do not leave it only to the Sunday school. Pray with your children, read the Gospel with them, and let them see you live it.

Isaiah sees all the nations streaming to the mountain of the Lord, saying, “Come, let us go up… that he may teach us his ways.” The word goes out from Jerusalem, and its fruit is peace: swords become ploughshares (Isaiah 2:3–4). This happened at Pentecost, when the apostles carried the word to the nations, and it happens wherever enemies are reconciled.

Saint Paul tells us that not everything we are allowed to do builds up others. Love thinks about the other person's conscience. And he gives a rule for every day: “whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). Our kitchen, our office and our classroom can all become places of worship.

In the Gospel, people tell Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate and about a tower that fell and killed eighteen people. Were they worse sinners? Jesus says, “No… but unless you repent, you will all perish” (Luke 13:3). When disaster strikes others, let us not judge them; let us help them, and look into our own hearts.

And Jesus tells of a fig tree without fruit, and a gardener who says, “let it alone for one more year.” That gardener is Jesus, who pleads for us and works on our roots. Today is our year of grace. Let us turn back to him, walk in the light of the Lord, and bear fruit for his glory. Amen.
kids: Children, Isaiah dreamed of a day when people would melt their swords and make them into tools for farming. That means: stop fighting and start helping!
Saint Paul says we can do everything for God, even eating and playing. Today, say a prayer before your meal, and if you have a fight with someone, be the first to make peace!

homily: Dear friends, today is the last Sunday of the Season of the Apostles. It began at Pentecost with tongues of fire, and the first reading takes us back to another fire, at Mount Horeb. There God spoke to his people: “You heard the sound of words but saw no form; there was only a voice” (Deuteronomy 4:12). Our God is not a statue; he is a God who speaks.

Moses says that the people must learn this word and teach it to their children. This month the schools have reopened and the faith formation classes have begun again. Parents, you are the first teachers of the faith. Ask your children what they have learned, and pray with them.

Isaiah warns against three woes: greed that joins field to field until no one else has room, strong drink from morning to night, and calling evil good and good evil (Isaiah 5:8, 11, 20). Our families know all three. Let us ask the Holy God to make us holy by righteousness.

Saint Paul asks the Corinthians to put something aside on the first day of every week for the poor in Jerusalem. Already then, Sunday was the day of the breaking of bread and the day of giving. And he gives us five words for the road: “Keep alert, stand firm in your faith, be courageous, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love” (1 Corinthians 16:13–14).

In the Gospel someone asks, “Lord, will only a few be saved?” Jesus does not give a number. He says: “Strive to enter through the narrow door” (Luke 13:24). It is not enough to have eaten and drunk near him; we must turn our lives to him.

But the door is open to all: people will come from east and west, from north and south, and sit at the table of the kingdom. The apostles carried this invitation to the whole world, and Mar Thoma brought it to us. As this season closes, let us enter the narrow door ourselves and hold it open for others. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says: try hard to go in through the narrow door. To go through a narrow door you must leave your big bags outside! Leave outside lies, selfishness and bad words.
And Jesus says people will come from every side of the world to sit at God's table. God wants everyone in his house. This week, help a friend to come closer to Jesus!

homily: Dear friends, today the whole Church celebrates Saint Peter and Saint Paul, the two great apostles. They were very different: a fisherman and a scholar, one who denied Jesus and one who persecuted his Church. Both were forgiven, both preached Christ, both died for him in Rome. Today is a day of obligation, and we gather with joy.

In the first reading the prophet Elisha raises a dead boy to life. In the second, Peter kneels, prays and says, “Tabitha, get up” (Acts 9:40), and gives her his hand. Peter learned that gesture from Jesus, who took his mother-in-law by the hand in his own house and lifted her up (Mark 1:31). The power of the apostles is the power of the risen Lord, given to lift up the poor and the fallen.

Paul does not boast of his success. He lists his sufferings: prisons, beatings, shipwrecks, hunger, cold, and his daily anxiety for all the Churches. “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness” (2 Corinthians 11:30). His glory is his wounds for Christ.

In the Gospel, by a charcoal fire, Jesus asks Peter three times, “Do you love me?” Three times Peter had denied him by another fire. Now three times he says, “Lord, you know that I love you.” And Jesus gives him the whole flock: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

This is the ministry that continues in the Pope, the successor of Peter: to feed, to strengthen the brethren, to keep the whole Church one. Our Syro-Malabar Church lives in full communion with him. Today let us pray for Pope Leo XIV, for our Major Archbishop and for all our bishops.

And let us hear the question that Jesus asks each of us: do you love me? Let us answer with Peter, “Lord, you know that I love you,” and let us show it by feeding his sheep and lifting up those who have fallen. Saint Peter and Saint Paul, pray for us. Amen.
kids: Children, today we celebrate Saint Peter and Saint Paul. Peter once said three times that he did not know Jesus. But Jesus forgave him and asked him three times, “Do you love me?”
Peter said, “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you!” Tonight, tell Jesus the same: “Jesus, I love you!” And pray for the Pope, who takes care of the whole Church.

homily: Dear friends, there are two ways to face tomorrow. One is the way of fear; the other is the way of trust. Today's readings show us both.

At Kadesh the people of Israel stood at the edge of the promised land. The land was good, but they were afraid, and they refused to go in, though the Lord had gone before them “in fire by night, and in the cloud by day” (Deuteronomy 1:33). Then, when God told them to wait, they rushed ahead without him and were defeated. Fear says, I will not go even with God. Presumption says, I will go even without God. Only Caleb followed the Lord with his whole heart.

Isaiah weeps over Jerusalem, a faithful city that has forgotten the orphan and the widow. But God's fire is the fire of a refiner: he burns away the dross to find the silver. When God allows trials in our lives, he is not destroying us; he is purifying us, so that we may again be called faithful.

Saint Paul tells the Corinthians, proud of their spiritual gifts: “Pursue love” (1 Corinthians 14:1). Every gift of the Spirit is for building up the Church. A trumpet that gives an unclear sound helps no one. Let our words and our gifts be clear and kind, for the good of others.

And Jesus says: do not worry. Look at the ravens; look at the lilies. Your Father knows what you need. “Do not be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). The kingdom is a gift. We do not have to grab it; we have only to receive it and share it.

This June, when schools reopen and fees fall due and the rains are heavy, many of us carry worries. Let us bring them to this altar. Let us strive first for the kingdom, give generously to the poor, and keep our treasure in heaven, for where our treasure is, there our heart will be also. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says: look at the birds. Nobody gives them a lunch box, but God feeds them. Look at the flowers. Nobody sews their clothes, but they are beautiful.
You are worth much more than birds and flowers! So when you feel worried about school or anything else, tell God your Father. He loves you and he will take care of you.

homily: Dear friends, today Saint Paul writes like a father. He says to the Corinthians: you have many guardians, but not many fathers; I became your father in Christ through the Gospel (1 Corinthians 4:15). Faith is not only taught; it is passed on by people who love us and whose lives we can copy.

This week children go back to school. Let us ask ourselves: who are the fathers and mothers in faith for our children? Not only priests and catechism teachers, but parents, grandparents and godparents. Children learn to pray by watching us pray.

Paul says: the kingdom of God depends not on talk but on power (1 Corinthians 4:20). It is easy to talk about God. The real sign of the kingdom is a life changed by the Holy Spirit: a temper calmed, a quarrel healed, a habit broken.

In the Gospel Jesus defends the little ones with strong words: it would be better to have a millstone around one's neck than to lead a little one into sin. Let us protect our children in every way. And let us be firm with ourselves: whatever leads us into sin, let us cut it off.

Today we remember Saint Justin. He searched for the truth among the philosophers, found it in Christ, and gave his life for him in Rome. He also told us how the first Christians celebrated the Eucharist on Sunday. When we say Amen at the Qurbana, we say it with Justin. May our faith, like his, be not only talk but power. Amen.
kids: Children, Saint Paul was like a father to the first Christians, because he told them about Jesus. Who told you about Jesus? Say thank you to them today!
Jesus loves children very much. If anyone ever makes you feel unsafe or asks you to do something wrong, tell your parents or a teacher you trust.

homily: Dear friends, today a whole town comes to Jesus because of one woman. She was not a priest or a scholar. She simply ran home and said: come and see a man who told me everything I have ever done. Many believed because of her word (John 4:39).
That is how faith spreads, in the time of the apostles and today: through ordinary people who tell what the Lord has done for them. Each of us has such a story. Let us not keep it hidden.

But the Samaritans went further. They asked Jesus to stay, and he stayed two days. Then they said to the woman: now we believe not because of what you said, but because we have heard for ourselves; this is truly the Saviour of the world (John 4:42). Our parents gave us the faith; but each of us must also meet Jesus personally, in prayer, in the Word and in the Holy Qurbana.

Saint Paul tells the Philippians: work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who is at work in you (Philippians 2:12–13). God gives the will and the strength; we must give our answer. Let us not be lazy with grace.

And he adds: do all things without murmuring, and you will shine like stars in the world. A Christian who complains about everything gives little light. Let us thank God instead, hold fast to his word, and shine where we live and work. Amen.
kids: Children, a woman met Jesus and ran to tell everyone in her town. Then the people met Jesus themselves and loved him too!
Your parents and teachers tell you about Jesus. Now talk to Jesus yourself every day, like a friend. And try not to grumble today: be a little star!

homily: Dear friends, the monsoon has come and the farmers are sowing. Jesus tells us about a sower who throws his seed everywhere, on the path, on the rock, among thorns and on good soil. God is that generous sower: he gives his word to everyone.

The seed is the word of God (Luke 8:11). Some hear it and the devil takes it away at once. Some receive it with joy, but have no root, and fall away when trouble comes. Some hear it, but the cares, riches and pleasures of life choke it. Which soil am I?

The good soil, Jesus says, is the heart that holds the word fast and bears fruit with patient endurance (Luke 8:15). Holding fast means remembering, praying over the word, living it. Patient endurance means not giving up when fruit is slow.

Saint Paul tells the Corinthians that their quarrels show they are still infants: one says, I belong to Paul, another, I belong to Apollos. Paul says: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. You are God's field. Let us never divide our parish into parties; we all belong to Christ.

Today the Latin Church remembers the Martyrs of Uganda, young men who received the Gospel only a few years before they died for it. The seed fell on good soil, and today their Church is full of life. May God's word find such soil in us. Amen.
kids: Children, a farmer threw seeds. Some fell on the path, some on rocks, some among thorns, and some on good soil, where they grew into a big harvest.
Jesus says his word is the seed, and your heart is the soil. Listen to Jesus and keep his word in your heart, and it will grow into kindness and goodness!

homily: Dear friends, on this First Friday the Church celebrates the Feast of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. In many of our homes the picture of the Sacred Heart hangs above the family altar, with a lamp before it. In the Bible the heart is the centre of the person. The Heart of Jesus means the whole love of Jesus for the Father and for us.

In the first reading Abram and Lot quarrel over land. Abram has the right to choose first, but he says: let there be no strife between us; we are kindred; you choose. Lot takes the best-looking land and goes toward Sodom. Abram gives up for peace, and God gives him the whole land. Here is a heart like the Heart of Jesus, who says: learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29).

Isaiah shows us the suffering Servant: he was wounded for our transgressions; by his bruises we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). The Heart of Jesus is a wounded heart. He does not love us from far away. He carries our sins and sorrows.

Saint Paul says: if you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved (Romans 10:9). Devotion to the Sacred Heart is faith with the heart and courage with the lips. Let us not be ashamed to show that we belong to Jesus.

In the Gospel a soldier pierces the side of Jesus, and blood and water come out (John 19:34). The Fathers saw in them Baptism and the Eucharist, and the Church born from the side of Christ. Eight days after Easter Jesus said to our father Thomas: put your hand in my side. And Thomas said: My Lord and my God!

Today let us look on the One whom we have pierced. Let us go to confession, receive him in the Qurbana, and renew the consecration of our families. And let us pray: Jesus, meek and humble of heart, make our hearts like yours. Amen.
kids: Children, when Jesus died, a soldier opened his side with a spear, and blood and water came out. It shows how much Jesus loves us: he gave us everything!
Look at the picture of the Sacred Heart at home. Say to Jesus: “Jesus, I love you. Make my heart gentle and kind like yours.”

homily: Dear friends, yesterday we looked at the Heart of Jesus; today we look at the Heart of his Mother. Simeon said to Mary: a sword will pierce your own soul too (Luke 2:35). The Heart of the Son and the heart of the Mother are joined in love and in suffering.

Her heart is called Immaculate because it was never stained by sin. God chose her before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in love (Ephesians 1:4), and preserved her from all sin from her conception, through the merits of Jesus, her Son and Saviour.

In the first reading God promises old Sarah a son, and Abraham laughs. But nothing is impossible with God. Sarah becomes the mother of a people; Mary becomes the Mother of all peoples, for Jesus gave her to us from the Cross: here is your mother.

Isaiah tells frightened King Ahaz: the Lord himself will give you a sign; the young woman shall bear a son, Immanuel. Saint Matthew sees it fulfilled in the Virgin Mary. Ahaz's heart was closed by fear; Mary's heart was open: here am I, the servant of the Lord (Luke 1:38).

In the Gospel Mary and Joseph search for the boy Jesus for three days in great anxiety. When they find him, they do not understand his words. But his mother treasured all these things in her heart (Luke 2:51). Mary did not understand everything, but she kept God's word and waited.

Parents, when you are worried about your children, bring them to Mary's heart. All of us, when God's ways are hard, let us keep his word as she did. And let us pray the rosary each day for peace, as she asked. Immaculate Heart of Mary, pray for us. Amen.
kids: Children, Mary and Joseph lost Jesus for three days, and they were very worried. When they found him, Mary kept everything in her heart.
Mary is our Mother too. When you are worried or sad, tell her: “Mother Mary, keep me in your heart.” And pray a Hail Mary for peace in the world!

homily: Dear friends, today's Gospel tells of a woman who was sick for twelve years. She had gone to many doctors and spent everything she had, and she only grew worse. Because of her illness she was also kept away from others. She was the kind of person a crowd walks past.

But she had heard about Jesus. And she said to herself: “If I but touch his clothes, I will be made well” (Mark 5:28). She reached out from behind and touched his cloak, and immediately she was healed.

Then Jesus stopped. “Who touched my clothes?” The disciples said: everyone is touching you! But there is a difference between pressing around Jesus and touching him with faith. Many were near him; one person reached for him. Every Sunday many of us come close to the altar. Do we press around him like a crowd, or do we reach out to him in faith?

The woman came trembling and told him the whole truth. And Jesus said: “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.” She came as a nameless sick woman; she went home as a daughter. Jesus heals not only the body but our place in God's family.

Saint Paul calls God “the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation”, who consoles us so that we may console others (2 Corinthians 1:3–4). The comfort God gives us is not meant to stop with us. In these days of rain and new school years, let us look for the person no one notices, and let us pass on the consolation we have received. Amen.
kids: Children, a sick lady was so sure of Jesus' power that she thought: if I just touch his clothes, I will be well. And she was! Jesus stopped and looked for her, because he wanted to be her friend, not only her doctor. Jesus sees you too, even in a big crowd or a big new classroom. And you can help him by being kind to the child nobody notices.

homily: Dear friends, today we celebrate St Mariam Thresia, a daughter of our own Church, born in 1876 at Puthenchira near Thrissur. She longed for a hidden life of prayer, but God sent her into the homes of her neighbours. She died on 8 June 1926, and in 2019 Pope Francis declared her a saint.

The first reading tells us how God called Abraham: “Go from your country… to the land that I will show you” (Genesis 12:1). Abraham did not know the way; he only trusted. Mariam Thresia also stepped onto a new road. With her companions she went from house to house to care for the sick, to pray with the dying, to make peace in quarrelling families and to teach children their prayers.

Sirach says, “when you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing” (Sirach 2:1). She was tested by spiritual darkness, by attacks of the evil one, and by being misunderstood. She remained humble and obedient to her bishop and her spiritual director. Gold is tested in the fire, and she came out as gold.

The secret of her life is in Paul's words: “it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Her service was not mere activity. It came from long hours at the feet of the Lord, like Mary of Bethany, and so she could serve like Martha without losing her peace.

In the Gospel Jesus says: “just as you did it to one of the least of these… you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40). She saw Jesus in the poorest families, and in 1914 she founded the Congregation of the Holy Family to serve families, so that every home might become a Nazareth.

Today let us ask her to bless our homes. Let us pray together as families, make peace where there is a quarrel, and visit one family that is carrying a burden alone. St Mariam Thresia, pray for us and for all the families of our land. Amen.
kids: Children, St Mariam Thresia grew up in Kerala, just like many of you. She loved Jesus so much that she went to help sick people and poor families in her village. She said that when we help someone in need, we are helping Jesus himself.
This week, help someone at home without being asked: your mother in the kitchen, your grandfather with his medicines, or a younger child with homework. You will be doing it for Jesus!

homily: Dear friends, today we celebrate Mar Aprem, St Ephrem the Syrian. He was born around the year 306 in Nisibis, served as a deacon and a teacher, and spent his last years in Edessa. He died in 373, and the Church declared him a Doctor of the Church. The Syriac tradition calls him “the Harp of the Spirit”.

Ephrem taught the faith in a special way: he sang it. He wrote hundreds of hymns, set them to tunes the people knew, and trained choirs to sing them. In this way ordinary people learned the truth about Jesus, about Mary and about the sacraments, not only in their heads but in their hearts.

Saint Paul tells us where such praise comes from: “God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). When the Spirit fills a heart, it begins to sing. Ephrem's heart became a harp, and the Spirit played on it.

Sirach praises Moses, to whom God spoke face to face, who received “the law of life and knowledge” in order to teach the people (Sirach 45:5). Ephrem too entered the mystery of God in prayer and came back to teach. He did not try to explain God away; he stood before God with wonder and love.

In the Gospel Jesus says: “You are the salt of the earth… You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:13–14). Ephrem's light shone not only in his hymns but in his service. At the end of his life, during a famine, he cared for the hungry and the sick.

Our Church has received the Syriac liturgy that Ephrem helped to shape. Let us love it, pray it with understanding, and teach it to our children. Let us sing our faith, and let our good works give glory to our Father in heaven. Mar Aprem, pray for us. Amen.
kids: Children, Mar Aprem loved Jesus so much that he wrote songs about him, hundreds of songs! He taught people to sing them in church, so that they could learn about God by singing.
When you sing in church, sing with your whole heart, because singing is praying twice. And like Mar Aprem, help someone who is hungry or sad. Then your light will shine for Jesus!

homily: Dear friends, today Jesus goes to the region of Tyre, outside Israel. He wants to stay hidden, but a mother finds him. She is a Gentile, a foreigner, and her little daughter is tormented by an evil spirit. She falls at his feet and begs for help.

Jesus answers with words that sound hard: the children must be fed first; it is not fair to give the children's bread to the dogs. He is testing her, and he is speaking of God's plan, which began with Israel. But notice the word “first”: after the children, someone else will be fed.

The woman does not give up. She says: “Sir, even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs” (Mark 7:28). She does not claim that she deserves the bread. She only trusts that there is so much bread at the Lord's table that a crumb will be enough. Jesus rejoices in her faith, and her daughter is healed.

Saint Paul tells the Corinthians that “knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1). The clever Corinthians were proud of what they knew. The foreign mother knew little, but she trusted much and loved much. And Paul reminds us of our faith: there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ.

We too were once outside the table. Through the apostles, the Gospel reached our land. Now at every Holy Qurbana we receive not crumbs but the Bread of life itself. Let us pray with this mother's persistence for the children we love, and let us use what we know of the faith to build others up. Amen.
kids: Children, a mother came to Jesus because her little girl was sick. Jesus tested her, but she did not give up! She said that even a crumb from his table would be enough. Jesus was so happy with her faith that he healed her daughter. When you pray, do not give up. Keep asking Jesus with trust, because he loves you very much.

homily: Dear friends, today we celebrate St Barnabas. His name was Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, but the apostles called him Barnabas, “son of encouragement” (Acts 4:36). He sold his field and gave the money to the apostles for the poor. Wherever he went, people were encouraged.

When Saul was converted, the Christians in Jerusalem were afraid of him. But Barnabas took him by the hand, brought him to the apostles and spoke for him (Acts 9:27). Without Barnabas, the Church might have kept Saul, the future Saint Paul, at a distance.

In today's reading the Church sends Barnabas to Antioch, where many Gentiles have believed. He does not come to find faults. “When he came and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced” (Acts 11:23). Scripture says, “he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.” Then he goes to look for Saul, and they teach together for a year. In Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.

While the church at Antioch was praying and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul” (Acts 13:2). The mission of the Church is born at prayer. The apostles in Jerusalem gave them the right hand of fellowship, and asked only that they remember the poor (Galatians 2:9–10).

Barnabas also gave a second chance to young Mark, who had once left the mission. Paul later wrote that Mark was useful in his ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). Jesus warns that his apostles go out like sheep among wolves, but the Spirit of the Father speaks through them (Matthew 10:16–20). Tradition says Barnabas died a martyr in Cyprus.

Every family and every parish needs a Barnabas. Let us look for God's grace in others and rejoice in it; let us welcome the newcomer and the one others fear; let us give a second chance; and let us remember the poor. St Barnabas, pray for us. Amen.
kids: Children, Barnabas was called the son of encouragement because he always made people feel brave and loved. When everyone was afraid of Saul, Barnabas became his friend.
This week, be a Barnabas! Sit with the child who is alone, say something kind to someone who is sad, and help a friend who made a mistake to try again.

homily: Dear friends, today a man with leprosy comes to Jesus. In those days such a person had to live alone, outside the town, and cry out “Unclean, unclean” so that no one would come near. Yet this man comes near. He kneels and says: “If you choose, you can make me clean” (Mark 1:40).

Mark tells us that Jesus was “moved with pity”. His heart was touched deep inside. And then he does something nobody expected: he stretches out his hand and touches the man. Perhaps no one had touched him for years. Before the healing comes the touch.

Jesus says: “I do choose. Be made clean!” And immediately he is clean. The man's prayer was “if you choose”; the answer of Jesus is “I do choose”. Jesus wants to heal us. Whatever makes us feel unclean or ashamed, he is willing to touch it and make it clean, especially in the sacrament of Reconciliation.

The healed man cannot keep quiet; he tells everyone. Now he can go into the town, and Jesus has to stay outside. Jesus takes the place of the outcast so that the outcast can come home. That is what he did for all of us on the Cross.

Saint Paul says that the apostles are “the aroma of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:15): wherever they go, they spread the fragrance of knowing him. Let us ask Jesus for his pity and his courage, to touch those whom others avoid, and to carry the fragrance of Christ into our homes and our town. Amen.
kids: Children, a man who was very sick with leprosy had no friends, because everyone was afraid to touch him. But Jesus touched him and healed him! Jesus is never afraid of us, even when we have done wrong. And Saint Paul says we can be like a sweet perfume of Jesus. When you are kind, people can smell Jesus' love!

homily: Dear friends, Saint Paul tells the Corinthians something surprising: “we were so utterly, unbearably crushed that we despaired of life itself” (2 Corinthians 1:8). The great apostle had a breaking point. If you feel today that you cannot go on, you are in good company.

Paul tells us why God allowed it: “so that we would rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:9). When our strength runs out, God's strength begins. The God who raised Jesus from the tomb can raise us from what crushes us.

And Paul asks for help: “join in helping us by your prayers.” Prayer for one another is real help. When we pray for the sick, the anxious, the poor, we carry them. And when God answers, we all give thanks together.

In the Gospel, Jesus tells his disciples that they will run away and leave him alone. “Yet I am not alone because the Father is with me.” Then he says: “In the world you face persecution. But take courage; I have conquered the world!” (John 16:32–33). He said this the night before he died. The victory was certain even before the battle.

So let us not carry our burdens alone. Let us bring them to the Lord who has conquered the world, and let us carry one another in prayer. Then many will give thanks for the blessings granted through the prayers of many. Amen.
kids: Children, sometimes even big people feel that their problems are too heavy. Saint Paul felt like that. But he trusted God, and his friends prayed for him. When you are sad or scared, tell Jesus, and ask your family to pray with you. And when a friend is sad, pray for them! Jesus says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world!”

homily: Dear friends, John the Baptist was in prison. He had prepared the way for Jesus, and now he sent a question: “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?” (Matthew 11:3). Even a great prophet can have a dark night. If you have ever asked God, are you really there?, you are not alone.

Jesus did not scold John. He sent him an answer from the Scriptures: “the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news brought to them” (Matthew 11:5). Look at what God is doing, he says. These are the signs of the kingdom.

Then Jesus adds: “blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.” Many people stumble over Jesus: he is too humble, too merciful, he goes to the Cross. Blessed are we if we keep following him even when he does not act as we expected.

Saint Paul warns the Colossians against a religion of rules without Christ: do not touch, do not taste, do not handle. These rules look wise, but they do not change the heart. Fasting and discipline are good, but only when they come from love of Christ, not from pride or from fear of unseen powers. We have died and risen with Christ; we belong to him.

So let us keep our eyes on Jesus himself. Let us look for the signs of his kingdom, especially where the poor are loved, and let us become such signs for others. Blessed are we if we do not stumble over him. Amen.
kids: Children, John the Baptist was in prison and he was sad. He asked Jesus, “Are you really the one?” Jesus said, “Look: blind people see, sick people are healed, poor people hear good news!” When you help someone in Jesus' name, people can see that Jesus is real. Be a sign of Jesus this week!

homily: Dear friends, Saint Paul tells the whole story of humanity in two men. Through Adam, sin and death came into the world. Through Jesus Christ, grace and life came. We all share Adam's wound; we can all share Christ's healing.

And the two are not equal. Paul says again and again, “much more.” Grace is much stronger than sin. “Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20). There is no sin so great that the grace of Christ cannot overcome it.

In the Gospel Jesus tells a story about a vineyard. The owner sends servant after servant to collect the fruit, and the tenants beat them and kill them. At last he sends his beloved son, and they kill him too. Jesus is speaking about himself, the beloved Son of the Father, who will soon be put to death.

But God does not let the story end there. “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Mark 12:10). The worst thing human beings ever did, killing the Son of God, became the foundation of our salvation. That is what grace does: it turns even death into life.

Today we are the tenants of God's vineyard: our family, our parish, our own life. The Owner is looking for fruit. Let us give him the fruit of prayer, forgiveness and charity, and if we have sinned, let us run to his grace, which is always greater. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus told a story about a man who sent his own dear son to his vineyard, and bad workers killed him. Jesus was talking about himself. But God made something wonderful out of it: Jesus rose again and saved us! God can bring good even out of bad things. And God's love is always bigger than our sins.

homily: Dear friends, Saint Peter tells us something astonishing: God has called us to “become participants of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4). Not just to be forgiven, not just to be good people, but to share the very life of God. That is our dignity as baptised Christians.

God has given us everything we need. But Peter says we must also “make every effort.” He gives us a ladder: faith, then goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, mutual affection, and at the top, love (2 Peter 1:5–7). We cannot skip the rungs in the middle.

In the Gospel, many disciples find Jesus' teaching about eating his flesh and drinking his blood too hard: “This teaching is difficult; who can accept it?” Jesus does not change his words. He says: “It is the spirit that gives life… The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:63). Only the Holy Spirit can open our hearts to this mystery.

Many turned away that day. But Peter said: “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.” When something in our faith is hard, let us not walk away. Let us stay with Jesus and ask the Spirit for light.

Every time we receive the Holy Qurbana, we receive the Body and Blood of the Son of God, and we share more deeply in God's own life. So let us climb Peter's ladder, rung by rung, from faith to love. Amen.
kids: Children, Saint Peter gives us a ladder. The first step is faith. Then come being good, learning about God, controlling ourselves, being patient, praying, loving our family, and at the very top, loving everyone! This week, try to climb one step higher. And remember: in Holy Communion Jesus gives himself to help you climb.

homily: Dear friends, Saint Peter wrote to Christians who were misunderstood and mistreated. He told them: “even if you do suffer for doing what is right, you are blessed. Do not fear what they fear… but in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord” (1 Peter 3:14–15). When Christ is Lord in our hearts, fear loses its power.

Peter adds: “Always be ready to make your defense to anyone who demands from you an accounting for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and reverence.” Many people around us, friends of other faiths, colleagues, even our own children, may ask us why we believe. Let us know our faith, and let us answer with gentleness and respect, never with pride or anger.

Today is Friday. Peter reminds us that “Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, in order to bring you to God” (1 Peter 3:18). The innocent One suffered for the guilty. When we suffer unjustly and do not return evil, we walk with him.

In the Gospel, an enemy sows weeds among the wheat. The servants want to pull them out at once, but the master says: wait until the harvest, or you will pull up the wheat too. God is patient. He gives everyone time to change. The Church is a field where good and bad grow together, and the weeds grow in our own hearts too.

So let us not despair when we see evil, and let us never use violence or contempt in the name of God. Let us pray for those we find hard to love, let us pull out the weeds in our own hearts, and let us trust the Lord of the harvest, who promises that “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43). Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus tells a story about a farmer. An enemy planted weeds among his wheat. The farmer did not pull them out at once, because he did not want to hurt the good wheat. God is patient like that farmer. He gives everyone time to become good. So be patient with others, and be kind, even to people who are not kind to you!

homily: Dear friends, Saint Paul asks a question today: is the law sin? And he answers, “By no means!” (Romans 7:7). God's commandments are holy and just and good. The problem is not the commandment; the problem is the heart.

Paul gives an example: “You shall not covet.” This is the only commandment about the heart. As soon as we hear it, we notice how much we want what others have: their phone, their house, their success, their life. Sin is like a parasite. It takes the good commandment and twists it against us.

That is why we need more than a law. We need the Holy Spirit. At Pentecost the Spirit came to write the law of love on our hearts. Saint Augustine said: the law was given so that we might look for grace; grace was given so that the law might be kept.

In the Gospel Jesus sits opposite the treasury of the Temple and watches. The rich put in large sums. A poor widow puts in two small coins. And Jesus says that she has given more than all of them, because she gave “everything she had, all she had to live on” (Mark 12:44).

The covetous heart grasps; the widow's heart lets go. She is a picture of Jesus himself, who a few days later gave his whole life on the Cross, and who gives himself to us today in the Holy Qurbana. Let us bring him not what is left over, but our whole life. Amen.
kids: Children, a poor lady put two tiny coins in the offering box at the Temple. Jesus said she gave more than all the rich people, because she gave everything she had, with love. God does not count how much we give; he looks at how much we love. What can you give to Jesus today with a big heart?

homily: Dear friends, at the end of a long and difficult argument, Saint Paul stops and sings: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33).

Paul has been thinking about his own people and about the Gentiles, and he sees that all are saved by the mercy of God. He does not understand everything, but he trusts. When we do not understand what God is doing in our lives, let us pray his words and trust.

In the Gospel Jesus says: “the tree is known by its fruit.” A good tree gives good fruit. Our words are fruit; our heart is the root. “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34).

Jesus warns us that we will give an account for every careless word. Think of gossip, cruel jokes, angry messages and rumours forwarded without checking. Words can destroy a person. But the answer is not only to keep quiet; it is to fill our hearts with God's word and love, so that good words overflow.

Today we remember St Aloysius Gonzaga, a young man who gave up riches to serve God and died at twenty-three caring for the sick. His heart was good, and his life bore good fruit. Let us ask him to pray for our young people, and for all of us, that our hearts may be good trees. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says a good tree gives good fruit. Your words are like fruit: if your heart is full of love, kind words will come out. Today, say three kind words to someone in your family, and ask St Aloysius to help you be good at school!

homily: Dear friends, Saint Paul was a tentmaker, and he tells us that our body is like a tent: good, but not permanent. “For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1).
God has already given us the Holy Spirit as a guarantee, like an advance payment, that we will have that eternal house. So we are confident, and we walk by faith, not by sight.
Jesus says that no one lights a lamp to hide it under a basket. Our faith is a lamp. It is meant to be seen, in our homes, at our work, in our words and choices.

Today we remember two men who did not hide their lamp: St John Fisher, a bishop, and St Thomas More, a husband, father and lawyer. When King Henry VIII demanded an oath against their conscience and against the unity of the Church, they refused. Both were beheaded in 1535. Thomas More said he died the king's good servant, but God's first.

Saint Peter says: if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but glorify God because you bear this name. May we love our country and serve it well, but put God first. And when our earthly tent is folded, may we find the house that God has prepared for us. Amen.
kids: Children, would you hide a lamp under your bed? No! Jesus says our faith is like a lamp. Today we remember St Thomas More, a father who loved to laugh, and St John Fisher, a bishop. They chose God first, even when the king was angry. Let your light shine today by being honest and kind!

homily: Dear friends, Saint Paul had changed his travel plans, and some people in Corinth said he could not be trusted. He answers: “this is our boast, the testimony of our conscience: we have behaved in the world with frankness and godly sincerity… by the grace of God” (2 Corinthians 1:12).
Paul has nothing to hide. His words mean what they say. That is a lesson for all of us, priests and people: let our yes be yes, in our accounts, our studies, our promises and our marriages.

In the Gospel Jesus tells of a woman who loses one of her ten silver coins. She lights a lamp, sweeps the house and searches carefully until she finds it. Then she calls her friends: “Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.”

God is like that woman. He searches for us, even when we are lost inside his own house, in the dark corners of the parish or the family. The coin bears the image of the king; we bear the image of God, and he does not rest until it shines again.

Tomorrow we celebrate the birth of John the Baptist, who called people to repentance. Let us light a lamp in our hearts, examine our conscience and go to confession, so that heaven may rejoice over us. And let us go and search for someone who is lost. Amen.
kids: Children, a woman lost a silver coin. She lit a lamp and swept the whole house until she found it, and then she had a party with her friends! Jesus says that God looks for each of us like that, because we are precious to him. Is there a child at school who feels alone? Be kind to them today!

homily: Dear friends, today the Church celebrates a birthday. Of most saints we celebrate the day of their death, but of John the Baptist we celebrate his birth, because his birth was already part of the Good News. The angel had said, “many will rejoice at his birth.”

Elizabeth, old and once barren, gives birth to a son, and her neighbours and relatives rejoice with her. On the eighth day the family want to call him Zechariah. But Elizabeth says, “No; he is to be called John,” and Zechariah writes, “His name is John” (Luke 1:63). This child belongs to God's plan. And when Zechariah obeys, his mouth is opened and he praises God.

God said to Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5). That is true of John, and it is true of every child. Every life in the womb is known and loved by God. Let us protect and welcome every child.

The first reading shows the prophet Nathan telling King David, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). A prophet tells the truth even to kings. John did the same with Herod, and it cost him his life. When our conscience says, ‘You are the man’, let us not argue; let us repent as David did.

Saint Paul says that when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, so that we might become children of God (Galatians 4:4–5). John stands at that door. He is the last of the prophets and points to Jesus: “Here is the Lamb of God.”

John's great word is, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). Parents, teachers, priests, every one of us: let us point to Jesus and step aside, so that he may grow in the hearts of others. What then will this child become? With the hand of the Lord upon us, we too can become voices that prepare his way. Amen.
kids: Children, today is John the Baptist's birthday! His old father Zechariah could not speak, but when he wrote, “His name is John,” he could talk again and he praised God.
God knew John before he was born, and God knew you before you were born too. Do you know what your name means? Ask your parents today, and thank God for calling you by name!

homily: Dear friends, today some clever men try to trap Jesus. They ask him: should we pay taxes to the emperor or not? Whatever he answers, they think, he will be in trouble.
Jesus asks for a coin. Whose picture is on it? The emperor's. “Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21).

The coin carries the emperor's image, so it goes back to him. But what carries God's image? You do. Every person is made in the image of God. So the coin may go to the government, but you yourself belong to God.

Saint Paul says that all authority comes from God, and that rulers are God's servants for our good (Romans 13:1, 4). So we pay our taxes, we keep the law, we vote with a good conscience, and we pray for those who govern. A Christian does not take or give bribes, even small ones.

But if any power commands what God forbids, we say with Peter and the apostles, “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (Acts 5:29). This week let us be honest citizens, and let us give back to God the only thing he asks for: our whole heart. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus looked at a coin with the king's picture on it and said: give the king what has his picture. Then he meant something wonderful: God's picture is on you! You belong to God. So be honest, obey good rules, and give your whole heart to God!

homily: Dear friends, Saint Paul writes to the Corinthians with the love of a father who has arranged his daughter's marriage: “I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). The Church is the bride of Christ, and each of us belongs to that bride.

Paul is afraid. Clever preachers have come with fine words and a different Jesus: a Jesus without the Cross, a gospel of success. The Corinthians accepted them easily. We too hear many voices today, on our phones and in new groups. Let us test every voice by the faith of the apostles that the Church has kept.

In the Gospel, people are surprised: how can Jesus teach so well when he has not studied? Jesus says: “My teaching is not mine but his who sent me” (John 7:16). A true teacher does not seek his own glory but God's.
Then he says: “Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment” (John 7:24). We often judge by appearance: by colour, caste, dress, money, or a photograph. But God looks at the heart.

On this Saturday let us look to Mary, the humble Virgin of Nazareth, wholly devoted to Christ. May she keep our love for her Son sincere and pure, and give us eyes that see others as God sees them. Amen.
kids: Children, some people did not believe Jesus because he had not gone to a famous school. They looked only at the outside. Jesus said: do not judge by appearances! God looks at the heart. This week, be kind to someone others laugh at because of how they look.

homily: Dear friends, today we remember Saint Irenaeus, a bishop of the second century. As a boy he listened to Polycarp, who had known the apostle John, who had known Jesus. Think of it: only a few links between Irenaeus and the Lord.

False teachers in his time said that they had secret knowledge that ordinary Christians did not have. Irenaeus answered: the apostles hid nothing. Their teaching is public, kept in the Churches they founded and handed on by the bishops who came after them. Paul says the same to Timothy: “continue in what you have learned and firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it” (2 Timothy 3:14).

The readings for his feast describe a true priest. Aaron carried the names of the tribes on his heart before God. Malachi says, “the lips of a priest should guard knowledge” (Malachi 2:7). And Jesus promises the Holy Spirit, who “will teach you everything, and remind you of all that I have said to you” (John 14:26).

Irenaeus was also a peacemaker; his name means peaceful. When a quarrel about the date of Easter threatened to divide the Church, he begged for patience. In the weekday reading Paul too asks for mercy: forgive and console the one who did wrong, reaffirm your love for him, so that Satan may not outwit you (2 Corinthians 2:7–11).

Irenaeus wrote: the glory of God is the human being fully alive. Tomorrow we celebrate Peter and Paul, the apostles whose Church in Rome Irenaeus honoured. Today let us thank God for those who handed on the faith to us, let us forgive, and let us continue in what we have learned. Amen.
kids: Children, Saint Irenaeus heard about Jesus from an old bishop who had known Saint John, Jesus' friend. The faith came to him like a chain, from hand to hand. Today, say thank you to the person who taught you to pray. And be a peacemaker, like Irenaeus!

homily: Dear friends, some of the first Christians thought that to follow Christ they had to change everything outside: their marriage, their customs, their work. Saint Paul says: “let each of you lead the life that the Lord has assigned, to which God called you” (1 Corinthians 7:17). Holiness is not somewhere else. It is where you are, if you remain there with God.

Paul also says: “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human masters” (1 Corinthians 7:23). Christ has paid for us with his Blood. So we must not sell ourselves to the opinion of others, to a habit, or to money.

In the Gospel Jesus says: “Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). Character is built in small things: the change returned, the honest exam, the hour of work truly worked.
And he says clearly: “You cannot serve God and wealth” (Luke 16:13). Money is a good servant but a bad master. Jesus tells us to use it to make friends with the poor, who will welcome us into heaven.

Today the Latin calendar remembers the first martyrs of Rome, ordinary believers who died in the same persecution as Peter and Paul. They served one Master only. As the Season of the Apostles comes to its end, let us ask ourselves whom we serve, and choose God. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says: if you are honest in small things, you will be honest in big things. Return the extra change, tell the truth, share your things. And remember: money is a helper, not a boss. Only God is our boss, and he loves us very much!

intro: Theme: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.”
On the Fourth Sunday of the Apostles: impartial justice, worship with clean hands, the discipline of the race, and mercy like the Father's.

points.h: Hear out the small and the great alike
sub: The citizen and the resident alien.
q: You must not be partial in judging: hear out the small and the great alike; you shall not be intimidated by anyone, for the judgment is God’s.
My brothers and sisters, do you with your acts of favoritism really believe in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ?
points.apply: Give the same fair hearing to everyone you deal with this week, and pay every worker fully and on time.

points.h: Wash yourselves; learn to do good
q: learn to do good; seek justice, rescue the oppressed, defend the orphan, plead for the widow.
leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.
points.apply: Before next Sunday's Qurbana, make peace with one person or make a good confession.

sub: The Way of Thomas in India.
q: but those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength, they shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint.
Do you not know that in a race the runners all compete, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may win it.
points.apply: Keep one spiritual discipline this week as faithfully as an athlete keeps training.

points.h: Merciful as your Father is merciful
q: The Lord passed before him, and proclaimed, “The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness,
Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.
points.apply: Pray by name each day this week for someone who has hurt you.

concl: The disciple of Jesus is just in judgment, clean of hands, disciplined in spirit and merciful as the Father.
Mercy can turn an enemy into a brother, as it did for Blessed Rani Maria's family.
2027-06-06.resolve: This week, judge fairly, wash your hands of injustice, keep one discipline, and bless someone who has hurt you.

intro: Theme: “No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all perish as they did.”
On the Sixth Sunday of the Apostles: the God who is near, the nations streaming to his mountain, a life lived for his glory, and the urgent, patient call to repentance.

sub: The commandments: so that you may live.
Make them known to your children.
q: For what other great nation has a god so near to it as the Lord our God is whenever we call to him?
And the Word became flesh and lived among us,
points.apply: Read one Gospel passage with your children or grandchildren this week.

points.h: All the nations shall stream to it
sub: The mountain of the Lord's house.
The word goes out from Jerusalem with the apostles.
q: they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
points.apply: Make peace this week with one person, or help two others to be reconciled.

points.h: Do everything for the glory of God
q: The earth is the Lord’s and all that is in it, the world, and those who live in it;
So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.
points.apply: Pray before every meal this week, and offer your daily work to God each morning.

sub: Suffering is not a verdict on the sufferer.
A call to my own conversion.
The gardener who asks for one more year.
q: For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, says the Lord God. Turn, then, and live.
He replied, ‘Sir, let it alone for one more year, until I dig around it and put manure on it.
points.apply: Make a good confession before the feast of Sts Peter and Paul.

concl: God is near; his word goes out to the nations and makes peace; every act of our day can give him glory.
Do not judge those who suffer; turn back to God yourself, for the gardener has asked for one more year.
2027-06-20.resolve: This week, hand on the faith to a child, make one peace, pray before every meal, and go to confession before 29 June.

intro: Theme: “Strive to enter through the narrow door; for many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able.”

On the last Sunday of the Season of the Apostles: the voice from the fire, the woes of the vineyard, the apostolic love that gives on the first day of the week, and the narrow door that opens on the feast of all nations.

sub: A God who speaks, not a statue.
q: Then the Lord spoke to you out of the fire. You heard the sound of words but saw no form; there was only a voice.
No one has ever seen God. It is God the only Son, who is close to the Father’s heart, who has made him known.
points.apply: Spend ten minutes this week with your children on what they are learning in the faith.

sub: Strong drink from morning to night.
q: Ah, you who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter!
And he said to them, “Take care! Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.”
points.apply: Name one woe that has a hold in your home and take one step against it.

points.h: Let all that you do be done in love
sub: The first day of the week.
A wide door and many adversaries.
q: Since there will never cease to be some in need on the earth, I therefore command you, “Open your hand to the poor and needy neighbor in your land.”
Let all that you do be done in love.
points.apply: Set aside a fixed amount every Sunday for the poor or the missions.

points.h: Strive to enter through the narrow door
sub: Not how many, but will I?
From east and west to the table.
q: This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it.
Then people will come from east and west, from north and south, and will eat in the kingdom of God.
points.apply: Choose one concrete effort of conversion this week.

concl: The Season of the Apostles closes with the voice of God, the call to justice, the love that gives and the door of the kingdom.
Let us enter the narrow door ourselves and hold it open for all peoples.
2027-06-27.resolve: This week, teach the faith at home, refuse one woe, set aside a Sunday gift for the poor, and make one real effort of conversion.

intro: Theme: “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.”

On the feast of St Peter and St Paul: the love that heals denial and receives the flock, the hand that lifts up the dead, the weakness that boasts only of Christ, and the rock on which the Church is built.

points.h: Do you love me? Feed my sheep
q: I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will make them lie down, says the Lord God.

He said to him the third time, “Simon son of John, do you love me?” Peter felt hurt because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” And he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.
points.apply: Answer Jesus tonight in your own words, and ask him whom you are to feed.

q: So he went in and closed the door on the two of them, and prayed to the Lord.
Peter put all of them outside, and then he knelt down and prayed. He turned to the body and said, “Tabitha, get up.” Then she opened her eyes, and seeing Peter, she sat up.
points.apply: Give your hand this week to someone who is down.

points.h: I will boast of my weakness
sub: Daily anxiety for all the Churches.
q: If I say, “I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name,” then within me there is something like a burning fire shut up in my bones; I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot.
If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
points.apply: Offer one weakness or suffering to God this week for the Church.

sub: Communion with the successor of Peter.
q: I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David; he shall open, and no one shall shut; he shall shut, and no one shall open.
And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
points.apply: Pray every day this week for Pope Leo, our Major Archbishop and your bishop by name.

concl: Peter and Paul, the fisherman and the scholar, forgiven and sent, are the two pillars of the Church.
Let us answer the Lord's question with love, lift up the fallen, carry the Churches in our hearts and remain one with the successor of Peter.
2027-06-29.resolve: This week, tell Jesus you love him, lift someone up, offer your weakness for the Church, and pray daily for the Pope and our bishops.

intro: Theme: “Do not be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.”
On the Fifth Sunday of the Apostles: a people who would not trust at Kadesh, a city refined by fire, gifts given to build up the Church, and the little flock that need not fear.

points.h: The God who goes before you
sub: Caleb's whole heart and the little ones who enter.
q: The Lord said to me, “Say to them, ‘Do not go up and do not fight, for I am not in the midst of you; otherwise you will be defeated by your enemies.’”
So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.
points.apply: Take the first step this week in one thing God has been asking of you, and ask his guidance before every big decision.

sub: Injustice to the weak is unfaithfulness to God.
God burns away the false to recover the true.
q: I will turn my hand against you; I will smelt away your dross as with lye and remove all your alloy. And I will restore your judges as at the first, and your counselors as at the beginning.
so that the genuineness of your faith… being more precious than gold that, though perishable, is tested by fire… may be found to result in praise and glory and honor when Jesus Christ is revealed.
points.apply: Do one concrete thing this week for a widow, an orphan or an elderly person living alone.

points.h: Pursue love, build up the Church
sub: A bugle with a clear sound.
Love as the measure of every gift.
q: Then afterward I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy,
So with yourselves; since you are eager for spiritual gifts, strive to excel in them for building up the church.
